Staff give first aid, CPR or the Heimlich maneuver only within their training, and follow the dispatcher's instructions. Staff keep the other clients safe and supervised throughout.
Staff do not move a seriously injured client unless there is immediate danger. Staff do not give medications that are not ordered for the client.

A staff member collects the emergency packet and gives it to the emergency medical personnel. Staff accompany the client to the hospital when staffing allows. If not, a staff member follows as soon as coverage is arranged.

As soon as the client is safe, staff call the guardian or legally responsible person, then the QP, the nurse consultant and the LME/MCO care coordinator. Staff record each call, with date, time and who was told.
Staff complete an incident report within the deadlines in GOV-06 if the event meets the reporting criteria. The Administrator makes any required reports to the LME/MCO and IRIS.
Staff write a progress note describing what happened, what care was given, who was notified, and the client's condition on transfer. The note goes in the record.

After a hospital visit, staff obtain discharge instructions and new medication orders, update the medication list and plan of care, and follow MED-02 for new orders. The QP updates the individual plan if needs have changed.
Within [NUMBER] days of any medical emergency, the Administrator and QP review the response, note any problems, and report findings to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05).
The Administrator reviews this plan at least annually and after any emergency that reveals a gap, and provides the updated plan to all staff.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures trained coverage on every shift, supplies are stocked, and this plan is reviewed.
Keeps records, consents and emergency contacts current, makes notifications, and updates plans after an emergency.
Advises on health needs, receives notifications, and reviews medical responses.
Respond to emergencies, call 911, give first aid within training, send the emergency packet with the client and document.
Know where emergency packets, first aid supplies and posted numbers are.

documentation: First aid/CPR/Heimlich certificates and coverage roster
Signed emergency-care consent in each record
Current face sheet, medication list and emergency contacts
First aid supply checks
Progress notes and notification log for each emergency
Incident reports where required
Post-emergency review notes and QA/QI minutes

policies.title: Use of Volunteers
policies.applies_to: Governing Body, Administrator, QP and any person who volunteers or offers to volunteer
policies.purpose: To state whether [AGENCY NAME] uses volunteers and, if volunteers are ever used, to protect clients through screening, training, supervision and confidentiality.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0201, Worksheet p.3, Item 9: whether volunteers are used, the services they provide, training, supervisor, and how client confidentiality is ensured.

Whether volunteers are used. [AGENCY NAME] does not use volunteers at this time. No volunteer provides direct care, supervises clients, transports clients, handles medication or manages client funds. Volunteers never count toward staffing minimums.

If the governing body later approves volunteers. Volunteers may only be used after the governing body approves and the Administrator documents the plan. Their services are limited to [SERVICES, e.g., helping with holiday events or community outings alongside paid staff]. Before any contact with clients, each volunteer gets a background check as for staff, signs a confidentiality agreement, and completes orientation on client rights and confidentiality. Any volunteer in direct client care is also trained in approved de-escalation techniques as described in TRN-01. Each volunteer reports to a named supervisor, a paid staff member designated in writing by the Administrator. A volunteer is never left alone with clients. Client information is shared with a volunteer only as needed, consistent with GOV-03 and the federal privacy rules at 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164.

definitions.definition: A person who gives unpaid services to the agency or its clients and is not an employee or contracted staff member.
Personal care, supervision, habilitation, transportation or other hands-on support to clients.
The number of paid, qualified staff the agency must have present based on the clients' needs and plans. Volunteers do not count toward it.

procedures: The Administrator informs anyone who offers to volunteer that [AGENCY NAME] does not currently use volunteers. The Administrator may refer the person to community resources, and clients may still receive visits from their own family and friends under IR-01.
The Administrator does not accept volunteer services unless the governing body has approved the use of volunteers in writing and the minutes record the services, supervisor and training requirements.

If approved, the Administrator defines in writing each volunteer's role, hours, location and limits, and states that the role is not direct care unless the person is trained and background-checked as set below.

Before the first client contact, the Administrator runs the same background and criminal record screening used for staff and checks the Health Care Personnel Registry, as described in HCP-01. A volunteer with a substantiated finding or disqualifying record is not accepted.
The volunteer signs a confidentiality agreement before any client contact, and the signed agreement is filed in the volunteer record.

Before client contact, a QP gives the volunteer orientation covering client rights, confidentiality, abuse/neglect reporting (HRM-01), emergency procedures and the volunteer's role. The QP documents the date and content.

Any volunteer who will have direct contact with clients receives approved de-escalation training under TRN-01 before that contact. Volunteers are not trained in or permitted to use restrictive interventions.
The Administrator names one paid staff supervisor for each volunteer in writing. The supervisor is present and in the same area with the volunteer when clients are present.
A volunteer never provides personal care, gives medications, handles client money, drives clients or covers a staff post. Volunteers are not counted in staffing minimums on any shift.

Volunteers are told to share client information only with the supervisor, and not to photograph clients, post about them or discuss them outside the home. Staff only give a volunteer the client information needed for the task.
Volunteers report any concern, injury or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the supervisor right away, and the supervisor follows HRM-01 and GOV-06.
The supervisor evaluates each volunteer at least annually and may end a volunteer's service at any time. A confidentiality breach ends volunteering at once and is reported to the Administrator.
The Administrator keeps a volunteer file with the approval, background check, signed confidentiality agreement, orientation record, schedule and supervisor assignment.
The governing body reviews this policy at least annually and records whether volunteers are used.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether volunteers are used and approves roles, supervisors and training.
Screens volunteers, assigns supervisors, keeps volunteer files and ensures volunteers are not counted toward staffing.
Directs and is present with the volunteer, protects confidentiality and reports concerns.
Provides orientation on rights, confidentiality and abuse/neglect reporting.
Follows the role limits, keeps client information private and reports concerns.

documentation: Governing body minutes recording whether volunteers are used
Written volunteer role description
Background and registry check results
Signed confidentiality agreement
Orientation and training record
Supervisor assignment
Annual evaluation

policies.title: Staff Training and Ongoing Education
policies.applies_to: All employees, including professional and paraprofessional staff, the Administrator and QPs
policies.purpose: To make sure every staff member has the training needed to serve people with developmental disabilities safely, that training is documented, and that education continues throughout employment.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0202, Worksheet p.4, Item 10: Policy on training for professional and paraprofessional staff, including what training is provided and how ongoing staff education is ensured. It also meets the training policy topic in 10A NCAC 27G .0201.

Required training. Training for all staff covers orientation, client rights and confidentiality, the needs identified in each client's individual plan, and bloodborne pathogens (10A NCAC 27G .0202; 29 CFR 1910.1030). At least one staff member trained in first aid, CPR and the Heimlich maneuver is on site at all times, and CPR must be taken in person. Medication administration training must be in person, delivered by an RN, pharmacist or other qualified trainer. Additional training is provided in de-escalation and restrictive interventions (TRN-01), fire and disaster procedures (EMG-01), incident reporting (GOV-06), abuse/neglect prevention and reporting (HRM-01), infection control (PER-02) and the special populations curriculum (REQ-02).

Professional and paraprofessional staff. Direct Support Professionals must hold a GED or high school diploma and are supervised under 10A NCAC 27G .0104 and PER-03. Professional staff (QPs and APs) meet the qualifications of 10A NCAC 27G .0104 and receive the same agency training, plus continuing education relevant to their roles.

Ongoing education. DHSR does not provide training. [AGENCY NAME] selects qualified trainers, pays for required training, schedules it on paid time and keeps training records. The annual training hours required by our accreditor and LME/MCO are adopted as the minimum, [ANNUAL TRAINING HOURS]. Training needs are reviewed at least annually and whenever a client's needs change, an incident shows a gap, or QA/QI identifies a need.

definitions.definition: Initial training given at hire that covers the agency, job duties, policies, client rights, confidentiality, emergency procedures and the home's clients.
A staff member who is not a QP or AP, as defined in 10A NCAC 27G .0104. This includes Direct Support Professionals.
A person with the license, certification or experience required for the topic, such as an RN or pharmacist for medication administration or a certified instructor for CPR.
The agency's list of required training topics, who must take each one, how often and when each person's training is due.

procedures: Before a new hire works alone with any client, the Administrator verifies the hire's qualifications (age 18 or older, GED or diploma for Direct Support Professionals) and confirms the hire has had orientation covering the agency, job description, client rights and confidentiality.

Before the new hire works alone with clients, a QP reviews each client's individual plan with the hire and trains the hire on that client's needs, supports, health concerns and communication methods. The QP documents it.
Within [NUMBER] days of hire, and before exposure to blood or body fluids on the job, each new hire completes bloodborne pathogen training under PER-02 and 29 CFR 1910.1030.
The Administrator makes sure every shift has at least one staff member with current first aid, CPR and Heimlich training. Staff complete CPR in person. Online-only CPR courses are not accepted.
Only staff who have completed in-person medication administration training from an RN, pharmacist or other qualified trainer, and who have passed the competency check, may give medications (MED-02).

The QP or Administrator arranges de-escalation training under TRN-01 for all staff who work with clients. Staff learn restrictive interventions only if the agency's governing body policy allows them (RRI-01).

Staff complete training on fire and disaster procedures, incident reporting, abuse/neglect reporting and the Health Care Personnel Registry as part of orientation, and refresher training as scheduled in the matrix.

The Administrator keeps a training matrix for each staff member listing required topics, dates completed, trainer, expiration dates and next due dates, as described in REQ-02. The Administrator reviews the matrix at least monthly.
Because DHSR provides no training, the Administrator identifies qualified outside trainers, confirms credentials and keeps records of trainer qualifications and course content.
The Administrator sets the annual training hours at the greater of what our accreditor and LME/MCO contract require, and builds a yearly training calendar approved by the governing body.
Staff sign an attendance sheet or receive a certificate for every session. The Administrator files the record in the personnel record within [NUMBER] business days.
Staff whose required training lapses are not scheduled for the duties that require the training until it is completed. The Administrator documents the corrective plan.
Supervisors identify additional training needs in the individualized supervision plan (PER-03), in annual evaluations and after incidents. The Administrator schedules training to meet those needs.
When a client's plan changes or a new client is admitted, the QP trains all staff on the new or changed needs before staff work alone with that client.
The QA/QI Committee (GOV-05) reviews training compliance at least quarterly and reports gaps to the governing body.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually and updates it when rules, accreditation or LME/MCO requirements change.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the training policy, budget and annual calendar.
Ensures staff meet qualifications, schedules training, checks coverage by trained staff and keeps the training matrix.
Trains staff on client plans, supervises paraprofessionals and identifies training needs.
Deliver and document training in their areas, such as CPR and medication administration.
Complete required training on time and apply it in daily work.

documentation: Personnel record training file, with certificates and attendance sheets
Training matrix with due dates
Orientation checklist signed by staff and trainer
Documentation of plan-specific training for each client
In-person CPR and first aid certificates
Medication administration training and competency records
Trainer credentials
Annual training calendar and QA/QI training review minutes

policies.title: Infection Control, Communicable Disease and Bloodborne Pathogens
policies.applies_to: All staff, clients, and anyone present in the home
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among clients and staff and to protect staff from exposure to blood and other potentially infectious material.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0202(i) and Worksheet p.4, Item 11: the policy on identifying, reporting, investigating and controlling infectious and communicable diseases affecting staff and clients, including training on infectious diseases and blood-borne pathogens.

Bloodborne pathogen training is required for all staff (10A NCAC 27G .0202(g)(4); 29 CFR 1910.1030). The policy includes an exposure control plan, universal precautions and sharps handling. Staff with a communicable disease follow work-restriction rules, and [AGENCY NAME] notifies the local health department when notification is required. Staff are trained on infectious disease during orientation and each year after.

Universal precautions. Staff treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious for every client, regardless of diagnosis. Client health information, including HIV status, stays confidential and is shared only as the law allows (GOV-03).

definitions.definition: An illness that can spread from person to person, such as influenza, COVID-19, norovirus, scabies, tuberculosis or hepatitis.
The practice of treating all blood and body fluids as if infected and using protective barriers and hand hygiene every time.
A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin or needle-stick contact with blood or other potentially infectious material.
A written plan identifying job tasks with exposure risk and the methods used to eliminate or reduce it, as required by 29 CFR 1910.1030.

procedures: The Administrator and nurse consultant write and maintain an exposure control plan that lists tasks with exposure risk (for example first aid, personal care, laundry, cleaning body-fluid spills, handling sharps) and reviews it at least annually.

At orientation and every year after, staff receive training on infectious and communicable diseases and bloodborne pathogens, given by a qualified trainer, with a chance to ask questions. Training is documented in the personnel record.

Staff practice universal precautions with every client. They wash hands with soap and water or use hand sanitizer where appropriate before and after client care, after glove removal and before preparing food.

The home keeps gloves, face protection, gowns, disinfectant, spill kits and hand-hygiene supplies in [LOCATIONS] and checks them monthly. The home provides personal protective equipment to staff at no cost.

Staff clean and disinfect body-fluid spills right away using gloves and an approved disinfectant. They place contaminated material in labeled, leak-proof bags or containers and dispose of it as directed by the exposure control plan.
The home keeps a puncture-resistant sharps container wherever sharps such as lancets are used. Staff do not recap, bend or break needles. A full container is sealed and disposed of as required.
Staff launder soiled linens and clothing promptly, wearing gloves, and keep them separated from clean items. Food prep and cleaning follow the home's sanitation routine under LIV-01.

If a staff member has an exposure incident, the person washes the area, flushes eyes or mucous membranes as needed, tells the supervisor immediately and seeks medical evaluation promptly. The Administrator makes available any post-exposure evaluation and follow-up that 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires, and records the incident.
The Administrator offers the hepatitis B vaccination series to staff with occupational exposure, as required by 29 CFR 1910.1030. Staff who decline sign a declination form.

Staff and clients who have symptoms of a communicable disease (for example fever, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, cough) report to the supervisor. The supervisor consults the nurse consultant or the person's health care provider.

Staff with a communicable disease do not work with clients until cleared under work-restriction guidance from their health care provider or the local health department. Staff are not penalized for reporting illness or staying home.

When a client has a communicable disease, staff follow the provider's orders, separate and care for the client as directed, increase cleaning and keep the person's privacy and dignity, and notify the guardian and QP.

The Administrator reports communicable diseases to the [LOCAL HEALTH DEPARTMENT] when notification is required, and follows its instructions on investigation and control. The Administrator documents the report date and instructions.

The Administrator investigates each suspected outbreak or cluster (two or more people with the same illness) by listing who is affected, when symptoms started and possible sources, and records the controls put in place.
Infection control incidents and reportable events are reported under GOV-06. The QA/QI Committee (GOV-05) reviews infection data at least quarterly.
Staff keep health information confidential. HIV or AIDS information is disclosed only as the law allows (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the exposure control plan, supplies, training and reporting to the health department.
Advises on infection control and communicable disease responses and helps review the plan.
Ensures client care follows medical orders and notifies guardians and care coordinators.
Use universal precautions, report exposures and symptoms, and complete training.

documentation: Written exposure control plan and annual review
Bloodborne pathogen and infectious disease training records
Hepatitis B vaccination or declination forms
Exposure incident reports and follow-up
Communicable disease log and health department reports
Outbreak investigation notes
Supply checks
QA/QI infection data review

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27G .0204 Competencies and Supervision of Paraprofessionals
policies.title: Individualized Supervision Plan for Paraprofessional Staff
policies.applies_to: All paraprofessional staff (including Direct Support Professionals), the QPs and APs who supervise them, and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure every paraprofessional is supervised by a qualified supervisor and has a written plan, started at hire, that addresses their areas of need and shows they have the knowledge and skills for the people served.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0204 and Worksheet p.4, Item 12: Policy on implementing and documenting an individualized supervision plan for all paraprofessional staff upon hire. It specifies who develops the plan, the staff's areas of need and methods to address them, and that the plan is reviewed and signed by both the staff member and the supervisor.

An individualized supervision plan is started at hire for every paraprofessional. A Qualified Professional (QP) or Associate Professional (AP) supervisor develops it with the staff member. Paraprofessionals are supervised by an AP or QP. Non-QPs are supervised by a QP with experience with the population served (10A NCAC 27G .0104). The plan lists the staff member's areas of need and the methods to address them. Both the staff member and the supervisor review and sign the plan. The plan is reviewed at least annually (10A NCAC 27G .0104) and sooner when needs change.

Paraprofessionals must show the knowledge, skills and abilities needed for people with developmental disabilities, as set out in 10A NCAC 27G .0204. Direct Support Professionals must hold a GED or diploma (10A NCAC 27G .0104).

definitions.definition: A staff member who is not a QP or AP, as defined in 10A NCAC 27G .0104. Direct Support Professionals are paraprofessionals.
A staff member who meets the QP definition for the developmental disability population in 10A NCAC 27G .0104.
A staff member who meets the AP definition for the developmental disability population in 10A NCAC 27G .0104.
A written plan, specific to one paraprofessional, that identifies areas of need and how the supervisor will address them.

procedures: At the time of offer or on the first day of work, and in all cases before the person works alone with clients, the Administrator assigns each new paraprofessional to a named QP or AP supervisor and records it in the personnel file.
The Administrator confirms that the assigned supervisor qualifies as an AP or QP and, for non-QP supervised staff, that supervision is by a QP with experience with the population served.

Within the first [NUMBER] days of hire and before the new hire works alone, the supervisor reviews the staff member's application, education, experience and the Direct Support Professional requirement (GED or diploma), and begins the plan.

The supervisor meets with the staff member to assess knowledge and skills for the clients served, including rights, individual plans, communication, behavior supports, medication, health and safety, and documentation.

The supervisor writes the individualized supervision plan with the staff member. It lists the staff member's areas of need and the methods to address them, for example shadowing, coaching, demonstration, observation, specific training, reading and review with feedback. It states who will do each activity and by what date.
The supervisor schedules regular supervision sessions, frequent at first, and states in the plan how often they will occur, where they will be held and how they will be documented.
The staff member and the supervisor both read and sign and date the plan. The staff member receives a copy, and the original goes in the personnel file by the end of the first week.
The supervisor observes the staff member working directly with clients, gives feedback and records competencies shown. The supervisor notes the date of each observation and what was observed.

The supervisor checks that the training in PER-01 (including plan-specific training, medication administration if applicable, CPR and de-escalation) is completed according to the plan and updates dates as training is finished.

The supervisor updates the plan when the staff member shows a new need, a client's needs change, an incident or complaint indicates a gap, or the staff member changes roles. The updated plan is re-signed by both people.

The supervisor and staff member review the plan at least once every 12 months, and no later than the anniversary of the previous review. They record progress, remove needs that are met, add new ones and sign and date the plan.
If competencies are not shown, the supervisor documents a corrective plan with deadlines. The Administrator is told. The staff member does not take on duties that they have not shown competence in.
The Administrator keeps a tracking list of every paraprofessional with the supervisor's name, plan start date, next review date and sign-off status, and reviews it monthly.
The QA/QI Committee (GOV-05) reviews supervision plan compliance at least annually and reports overdue plans to the governing body.
Supervision plans are confidential personnel records, kept separately from client records, and available to DHSR surveyors on request.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns qualified supervisors, makes sure plans start at hire, tracks reviews and keeps plans on file.
Develops the plan with the staff member, supervises and observes, documents progress, and reviews and signs the plan at least annually.
Takes part in developing the plan, completes the activities, asks for help and signs the plan.
Receives QA/QI reports on supervision compliance.

Record of supervisor assignment and supervisor qualifications
Supervision session notes and observation records
Competency documentation
Annual review sign-offs by staff and supervisor
Corrective plans, if any
Tracking list of start and review dates

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27G .0205 Assessment and Treatment/Habilitation or Service Plan
policies.title: Referral, Admission and Assessment
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] Supervised Living 'C' homes: the Administrator, Qualified Professionals (QPs), and all staff who take referrals or take part in admissions and assessments.
policies.purpose: To make sure every person admitted to a [AGENCY NAME] home is eligible and appropriate for the program, is admitted lawfully, and has an assessment completed before services begin.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0205, Worksheet pp.4-5, Item 13 (Admission and Assessment policy). [AGENCY NAME] operates a Supervised Living facility with 'C' designation under 10A NCAC 27G .5601. It serves adults whose primary diagnosis is a developmental disability. Minors and adults do not live together. No more than six clients live in a home (10A NCAC 27G .5603). Under N.C.G.S. 122C-28, operating a licensable facility without a license is a Class H felony with a $1,000 per day fine. A facility serving two or more adults must be licensed, so [AGENCY NAME] admits no second adult before the DHSR license is issued. Admissions come through the LME/MCO Tailored Plan choice list and authorization. Before any services are provided, a written assessment is completed and placed in the client record. It covers (a) the presenting problem; (b) the person's needs and strengths; (c) a provisional or admitting diagnosis, with an established diagnosis within 30 days; (d) a pertinent social, family and medical history; and (e) evaluations appropriate to the person's needs. If services begin before the habilitation plan is in place, the strategies being used are documented in the record. Admission follows the requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c), including the client's choice and person-centered planning.

definitions.definition: The written, pre-service gathering of information about the person's presenting problem, needs, strengths, diagnosis and history, used to plan services.
The working diagnosis recorded at admission by a qualified professional, which must be confirmed as an established diagnosis within 30 days.
A staff member who meets the North Carolina definition of qualified professional for developmental disabilities services and is designated by [AGENCY NAME] to complete assessments and plans.
The list through which the Tailored Plan offers eligible individuals a choice of providers and which authorizes admission to Innovations Residential Supports.
A parent of a minor, legal guardian, or other person with legal authority to make decisions for the client.

procedures: The Administrator or designee ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) records every referral on the Referral Log with the date, source, person's name, and LME/MCO and care coordinator contact details.

Before accepting a referral, the Administrator confirms the person is an adult (18 or older), has a primary diagnosis of a developmental disability, and fits the 'C' designation. Referrals for minors are declined and referred back to the LME/MCO.

The Administrator confirms there is a vacancy within the six-client maximum. The Administrator also confirms that any shared bedroom would hold no more than two people of the same sex and meets the space requirements described in EMG-01.

Licensure gate: before any second adult is admitted, the Administrator confirms the DHSR license has been issued and a copy is on file. Admission is prohibited until then. The Administrator signs and dates the Admission Readiness Checklist to show the check was made.

The Administrator confirms the referral came through the LME/MCO Tailored Plan choice list and obtains the written service authorization. The Administrator also confirms Innovations eligibility and the approved level of support, and files copies in the client record.

The Administrator arranges a pre-admission meeting or visit with the person, the legally responsible person (if any) and the care coordinator, so the person can see the home and meet housemates. The person's and LRP's choice to enter the home is documented.

The Administrator asks for existing records: prior assessments, psychological and adaptive evaluations, medical records, current medication orders, guardianship papers, and the Innovations person-centered plan.

A QP completes the assessment before services begin, using the Admission Assessment Form. The form documents the presenting problem, needs and strengths, and the provisional or admitting diagnosis. It also records the social, family and medical history, and any evaluations needed.

The QP records the provisional or admitting diagnosis and who made it. The QP sets a 30-day tickler date to obtain the established diagnosis, in writing, from a qualified clinician. The Administrator checks the tickler weekly.

The QP identifies evaluations suited to the person's needs (for example medical, dental, psychological, speech, occupational therapy, behavioral, vision and hearing). The QP arranges any that are missing and records the date requested and the date completed.

If services must start before the habilitation plan (ASM-02) is complete, the QP writes down the strategies staff will use for the person's needs from day one. These are signed and dated in the record on the day of admission and given to direct care staff.
The QP coordinates with the QPs responsible for habilitation or case management and with the LME/MCO care coordinator, and records those contacts in the record.

On admission day the Administrator reviews rights, house rules and fees with the person and the LRP (INF-01, GOV-07, CON-01) and states that Medicaid does not pay room and board. The person or LRP signs the admission agreement and consents, or the reason a signature was not obtained is written down.
The Administrator documents the admission decision. If the person is not admitted, the Administrator tells the referral source and the LRP the reasons in writing within five business days.
The QP updates the assessment when the person's needs change significantly and uses it at each plan review. The Administrator keeps all assessment documents in the client record per GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Screens referrals, enforces the licensure gate and six-client maximum, confirms LME/MCO authorization, and makes and documents admission decisions.
Completes the assessment before services, tracks the 30-day established diagnosis, arranges evaluations, and documents interim strategies.
Use the documented interim strategies and report new information about the person's needs to the QP.
Approves admission criteria and reviews admission and licensure compliance.

documentation: Referral Log
Admission Readiness Checklist with licensure verification
LME/MCO choice list documentation, authorization, Innovations eligibility and level of support
Admission Assessment Form with provisional/admitting diagnosis and 30-day established diagnosis
History and evaluation records
Interim service strategies
Admission agreement and consents
Denial letters, if any

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27G .0205 Assessment and Treatment/Habilitation or Service Plan
policies.title: Person-Centered Habilitation Plan and Individual Plan
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] Administrator, Qualified Professionals, direct care staff, clients and legally responsible persons.
policies.purpose: To make sure each client has a written, person-centered habilitation plan developed with the client and legally responsible person within 30 days of admission, matched to the Innovations plan, and reviewed at least annually.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0205, Worksheet p.5, Item 14 (policy on developing a treatment/habilitation plan within 30 days). [AGENCY NAME] develops a habilitation plan for every client within 30 days of admission, or before if applicable, together with the client and/or the legally responsible person. Each plan includes (a) anticipated outcomes with projected dates; (b) strategies; (c) the staff responsible; (d) a review at least annually; and (e) the basis for evaluating outcomes. The plan must have the written consent of the client or legally responsible person, or a written statement of why consent was not obtained. The plan is built around the person's preferences and strengths and is aligned with the Innovations person-centered plan from the LME/MCO care coordinator (42 CFR 441.301(c)). Residential Supports are paid through the LME/MCO Tailored Plan under the NC Innovations Waiver, and Medicaid does not pay for room and board. As required by 10A NCAC 27G .5603, [AGENCY NAME] sends an annual progress report to the legally responsible person.

definitions.definition: The written plan of outcomes, strategies and responsible staff that guides a client's services in the home. It is also called the individual plan.
The plan developed by the LME/MCO care coordinator with the person that authorizes and describes waiver services.
A measurable result the client is working toward, with a projected date.

procedures: On admission day the Administrator assigns a QP to lead plan development and enters the 30-day plan due date (counted from the admission date) on the Plan Tracking Calendar.
The QP obtains the current Innovations person-centered plan from the care coordinator and reviews it, along with the admission assessment (ASM-01), so the habilitation plan fits the Innovations plan.

The QP schedules a planning meeting at a time and place convenient to the client and the legally responsible person. The QP invites the care coordinator and anyone else the client chooses, and offers communication supports (IR-01).

At the meeting the QP asks the client and LRP about preferences, goals, strengths, health and safety needs, and the activities and relationships the person wants. The QP records their words in the plan.
The team writes each anticipated outcome so it can be measured and gives each a projected achievement date.
For each outcome the plan states the strategies staff will use, the staff position responsible, and the basis for evaluating progress (for example data sheets, observation or skill checklists).
The plan includes supports for health, medication (MED-02), behavior, community inclusion (SOC-01) and family contact, using the least restrictive alternative (LRA-01).
The QP and Administrator confirm the plan is complete and meets the requirements before the 30-day due date. Any gap is corrected before sign-off.
The client or LRP is asked to sign the plan to show written consent. If consent is not obtained, the QP writes a statement of why not and the follow-up steps, and files it with the plan.
The QP gives a copy of the signed plan to the client and LRP, to the care coordinator, and to the direct care staff who carry it out. Staff sign a read-and-understood sheet.
Direct care staff record progress on each outcome as the plan requires. The QP reviews the data at least quarterly and writes a short summary.

The QP reviews the plan with the client and LRP at least annually, and sooner if the person's needs change, an outcome is met, or the Innovations plan changes. The QP revises outcomes, dates and strategies, and obtains new consent.

Within [NUMBER OF DAYS] days after each annual review, the QP prepares an annual progress report. The Administrator sends it to the legally responsible person and files a copy of the report and the transmittal date in the record.
The Administrator checks the Plan Tracking Calendar monthly and reports overdue plans or reviews to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05).
All plans, consents, reviews and progress reports are filed in the client record (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Leads plan development, writes outcomes, obtains consent, reviews data and conducts annual and interim reviews.
Assigns the QP, tracks due dates, approves plans, and sends annual progress reports to the legally responsible person.
Carry out strategies, collect progress data and report changes to the QP.
Take part in planning, state preferences, and give or withhold written consent.
Provides the Innovations person-centered plan and takes part in planning.

documentation: Plan Tracking Calendar
Habilitation plan with outcomes, dates, strategies, responsible staff and evaluation basis
Signed consent or written statement of why consent was not obtained
Copy of the Innovations person-centered plan
Staff read-and-understood sheets
Quarterly data summaries
Annual review and progress report with transmittal date

policies.title: Fire Safety Plan, Disaster Plan, Drills and Emergency Supplies
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] Administrator, all direct care staff, clients, and visitors in each Supervised Living home.
policies.purpose: To protect clients and staff in a fire or disaster by maintaining approved written plans, posted evacuation routes, regular drills and basic first aid supplies.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0207, Worksheet pp.5-6, Item 15 (Emergency Plans and Supplies policy). It also provides Required Materials for Licensure Review items RM-DP-1 (Written Disaster Plan) and RM-DP-2 (verification of the disaster plan from local Emergency Management (OEM)). [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written fire safety plan for each facility and a written disaster plan approved by the appropriate local authority. A copy of the OEM verification is kept for the licensure review. Plans are accessible to all staff. Evacuation procedures and routes are posted in the home. Fire and disaster drills are held at least quarterly in this 24-hour facility and repeated for each shift. Drills simulate actual fire emergencies. Basic first aid supplies are kept accessible. [AGENCY NAME] complies with the NC Building Code and keeps documented evidence of compliance with fire, sanitation and building codes, including an annual fire inspection (10A NCAC 27G .0301). Homes serving four to six clients, or two-story homes, must have two remotely located exits per occupied story.

definitions.definition: A written plan for each facility describing how to prevent fire, raise the alarm, evacuate clients, account for everyone and contact emergency services.
A written plan covering natural and other disasters (such as severe weather, power or water loss, and hazardous events), approved by the local authority.
A practice evacuation or sheltering exercise that simulates an actual emergency and is documented.
The county or local Emergency Management office that verifies the disaster plan.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) writes a facility-specific fire safety plan for each home. It includes floor plan with exits, alarm and extinguisher locations, evacuation steps for each client (including those who need physical help, prompting or communication supports), the outside meeting place, and the emergency numbers.

The Administrator writes a disaster plan covering severe weather, flood, power or water loss, loss of the home, shelter-in-place, and evacuation. It lists the transportation, relocation sites, medication, medical record, and family and LME/MCO contacts that go with clients, and the emergency supplies on hand.

The Administrator submits the disaster plan to local Emergency Management (OEM) for approval and keeps the written verification with the plan. The plan is not treated as final until verification is on file. A copy goes into the licensure submission (REQ-01).

The fire safety plan is reviewed with the local fire authority. The Administrator arranges the annual fire inspection and files each inspection report as evidence of compliance with fire, sanitation and building codes (10A NCAC 27G .0301).

The Administrator consults the DHSR Construction Section and local building and fire officials, and obtains all required local permits, before any construction, change of use, alteration or addition (10A NCAC 27G .0302).

The Administrator checks that the home has two remotely located exits per occupied story where the home has four to six clients or two stories. No client sleeps in an unfinished basement or attic, and mattresses are fire-retardant (10A NCAC 27G .0304).
Copies of both plans are kept in the staff office in a place known to all staff. Each new employee reads them during orientation and signs an acknowledgment (PER-01).
Evacuation routes and procedures are posted near exits and in each hallway and bedroom area, with a floor plan showing 'You Are Here'. The Administrator checks the postings monthly.

The Administrator schedules fire drills and disaster drills at least once each calendar quarter, with the drills repeated for each shift (day, evening and overnight). Fire drills simulate an actual fire emergency, for example by blocking a primary exit or using a simulated smoke or alarm scenario.

During each drill the staff in charge times the evacuation, checks that every client reached the meeting place, and notes any client who needed help, any obstacle, and any alarm or equipment problem. Clients are given support to take part safely.

The staff in charge completes a Drill Record for each drill: date, time, shift, type of drill, scenario, evacuation time, participants, problems found and corrective action. The Administrator reviews and signs it within three business days.
If a drill shows a problem, the Administrator corrects it and holds a repeat drill as soon as practical. The Administrator reports unresolved issues to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05).

The Administrator keeps basic first aid supplies in a known, accessible place in each home and in each facility vehicle. A staff member checks them monthly and replaces used or expired items, recording the check on the Supply Log.
Staff test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and check extinguishers monthly, and record the results. Broken equipment is reported to the Administrator the same day and fixed or replaced right away.
After a real fire or disaster, the Administrator reports it as required by GOV-06, reviews how the plan worked, and updates the plan within 30 days.
The governing body reviews both plans at least annually and whenever the home, population or local conditions change.

responsibilities.duty: Writes and maintains the plans, obtains OEM verification and annual fire inspection, schedules drills, and signs Drill Records.

responsibilities.role: Staff in charge on each shift
responsibilities.duty: Lead drills and real emergencies, account for all clients, and complete the Drill Record.
Know the plans and routes, take part in drills, and keep exits clear.
Approves the plans and reviews drill results and inspection reports.
Approve or verify the disaster plan and carry out fire inspections.

Written disaster plan (RM-DP-1)
OEM verification of the disaster plan (RM-DP-2)
Annual fire inspection reports and building, sanitation and fire code compliance evidence
Drill Records by quarter and shift
First aid and alarm/extinguisher check logs
Staff acknowledgment of plans
Permits and Construction Section correspondence

policies.title: Medication Program Scope, Dispensing, Packaging and Labeling
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] Administrator and all staff who receive, check, store or administer client medications.
policies.purpose: To state the scope of [AGENCY NAME]'s medication program and set the rules for dispensing, packaging and labeling so clients receive only properly ordered, properly labeled medication.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0209 (Medication Requirements) and the medication policy topic required of the governing body by 10A NCAC 27G .0201. Item 16 (Worksheet p.6): [AGENCY NAME] does not adopt the statement that it chooses not to handle medications. The home administers and stores medications for clients, so the medication procedures in MED-01 through MED-04 apply and Item 16 is not completed. Item 17 (Medication Dispensing Procedure, Worksheet p.6): staff do not prescribe or dispense medication and keep no stock of prescription drugs. Dispensing is done only by a registered pharmacist, physician or other person authorized by law and registered with the NC Board of Pharmacy, and only on the written order of a licensed physician. The take-home methadone clause does not apply because [AGENCY NAME] is not licensed to distribute methadone. Item 18 (Medication Packaging and Labeling Procedures, Worksheet p.7): non-prescription containers not dispensed by a pharmacist keep the manufacturer's label and a visible expiration date. Prescription medications, including samples, are in tamper-resistant packaging. Prescription labels show the client's name, the prescriber, the dispensing date, directions for use, the drug name, strength, quantity and expiration date, and the pharmacy or dispensing location details and the dispensing practitioner.

definitions.definition: Preparing and delivering a prescription drug to a client under a prescriber's order, which only a pharmacist, physician or other person authorized by law may do.
A signed order from a legally authorized prescriber stating the drug, dose, route, frequency and any other directions.
Packaging that shows visible evidence if it has been opened or altered.
A medication that can be bought without a prescription, administered here only under a written order.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) states in the admission packet and orientation that the home administers and stores medication, and that Item 16 of the Worksheet is not adopted.
Staff never prescribe, never change a dose on their own, never share a client's medication with another person, and never repackage or relabel medication.

Staff do not keep stock supplies of prescription drugs for dispensing. Only medication prescribed to a specific client by a legally authorized prescriber and dispensed for that client is kept in the home.

The Administrator obtains a written order from the client's physician or other authorized prescriber for every prescription and non-prescription medication, vitamin, supplement and treatment given in the home, and files it in the client record.

All prescriptions are filled by a registered pharmacist, or are dispensed by a physician or other person authorized by law. Staff use a pharmacy of the client's or LRP's choice and record the pharmacy name and phone number.

When a medication is received, the trained staff member checks the label against the written order for client name, drug name, strength, directions, quantity and prescriber, before putting it into use. A second staff member verifies when one is available.

The staff member checks that prescription packaging is tamper-resistant and intact, and that the label shows the client's name, prescriber, dispensing date, directions for use, drug name, strength, quantity, expiration date, and pharmacy or dispensing location details and the dispensing practitioner.
Samples must be in tamper-resistant packaging and carry a complete label, and must come with a written order. Staff do not accept samples that fail these checks.
For non-prescription medication not dispensed by a pharmacist, staff check that the manufacturer's label and a visible expiration date are present. Items missing either are not used.

If a label does not match the order, is unreadable, incomplete or mislabeled, staff do not use the medication. They set it aside, notify the Administrator the same day, and return it to the pharmacy for correction. The Administrator documents the event.

The Administrator calls the pharmacy or prescriber right away to get a corrected label or order, and makes sure the client has no gap in medication. Any gap is reported under MED-04 and GOV-06 if it is a medication error.
After the check, the staff member signs the Medication Receipt Log with date, time, client, drug, strength, quantity and name of staff. The medication is placed into locked storage (MED-03).
Only labeled medication in its original container is sent with a client on outings or visits, as set out in MED-02, and staff record what leaves and returns.
The Administrator reviews the Medication Receipt Log monthly, and the QA/QI Committee reviews labeling and order findings at least quarterly (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures orders are on file, labels are checked, mislabeled items are returned, and the policy is followed.
Verify each label against the written order on receipt and never dispense, repackage or relabel.
Issue written orders and dispense and label medication as the law requires.
Adopts this policy and reviews medication program findings.

documentation: Written prescriber orders
Medication Receipt Log
Pharmacy contact record
Records of mislabeled medication returned to the pharmacy
Monthly Administrator review and QA/QI minutes

policies.title: Medication Administration and MAR
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] Administrator, nurses, and all staff who administer or assist with medication, and clients who self-administer.
policies.purpose: To ensure medication is given only on written orders, by qualified and privileged staff, and recorded immediately on a current medication administration record (MAR).
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Worksheet pp.7-8, Item 19 (Medication Administration procedures). [AGENCY NAME] administers medication only on the written order of a legally authorized prescriber. A client self-administers only if the physician authorizes it in writing. Only licensed persons, or unlicensed staff who have been trained by a registered nurse, pharmacist or other qualified professional and who are privileged by [AGENCY NAME], may administer medication. A current MAR is kept for each client. Each dose is recorded on the MAR immediately after administration and shows the client's name, the drug name, strength and quantity, the instructions, the date and time, and the name or initials of the person who gave it. When a client asks to change a medication, the request is documented and filed with the MAR, and the physician is consulted. Training and privileging meet the personnel requirements of 10A NCAC 27G .0202.

definitions.definition: Medication Administration Record, the client-specific record of each dose given, refused or missed.
Authorized in writing by [AGENCY NAME] to administer medication after completing training and a competency check.
A client taking his or her own medication, which requires the physician's written authorization.
A physician or other practitioner licensed to prescribe medication in North Carolina.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) keeps a Medication Administration Roster listing every staff member who may administer, with credential (license) or training date, trainer's name and credential, competency date and privileging date.

Unlicensed staff must complete medication administration training taught by an RN, pharmacist or other qualified professional (PER-01), pass a written and observed competency check, and be privileged in writing by the Administrator before giving any medication. Unprivileged staff may not administer.
On admission and at each change, the Administrator obtains the written order and the MAR is set up from the order. A second trained staff member verifies the transcription, and both initial it.
Each MAR shows the client's name, drug name, strength, quantity, instructions (dose, route, frequency, time), start and stop dates, allergies, prescriber, and a signature/initial key.
Before each administration the staff member washes hands, takes the client's medication from locked storage, and checks the client, drug, dose, route and time against the order and MAR.

The staff member watches the client take the medication and records it on the MAR immediately, with the date, time and the staff member's name or initials. Staff never pre-record or record later from memory.
If a dose is refused, missed, spit out or not available, the staff member records it on the MAR at once and follows MED-04.

If the physician authorizes self-administration in writing, the written authorization is filed, the plan reflects it, and the medication is kept in secure storage (MED-03). A staff member watches or checks as the authorization and plan state, and records what happened.

When a client asks to change, stop or refuse a medication, the staff member records the request, signs and dates it, and files it with the MAR. The staff member notifies the Administrator the same day and contacts the physician for consultation, recording the date, time, person spoken to and outcome.

Staff do not change doses, times or routes without a new written order. A telephone order is written down, read back to the prescriber, and followed by a signed written order within the time set in the order policy of [AGENCY NAME].
For outings and visits, a trained staff member gives the client's labeled medication in its original container or a pharmacy-prepared container, and records what was sent and returned.
The Administrator reviews each MAR at least weekly for blanks, mismatches and missing orders, and signs the review. Nurse or pharmacist reviews are held as set out in MED-04.
Any medication error is handled and reported under MED-04 and GOV-06.
Completed MARs are filed in the client record (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the roster, privileges staff, verifies orders, reviews MARs weekly and follows up on gaps.

responsibilities.role: Licensed staff and privileged unlicensed staff
responsibilities.duty: Administer only per written order, record each dose immediately and report refusals and errors.

responsibilities.role: RN, pharmacist or other qualified trainer
responsibilities.duty: Trains unlicensed staff and verifies competency.
Writes orders and authorizes self-administration.
May ask for medication changes, which staff document and take to the physician.

documentation: Written orders and physician authorization for self-administration
MAR for each client
Medication Administration Roster with training, competency and privileging records
Documented client requests for medication changes and physician consultation notes
Weekly MAR review sign-off

policies.title: Medication Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] Administrator and all staff who store, handle, count or dispose of client medications.
policies.purpose: To keep client medications secure, at the correct temperature and separated by client, and to dispose of them safely with a witnessed record.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Worksheet pp.8-9, Item 21 (Medication Storage procedures) and Worksheet p.8, Item 20 (Medication Disposal procedures). Storage (Item 21): medications are kept in a securely locked cabinet in a clean, well-lit, ventilated room at 59-86 degrees F. Any refrigerator used runs at 36-46 degrees F, and if food is also stored in it the medications are in a separate locked compartment. Each client's medication is stored separately, and external-use products are stored apart from internal-use products. If a physician approves self-medication, secure storage is provided for the client. Disposal (Item 20): medication is disposed of in a way that prevents diversion or accidental ingestion. A disposal record is kept showing the client, drug, strength, quantity, date and method, and signed by the person disposing and a witness. For non-controlled substances the methods are incineration, flushing into a septic or sewer system, or transfer to a local pharmacy. Remaining medication is disposed of promptly, or held no more than 30 days after discharge unless the client is expected to return.

definitions.definition: The use, taking or transfer of medication by anyone other than the client it was prescribed for.
The written, witnessed record of each medication destroyed or transferred.
A medication applied to the skin, eyes, ears or other outside area, rather than taken by mouth or other internal routes.
A medication not scheduled as a controlled substance under state or federal law.

procedures: The Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) designates one locked medication cabinet in a clean, well-lit, ventilated room in each home. It is kept locked at all times except during use.

Keys or access codes are held only by staff on the Medication Administration Roster (MED-02). The staff in charge on each shift controls them and never leaves them where clients or visitors can reach them.

A staff member records the room temperature on the Temperature Log at least daily. It must stay between 59 and 86 degrees F. If it is outside the range, the staff member tells the Administrator at once, moves the medication to a suitable place, and asks the pharmacist whether it is still usable.

If medications need refrigeration, they are kept in a refrigerator with a thermometer at 36-46 degrees F. Staff record the temperature daily on the log. Out-of-range readings are reported and handled as above.
If food is stored in the same refrigerator, medications are kept in a separate, locked compartment or box inside it.
Each client's medication is stored separately, in a labeled bin or section with the client's name. Medications are never mixed between clients.
External-use products are stored apart from internal-use products, on a separate shelf or in a separate bin.

If a physician approves self-medication in writing (MED-02), the Administrator provides secure storage for that client, such as a locked drawer or box in the client's room. The client holds the key and the arrangement is recorded in the plan.

Each month the Administrator checks all medications for expiration, discontinued orders, damaged containers, and labels that no longer match orders. Expired, discontinued, contaminated or unneeded medication is pulled for disposal.
Disposal is carried out so as to prevent diversion or accidental ingestion. Two staff, the person disposing and a witness, handle it together.

For non-controlled substances, staff use one of these methods only: incineration, flushing into a septic or sewer system, or transfer to a local pharmacy. Controlled substances are not disposed of by these methods. The Administrator consults the dispensing pharmacist and follows applicable state and federal law.

At the time of disposal, the staff member completes the Medication Disposal Record: client, drug, strength, quantity, date, method, and the signatures of the person disposing and the witness. The record is filed with the client record.

When a client is discharged, remaining medication goes with the client or LRP if ordered and receipted. Otherwise it is disposed of promptly, or held in locked storage no more than 30 days after discharge unless the client is expected to return, and then disposed of per steps 10-12.
If medication is found missing or suspected of diversion, the Administrator investigates immediately, reports under GOV-06 and, when required, notifies law enforcement and the pharmacist.
The Administrator reviews the Temperature Logs and Disposal Records monthly and reports findings to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Sets up secure storage, controls access, performs monthly checks, and reviews logs and disposal records.
Hold the keys, record temperatures, and report out-of-range readings and missing medication.
Dispose of medication properly and both sign the Disposal Record.
Advises on temperature excursions and disposal of controlled substances.

documentation: Temperature Log for storage room and refrigerator
Medication Disposal Record with signatures of disposer and witness
Monthly storage check records
Discharge medication receipts or disposal records
Incident reports for missing medication

policies.title: Medication Review, Errors and Refusals
policies.applies_to: All staff who administer, assist with, or oversee medications; the Administrator; the Qualified Professional; contracted prescribers and pharmacists
policies.purpose: To make sure medication regimens are reviewed on schedule, that every medication error, significant adverse drug reaction and refusal is reported and documented, and that clients are protected from harm related to medications.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will have a physician or pharmacist review the drug regimen of every client who takes psychotropic medication at least every 6 months. Findings and any corrective action are recorded in the client record. This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Medication Review Procedures (official checklist item 22; Worksheet p.9). [AGENCY NAME] will report every medication error and every significant adverse drug reaction immediately to the client's physician or pharmacist. Each error is documented in the client record as required by 10A NCAC 27G .0206 and evaluated against the incident level definitions in GOV-06. Every refusal of medication is documented. This policy meets 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Medication Errors Procedures (official checklist item 23; Worksheet p.9). Staff will never force, hide, or trick a client into taking medication. A client's refusal is handled under the rights policies, and the prescriber decides any change in treatment.

definitions.definition: A medication prescribed to affect mood, thought, behavior or perception, including antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilizers, anti-anxiety agents and similar drugs, whatever the reason prescribed.

Any deviation from the prescriber's written order, including a wrong client, wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong time, wrong route, a missed dose, an unauthorized extra dose, or a dose given from a wrong or mislabeled container.
An unintended and harmful reaction to a medication that needs medical attention, changes treatment, or poses a risk to the client's health or safety.
A client's declining, spitting out, or otherwise not taking a prescribed medication when it is offered.
A documented review by a physician or pharmacist of all of a client's medications for appropriateness, dose, interactions, side effects and continued need.

procedures: The Qualified Professional (QP) keeps a Psychotropic Review Tracking Log listing every client on a psychotropic medication, the date of the last review, and the date the next review is due (no more than 6 months later).
At admission and at each plan update, the QP checks the medication list and adds any client who takes a psychotropic medication to the log.

At least 30 days before each due date, the QP schedules the review with the client's prescribing physician or a pharmacist and sends the current medication list, the MAR, and any notes on side effects, refusals or errors.
The physician or pharmacist reviews the regimen and records the findings. Findings are filed in the client record. The review is not complete until the findings are in the record.

Within 3 working days of receiving findings, the QP gives them to the prescriber and the Administrator. If the findings recommend a change or other corrective action, the QP gets the prescriber's written order before anything changes.

The QP records the corrective action taken, the date, and the person responsible in the client record. The QP informs the client and legally responsible person of any change and updates the individual plan if needed.
If a review is overdue, the QP tells the Administrator, schedules it right away, and documents the reason for the delay. Overdue reviews are reported to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05).
When staff find or cause a medication error, they first make sure the client is safe. They check the client's condition and call 911 if the client appears to be in danger.

Immediately after discovering an error or a significant adverse drug reaction, the staff member reports it by telephone to the client's physician or the dispensing pharmacist. The staff member follows the instructions given and records the name of the person contacted, the time, and the instructions.
The staff member notifies the Administrator or on-call supervisor on the same shift and, as directed, the legally responsible person.

Before the end of the shift, the staff member documents the error in the client record (progress note and medication error form) per 10A NCAC 27G .0206. The documentation states what happened, the medication and dose involved, the time, the client's condition and response, who was notified, and what follow-up was ordered.

Within 1 working day, the Administrator reviews the error, decides the incident level under GOV-06 (Level I, II or III), and files any required report in IRIS or notifies the LME/MCO and others as GOV-06 directs.

The Administrator reviews the cause of each error (for example, labeling, staffing, interruptions, or training gaps) and puts a corrective action in place. This may include retraining by the RN or pharmacist who trained the staff member or suspending the staff member's medication privileges until retraining is complete (MED-02).

When a client refuses a medication, staff do not force it. They calmly ask what the concern is, offer the medication again after a reasonable time if the order allows, and offer help or a different explanation in a form the client understands.
Staff document the refusal on the MAR with the date, time, medication and reason given, and write a progress note describing the circumstances.

Staff notify the prescriber of the refusal as the prescriber has directed. Staff report any refusal of a critical medication, such as an anti-seizure drug, or any pattern of refusals, to the prescriber and the QP on the same day and follow the instructions given.
The QP reviews refusals at each plan review and brings recurring refusals to the person-centered team and the prescriber to address the cause (ASM-02).
Each quarter the Administrator gives the QA/QI Committee a summary of medication errors, adverse reactions, refusals and overdue reviews, including trends and corrective actions (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures reviews are completed every 6 months, reviews every error, assigns the incident level, ensures corrective action and reports trends to the QA/QI Committee.
Maintains the psychotropic review tracking log, schedules reviews, files findings, records corrective action and coordinates with prescribers on refusals.
Report errors, adverse reactions and refusals immediately and document them accurately. Never force or conceal medication.
Conducts the 6-month regimen review, records findings and gives instructions on errors, reactions and refusals.
Reviews summary data and recommends system changes.

documentation: Psychotropic Review Tracking Log
Signed 6-month drug regimen review findings and corrective action in the client record
Medication error report and progress note in the client record (10A NCAC 27G .0206)
Record of the telephone report to the physician or pharmacist (name, time, instructions)
Incident report and IRIS entry when the incident level requires it
MAR entries and progress notes documenting each refusal
Quarterly medication error and refusal summary for the QA/QI Committee

policies.title: Search and Seizure
policies.applies_to: All staff, contractors and volunteers in the home; the Administrator and QP who may authorize a search
policies.purpose: To protect each client's privacy, dignity and property while allowing a limited, lawful response when there is an imminent threat to safety.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27D .0103 Search and Seizure Policy (official checklist item 24; Worksheet p.9). [AGENCY NAME] does not conduct routine or random searches of clients, bedrooms, closets, belongings or vehicles. A client or living space may be searched, and belongings may be seized, only when staff have a reasonable, specific belief that the client has an item that creates an imminent risk of serious harm to the client or others (for example, a weapon, or a substance or object the client could use to cause injury), and a less intrusive step has not resolved the risk. Under 10A NCAC 27D .0103 (official checklist item 25; Worksheet p.9), clients will be free from unwarranted invasion of privacy. Bedrooms are the client's private space. Staff will not enter or search them except as this policy allows, and will knock and wait for permission to enter. Strip searches and body-cavity searches are never permitted. Under 10A NCAC 27D .0103 (official checklist item 26; Worksheet p.9), every search and seizure is documented, including the scope of the search, the reason, the procedures followed, a description of any property seized, and an account of the disposition of the property. Clients and legally responsible persons are told of this policy within 72 hours of admission under 10A NCAC 27D .0201 (see INF-01).

definitions.definition: A purposeful examination of a client's person, clothing, bedroom, personal belongings, or private storage space to find an item.
Taking and holding an item from a client's possession or living space.
A situation in which there is a reasonable belief that serious harm to the client or another person is likely to happen right away unless action is taken.
An item that is illegal for the client to possess, or that creates an imminent safety risk in this setting, such as a weapon or illegal drugs.
The Administrator, QP or designated on-call manager who may approve a search under this policy.

procedures: Staff do not search clients or their living space routinely, as a precaution, or as a form of discipline or punishment. A search is never used because of a general suspicion or to enforce house rules.

When a staff member has a reasonable belief that a client has an item that creates an imminent safety risk, the staff member first tries less intrusive steps: talking with the client, asking the client to hand over or show the item, and offering support.

If those steps do not resolve the risk, the staff member calls the Administrator, QP or on-call manager (the authorizing person) before any search, unless waiting would put someone in immediate danger. In that case, the staff member acts to protect people, calls 911 if needed, and notifies the authorizing person as soon as it is safe.

The authorizing person decides whether the conditions in this policy are met and states the limits of the search (the area to be searched and the item sought). The authorizing person documents the decision.
Whenever possible, the client is told why the search is occurring and is invited to be present and to take part. The explanation is given in a way the client understands.

At least two staff members are present for a search. The search is done in a private place, respectfully, and without unnecessary touching. If a search of the person is unavoidable, it is limited to a pat-down over clothing by a staff member of the gender the client requests when possible. No client is ever asked to remove clothing for a search.
Staff search only the areas covered by the authorized scope. They handle belongings carefully and return them neatly to their places.
Items lawful for the client to possess that pose no ongoing risk are returned to the client right away.

Items that create a continuing safety risk are held only as long as needed. Staff give the client a written, signed receipt listing each item, store it in a secured place, and return it as soon as the risk has passed or when the client leaves the home.

Weapons and illegal items are not returned. The Administrator contacts law enforcement to take them. Prescription medications found in the client's possession are secured under MED-03 and reported to the prescriber.
The Administrator informs the legally responsible person (if any) and the client's case manager or care coordinator of the search and seizure within 24 hours.

The staff member who conducted the search completes the Search and Seizure Record before the end of the shift. It records the date and time, who authorized it and who took part, the scope of the search, the reason, the procedures followed, a description of each item seized, and what happened to each item (returned, secured, or given to law enforcement, with dates).
The Administrator reviews each record within 1 working day, signs it, files it in the client record, and decides whether the event is also reportable under GOV-06.

If a search shows that the client may need a rights restriction or a change in supports, the QP brings the matter to the person-centered team under RRI-01 and RRI-02. A rights restriction is never put in place through this policy alone.
During the 72-hour orientation, staff explain this policy to the client and legally responsible person at the person's level of understanding and document it in the record (INF-01).
The Administrator reports the number and nature of searches and seizures to the QA/QI Committee each quarter and in the periodic rights compliance review (GOV-05, PIR-01).

responsibilities.duty: Authorizes or delegates authorization of searches, reviews and signs every search record, ensures notifications and reports data to the QA/QI Committee.
May authorize a search when the Administrator is unavailable, supports the client afterward and brings any needed plan changes to the team.
Use less intrusive steps first, request authorization, conduct only authorized searches with a second staff member present, and document completely.
Are informed of this policy and notified when a search or seizure occurs.

documentation: Search and Seizure Record (scope, reason, procedures, property seized, disposition) signed by staff and the Administrator
Signed receipt for any property held
Record of notifications to the legally responsible person and case manager
Law enforcement report number when items are turned over
Incident report if reportable under GOV-06
Documentation of the 72-hour explanation of this policy in the client record

policies.title: Periodic Internal Review of Client Rights Compliance
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator, QA/QI Committee and any staff assigned to the review
policies.purpose: To make sure the governing body regularly checks that the Client Rights Rules are being carried out in practice, and that problems are corrected.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27D .0104 Periodic Internal Review (official checklist item 27; Worksheet p.10). The governing body of [AGENCY NAME] will ensure that a compliance review of the implementation of the Client Rights Rules is completed at least every 3 years. The agency will keep the 3 most recent written review reports on file. As agency practice, the first review is done within the first 12 months of operation, and the QA/QI Committee checks rights data each year between reviews. The review is done by a person designated by the governing body who does not have day-to-day responsibility for the area being reviewed. Findings are acted on through a written corrective action plan. The review includes checks of the Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) settings requirements in 42 CFR 441.301(c). If the LME/MCO requires [AGENCY NAME] to form a Client Rights Committee, the agency will report rights incidents as 10A NCAC 27G .0504 requires. Because the core rules in 27G apply to all facilities (10A NCAC 27G .0101), failure to meet them can be grounds for the Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR) to deny or revoke the license, so this review is taken seriously.

definitions.definition: The rules in 10A NCAC 27C, 27D, 27E and 27F, and G.S. 122C Article 3, on client rights, restrictions and interventions, as applicable to this facility.
A planned, documented review by the agency of its own compliance, using record review, observation and interviews.
A written plan listing each problem, the action to be taken, who is responsible and the completion date.
A review of whether the home meets the HCBS settings requirements for privacy, choice, access, visitors, control of schedule and personal space.

procedures: The governing body designates in writing a reviewer for each review (for example, the QA/QI Committee chair, a board member, or an outside consultant) who is not the person primarily responsible for the practices being reviewed. The designation names the reviewer and the review period.

The Administrator keeps a Rights Review Calendar showing the date of the last review and the date the next is due, no later than 3 years after the last. The first review is scheduled within 12 months of opening.

The reviewer builds a review tool covering every area of the Client Rights Rules: informing clients and staff (INF-01, INF-02), search and seizure (SRH-01), social integration and self-governance (SOC-01), rights restrictions and interventions (RRI-01, RRI-02, RES-01, RES-02), prohibited procedures (PRO-01), grievances (IR-02), confidentiality (GOV-03), and personal funds and possessions (LIV-02).

The reviewer examines a sample of client records, including every record with a rights restriction, restrictive intervention or protective device. The reviewer checks that the documentation, consents, authorizations and reviews required by policy are present and current.
The reviewer examines personnel files to confirm that staff signed their client rights acknowledgments and completed required training (INF-02, PER-01, TRN-01).
