The reviewer carries out the HCBS settings checks: whether clients have privacy in bedrooms and bathrooms, lockable bedroom doors where appropriate, control over their schedules and visitors, access to food at any time, freedom to use their own money, ability to personalize their rooms, and access to the community (IR-01).
The reviewer observes the home and routines at different times of day and interviews clients, legally responsible persons and staff. Interviews use communication supports where a client needs them.
The reviewer reviews grievances, incident reports, search and seizure records, and data on rights restrictions and restrictive interventions for the review period (GOV-06, IR-02, SRH-01, RES-02).

Within 30 days after the fieldwork, the reviewer prepares a written report with the scope, methods, findings of compliance and non-compliance, and recommendations. The report is signed and dated by the reviewer.
The Administrator presents the report to the governing body and the QA/QI Committee within 30 days of receiving it.
For each finding of non-compliance, the Administrator prepares a corrective action plan with the action, the person responsible and a due date, and the governing body approves it.

The Administrator follows up on each corrective action and reports progress to the QA/QI Committee at its next quarterly meeting until all items are closed. The reviewer verifies closure and documents it.

The Administrator files the written report and corrective action plan in the Rights Review file and keeps the 3 most recent reports available for DHSR and LME/MCO review. Older reports are kept under the agency's record retention schedule.

If the LME/MCO requires [AGENCY NAME] to form a Client Rights Committee under 10A NCAC 27G .0504, the committee reviews grievances, alleged rights violations and restrictive procedures. The Administrator reports rights incidents to the area director within 30 days and to the area board within 90 days, as that rule requires.
The governing body reviews this policy at each periodic review and revises it when the rules change (REQ-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the review occurs at least every 3 years, designates the reviewer, approves corrective action plans and receives reports.
Schedules reviews, gives the reviewer access to records and staff, prepares corrective action plans and keeps the 3 most recent reports.
Conducts the review, includes the HCBS settings checks, and writes and signs the report.
Tracks corrective actions and reviews rights data between periodic reviews.

documentation: Written designation of reviewer
Rights Review Calendar
Completed review tool and sample list
Signed written review report (3 most recent kept on file)
HCBS settings checklist
Corrective action plan and follow-up verification
Governing body and QA/QI Committee minutes showing review of the report
Rights incident reports to the area director and board, if a Client Rights Committee is required

policies.title: Informing Clients of Rights and Facility Policies
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Qualified Professional, all direct support staff, and every client and legally responsible person
policies.purpose: To make sure every client and legally responsible person is told, in a way they can understand and within required time frames, about client rights and the facility's policies.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27D .0201 Informing Clients (official checklist item 28; Worksheet pp.10-11). [AGENCY NAME] will give each client and legally responsible person a written summary of client rights (G.S. 122C Article 3), and will tell each of them that they may contact Disability Rights North Carolina (the rule text names the Governor's Advocacy Council). Because this is a 24-hour facility, within 72 hours of admission staff will explain, at the person's level of understanding: the house rules and the penalties for breaking them; confidentiality protections (G.S. 122C-52 through -56); how to get a copy of the habilitation plan; the governing body policies on fee assessment and collection, grievance procedures (with contact information and help to use them), suspension and expulsion, and search and seizure. [AGENCY NAME] will give written notice of the right to contact the LME/MCO, the NC Division of Mental Health, Developmental Disabilities and Substance Abuse Services (DMH/DD/SAS), the Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR), the county Department of Social Services (DSS) and Disability Rights North Carolina (10A NCAC 27G .7002). Staff will also explain the facility's behavior management system, any possible rights restrictions, notification after emergency use of restrictive interventions, notification of legally responsible persons, and notification of any rights restrictions. Staff will document in the client record that rights were fully explained. Protected health information is handled under HIPAA (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164).

definitions.definition: A guardian, or a parent of a minor, or another person with legal authority to make decisions for the client.
Explaining information using the words, format, pace, language and communication supports that the person can understand, such as plain language, pictures, interpreters or assistive technology.
The written summary of client rights under G.S. 122C Article 3 and the Client Rights Rules, provided to clients and legally responsible persons.
The positive supports, de-escalation methods and any permitted restrictive interventions that the facility uses to address behavior.

procedures: Before or on the day of admission, the QP gives the client and the legally responsible person the written rights summary and tells them that they may contact Disability Rights North Carolina. The contact information is [PHONE] and [ADDRESS] for the local office or the number on the rights summary.

The QP uses the client's preferred language and communication method. Where needed, staff use plain language, pictures, read-aloud, large print, interpreters or assistive technology (IR-01) and note which supports were used.

Within 72 hours of admission, the QP or Administrator meets with the client and legally responsible person to explain the house rules and the penalties for breaking them. The house rules are written in plain language, and no penalty may be a prohibited procedure (PRO-01) or an unauthorized rights restriction (RRI-01).

At the same meeting, staff explain confidentiality and the limits of confidentiality under G.S. 122C-52 through -56 and the HIPAA notice of privacy practices, and obtain any releases the client or legally responsible person chooses to sign (GOV-03).
Staff explain how to get a copy of the client's habilitation plan and individual plan and how the client and legally responsible person take part in planning (ASM-02).
Staff explain the agency's fee assessment and collection policy, what the client will be charged and how (GOV-07).

Staff explain the grievance procedure (IR-02), including who to give a grievance to, the contact information, how staff will help the client write or voice a grievance, and that the client will not be punished for complaining.
Staff explain the suspension, expulsion and involuntary discharge policy and the discharge notice process (SUS-01, GOV-02).
Staff explain the search and seizure policy, including that there are no routine searches and that searches occur only for an imminent safety risk (SRH-01).

Staff give written notice of the right to contact the LME/MCO, DMH/DD/SAS, DHSR, DSS and Disability Rights North Carolina, with current contact information, as 10A NCAC 27G .7002 requires. A copy is posted where clients can see it.

Staff explain the behavior management system, including positive supports, which rights restrictions or restrictive interventions are possible under the agency's policies, that the legally responsible person will be notified after any emergency use of a restrictive intervention, and that the legally responsible person and client will be notified of any rights restriction (RRI-01, RRI-02, RES-01, RES-02).
Staff check the client's understanding by asking the client to explain key points in their own words or in their own way, and re-explain anything not understood.

The QP documents in the client record, before the end of the 72-hour period, that rights and each required topic were fully explained, noting the date, the people present, the communication supports used and the person's level of understanding. The client, the legally responsible person and the staff member sign the acknowledgment form. If a person declines to sign, the staff member documents that.

If any item cannot be completed within 72 hours (for example, because the client is ill or the legally responsible person is unavailable), the QP documents the reason, completes it as soon as possible, and notifies the Administrator.

The QP repeats the explanation and documents it at least annually, at plan reviews, whenever a policy changes, and whenever a client asks. The QP notifies clients in writing of any change to house rules or policies.
The Administrator reviews a sample of new admission records each quarter to verify timely and complete documentation and reports results to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05, PIR-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the rights summary, house rules and notices are current, posted and given on time, and audits admission records.
Delivers the information within 72 hours at the person's level of understanding and documents it in the record.
Reinforce rights information day to day, help clients use the grievance process and report any rights concerns.
Receives the rights summary and information and takes part in decisions as the client's representative.

documentation: Signed Client Rights Acknowledgment form showing each topic, date, persons present and communication supports used
Copy of the written rights summary given to the client and legally responsible person
Written notice of the right to contact the LME/MCO, DMH/DD/SAS, DHSR, DSS and Disability Rights North Carolina
House rules and penalties acknowledged by the client
Progress note documenting that rights were fully explained, within 72 hours of admission
Records of annual and as-needed re-explanations
Quarterly admission documentation audit

policies.title: Informing Staff of Client Rights
policies.applies_to: All employees, including management, direct support staff, relief and contract staff, and volunteers who have contact with clients
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who works in the home knows and carries out client rights, and that this training is documented.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27D .0202 Informing Staff (official checklist item 29; Worksheet p.11). [AGENCY NAME] will inform all staff of client rights and of the facility's rights policies at hire (as part of orientation, before working alone with clients) and at least annually. Training on rights and confidentiality is part of the required orientation under 10A NCAC 27G .0202. Each staff member will sign an acknowledgment of receipt, kept on file in the personnel file. The date of training and the name of the trainer are documented. All staff are also trained on the rights restriction policy (RRI-01) as required by 10A NCAC 27D .0101.

definitions.definition: The rights of clients under G.S. 122C Article 3 and the Client Rights Rules, including privacy, dignity, freedom from abuse and neglect, confidentiality, and freedom from unauthorized restraint or restriction.
A signed and dated statement by a staff member that they have received, been trained on, and understand the client rights information and policies.
Training on client rights repeated at least once every 12 months.

procedures: The Administrator prepares and keeps current a Client Rights Training packet with the rights summary, the rights policies in this manual (including INF-01, SRH-01, HRM-01, PRO-01, RRI-01, IR-01 and IR-02) and a short test or discussion guide.

On or before a new employee's first day, the Administrator or a designated trainer provides client rights training as part of orientation. New staff do not work alone with clients until they have completed the rights training.

Training covers: the rights in G.S. 122C Article 3; confidentiality and HIPAA; protection from abuse, neglect and exploitation and mandatory reporting; prohibited procedures; privacy and search/seizure; the grievance procedure; respect for choice and dignity; and communication access.

Training includes the agency's policy on rights restrictions and restrictive interventions (RRI-01): which are permitted, who informs the client, due process, who authorizes and reviews, and the appeal process.
Training is delivered in person or through an approved format with a chance to ask questions. The trainer assesses understanding.
After training, each staff member signs and dates the Client Rights Acknowledgment of Receipt form. The trainer signs to confirm the training date and the topics covered.
The Administrator places the signed acknowledgment in the staff member's personnel file within 5 working days and records the training date and the trainer's name on the staff training log (PER-01).
Contract and relief staff and volunteers who have contact with clients receive the same training and sign the same form before working with clients (GOV-09).
The Administrator keeps a Staff Rights Training Tracker showing each person's hire date, orientation date and next annual due date.

At least 30 days before the annual due date, the Administrator schedules the annual refresher training. Refresher content includes any policy changes, lessons from grievances and incidents, and recent rule changes.
Staff who miss or are overdue for annual training are not scheduled to work alone until the training is completed. The Administrator documents the reason and the completion date.
When a rights policy changes, the Administrator informs all staff within 14 days, and staff sign a new acknowledgment.
The Administrator reviews the tracker and a sample of personnel files each quarter and reports completion rates to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures all staff are trained at hire and annually, keeps signed acknowledgments on file and tracks due dates.
Delivers training, checks understanding, signs training records.
Complete training, sign the acknowledgment, follow client rights policies and report concerns.

documentation: Signed Client Rights Acknowledgment of Receipt in each personnel file
Training sign-in sheet with date, topics, trainer's name and signature
Staff Rights Training Tracker
Records of annual refresher training and training on policy changes
Quarterly personnel file audit results

policies.title: Social Integration, Community Inclusion and Client Self-Governance
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Qualified Professional, the Administrator, and all clients of the home (maximum of six adults with developmental disabilities)
policies.purpose: To support clients to build relationships, take part in community life and have a real voice in how the home is run, consistent with HCBS community-living expectations.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27D .0301 Social Integration (official checklist item 30; Worksheet pp.11-12), which applies to this 24-hour facility. [AGENCY NAME] will encourage and facilitate appropriate social interaction among clients and with community non-clients, and will encourage clients to take part. Staff will not prohibit social interaction unless a written restriction is in the client's record, authorized under RRI-01 and RRI-02. Appropriate interaction includes friendly conversation, shared activities, visits with family and friends, community outings, work, volunteering, worship, recreation and relationships that the client chooses, that are respectful and that are safe for all involved. Under 10A NCAC 27G .5603, [AGENCY NAME] will offer choice-based, community-inclusive activities, will support family contact, and will keep the home to no more than six clients. Under 10A NCAC 27G .0208, activities are suitable for adults, and clients help plan them. Integrated employment and day choices are supported through each individual plan. This policy also meets 10A NCAC 27D .0302 Client Self-Governance (official checklist item 31; Worksheet p.12). Clients will have input into how the home is run through house meetings, a client feedback mechanism, client groups and written protocols for communication between clients and staff, and staff and clients will be trained and supported to use them.

definitions.definition: Meaningful participation in community life, including relationships and activities with people who are not clients or paid staff.
A person who does not live in or receive services from the home, such as a family member, friend, neighbor, co-worker or community member.
A client's and clients' collective say in decisions about the home's routines, activities, rules, menus and improvements.
A regular meeting where clients and staff discuss the home, make plans and raise concerns.
A rights restriction documented in the client record and authorized under the agency's rights restriction policy (RRI-01, RRI-02).

procedures: During assessment and at each plan review, the QP asks the client (and, when the client wishes, family or the legally responsible person) about the client's interests, friendships, family contacts, faith, work and community preferences, and records them in the individual plan (ASM-02).

The individual plan identifies supports and goals for community participation and for employment and day choices, including integrated competitive employment where the client chooses it. The QP coordinates with the case manager or care coordinator and any day or employment provider.

Each week, staff and the client plan at least one community-based activity chosen by the client, and the home offers a variety of choice-based activities (such as shopping, dining out, faith activities, recreation, classes, volunteering and visits) in line with 10A NCAC 27G .5603. Activities are age-appropriate for adults and are not limited to group outings if the client prefers something else.
Clients help plan activities and menus at house meetings and individually. Staff record client choices and the activities actually offered and done.

Staff support family contact: they help clients call, write, video chat or visit, share the annual progress report with the legally responsible person, and welcome families and friends to the home at times the client chooses, unless a written restriction applies.

Staff do not prohibit or discourage a client's contact or interaction with others for convenience, as a consequence, or as punishment. If a client's safety requires a limit, the limit must be a written rights restriction authorized and reviewed under RRI-01 and RRI-02 and placed in the client record, and the least restrictive alternative applies (LRA-01).
Staff help clients arrange transportation, communication supports and the support they need to take part, and transport clients safely under GOV-04.

Staff teach and model respectful interaction and, where a client wants, help them learn social skills, resolve conflicts and set personal boundaries. Staff respond promptly to bullying, harassment, abuse or exploitation of or by a client (HRM-01).

The Administrator and QP set up house meetings at least monthly. Each client may attend and take part, with support. Meetings are held at times that suit clients and are led or co-led by a client where possible.

At each meeting, clients may raise ideas and concerns about activities, menus, house rules, chores, visitors and house improvements. Staff write down each item, who will follow up and the due date, and report back at the next meeting.

The home provides ways for clients to give feedback at any time, apart from meetings, such as a suggestion box, one-to-one conversations with the QP, picture-based or easy-read feedback forms, and help to contact a person of the client's choosing. This is separate from, and does not replace, the grievance procedure (IR-02).

Clients who want to may form a client group, for example a house council or a self-advocacy group, and may link with local or statewide self-advocacy organizations. The Administrator provides a meeting space and a staff liaison who supports without controlling the group.

The written meeting protocol states how meetings are scheduled and announced, how clients speak and are heard, how decisions are made, how minutes are kept in accessible form, and how requests for changes get an answer from the Administrator within 14 days.

At orientation (within 72 hours of admission) and at least annually, staff and clients are trained on self-governance: how house meetings and the feedback process work, how to take part, and how staff will support them (INF-01, PER-01). Staff learn how to support choice and speak with clients as equals.

The Administrator reviews meeting minutes, the activity log and community participation data each quarter, looks for clients who are isolated, and reports to the QA/QI Committee with improvements planned (GOV-05). The periodic rights compliance review includes these items (PIR-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures community-inclusive activities and self-governance mechanisms are in place, answers client requests and reports data to the QA/QI Committee.
Identifies each client's goals and preferences, coordinates community, employment and day supports and ensures restrictions on social contact are only by written authorized restriction.
Offer and support choices, help clients take part in the community, facilitate house meetings and record outcomes.
Take part in planning and meetings as they choose, and may form groups and give feedback.

documentation: Individual plan sections on community participation, employment and day choices
Weekly activity plans and activity log showing client choice and participation
House meeting schedule, sign-in sheets and minutes in accessible format, with follow-up items
Client feedback records and responses
Documentation of family contact support and annual progress reports sent to legally responsible person
Written restriction authorizations (if any) limiting contact, with review dates
Training records for staff and clients on self-governance
Quarterly community participation review for the QA/QI Committee

policies.title: Informed Consent and Decision-Making Support
policies.applies_to: All clinical and direct care staff, the Qualified Professional (QP), the Program Director, and any person who obtains, records or relies on a client's consent
policies.purpose: To make sure every adult served by [AGENCY NAME] is given the information needed to make his or her own decisions, that consent is voluntary, written where required, time-limited and revocable, and that every consent, refusal and withdrawal is documented in the client record.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27D .0303 Informed Consent (Worksheet item 32). [AGENCY NAME] presumes that every adult client can make decisions. We do not provide a service, intervention, medication-related treatment or release of information that requires consent without valid consent from the client or, where the client has one, the legally responsible person (LRP). The definition of 'client' in the licensure rules includes the LRP for the purpose of consent. (1) INFORMING: Before asking for consent, staff explain in plain language, at the client's communication level and in the client's preferred language or mode: the benefits, the risks, the alternatives (including doing nothing), how long the consent is valid, and how to withdraw it. (2) WRITTEN CONSENT: Written consent is obtained for planned interventions as required by G.S. 122C-57(f) and Subchapter 27E .0100, and written consent is required for Antabuse and Depo-Provera when they are used for non-FDA-approved purposes. Consent for a planned restrictive intervention may not be valid for more than six months. This home does not permit planned restrictive interventions (see RRI-01), so this limit applies only if the governing body later adopts one by formal action. (3) RIGHT TO CONSENT OR REFUSE: Each client has the right to consent to or refuse treatment under G.S. 122C-57(d). Refusal is never used as the sole ground for termination or discharge except as the statute states. Any proposed discharge after a refusal goes to the Administrator and is handled under GOV-02 and SUS-01. (4) LRP AND SUPPORTED DECISION-MAKING: Where an LRP gives consent, staff still seek the individual's own assent or preference, use supported decision-making (plain-language explanation, visuals, extra time, a trusted supporter of the client's choice) and record the client's views. A client's objection is brought to the QP and the LRP before the activity proceeds. (5) DOCUMENTATION: Every consent, refusal, assent and withdrawal is documented in the client record, dated and authenticated.

definitions.definition: A voluntary, documented agreement given after the person has been told the benefits, risks and alternatives, how long the consent lasts and how to withdraw it.
A guardian or other person with legal authority to consent for an adult client, as shown by court or other legal documentation kept in the record.
The client's own agreement or preference, sought and recorded even when an LRP has legal authority to consent.
Helping a person understand choices and express a decision using accommodations and trusted supporters, without substituting the supporter's judgment.
An intervention that restricts a client's movement or rights and is written into a plan in advance. Not permitted in this home unless the governing body adopts it by formal action (see RRI-01).
A dated and authenticated entry in the client record.

procedures: At admission, the QP identifies whether each client has a guardian or other LRP, obtains a copy of the legal authority (guardianship order or other document) and files it in the record. If there is none, the client is treated as his or her own decision-maker.

Before any consent is requested, the staff member responsible (QP for treatment, habilitation and plan matters; Administrator for fees, admission and releases of information; the medication-trained staff member working with the prescriber for medication matters) prepares a plain-language explanation and any visuals the client needs.
The staff member meets with the client, and the LRP if any, in a private setting with enough time and, when needed, an interpreter, communication device or supporter chosen by the client.

The staff member explains the benefits, risks and alternatives, how long the consent will be valid and how to withdraw it. The client is asked to say back or show his or her understanding in his or her own way. Questions are answered and the client is told that he or she may say no.
The client's own decision is recorded. If an LRP consents, the staff member records the client's assent, objection or preference separately and the supports used.

For planned interventions under G.S. 122C-57(f) or Subchapter 27E .0100, written consent is obtained on the agency consent form before the intervention begins. The form shows the intervention, the reasons, the expected duration and the date the consent expires. A consent for a planned restrictive intervention is never written for more than six months.

Before Antabuse or Depo-Provera is used for a non-FDA-approved purpose, the QP confirms that a prescriber's written order exists and that the client or LRP has signed a specific written consent for that use. Staff do not administer the drug without it. The QP notifies the Administrator the same day.

The consent form shows the effective date, the expiration date or the plan-review date at which consent will be revisited, and the signature, date and relationship of each signer. Staff give the client or LRP a copy.

Each consent is reviewed at every person-centered plan review (see ASM-02) and whenever the service, medication or risk changes. The QP obtains renewed consent before the earlier consent expires. A consent with no renewal on file is treated as expired.

If a client or LRP withdraws consent, in any form including words, behavior or gesture, staff stop the activity unless stopping would create imminent danger. Staff notify the QP the same shift, and the QP documents the withdrawal and meets with the client and LRP within [NUMBER] business days.

If a client refuses a service or treatment, staff respect the refusal, offer alternatives, explain consequences in plain language, and document the refusal. Staff notify the QP the same day. Medication refusals are also handled under MED-04.
Refusal alone is never the sole ground for discharge or for any adverse action. If other concerns exist, the Administrator documents them and follows GOV-02, SUS-01 and the notice requirements.

If a client's ability to understand appears to change, the QP arranges an assessment of decision-making support needs, tries more supports first, and refers to the LME/MCO care coordinator and, if needed, to the LRP or guardianship process. The agency never self-declares a client incompetent.
Releases of protected health information require a separate signed authorization consistent with 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164 and GOV-03. A consent for treatment is not a release of information.
The QP documents every consent, assent, refusal and withdrawal in the client record, dated and authenticated, and files the signed form in the consent section.

The Program Director audits at least [NUMBER] records per quarter for current consents, expiration dates, LRP documentation and documented assent, and reports results to the QA/QI Committee (see GOV-05).
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (see PER-01 and INF-02).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, makes sure forms are available, decides on any discharge following a refusal, and reports audit results to the governing body.
Obtains and documents consent for plan, treatment and interventions, tracks expiration dates, seeks the client's assent, and arranges decision-making supports.
Support clients' understanding, respect refusals and withdrawals, and report them to the QP the same shift.
Provides decisions within the scope of legal authority, together with the client's own views.
Reviews quarterly audit results and corrective actions.

documentation: Signed written consent forms with effective and expiration dates
Copy of guardianship or other LRP authority
Record of the information given and the supports used
Documented assent, objection, refusal or withdrawal
Prescriber's order and specific consent for Antabuse or Depo-Provera for non-FDA-approved use
Quarterly consent audit results

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27D .0304 Protection From Harm, Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation
policies.title: Protection From Harm, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation: Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors, the Administrator and the governing body
policies.purpose: To protect every client from harm, abuse, neglect and exploitation, and to make sure that every alleged or suspected incident is stopped, documented and reported to the County Department of Social Services (DSS) and all other required parties.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27D .0304 Protection From Harm, Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation (Worksheet item 33) and the reporting requirement of 10A NCAC 27D .0101 (Worksheet item 36). [AGENCY NAME] protects each client from harm under G.S. 122C-66. Abuse and neglect are defined and prohibited as set out in 10A NCAC 27C .0102 and in the definitions below. Exploitation is also prohibited. (1) PROHIBITION: Staff, volunteers and contractors may not abuse, neglect or exploit any client, and may not use any procedure prohibited by PRO-01, including corporal punishment. (2) REPORTING OF ALL INSTANCES: ALL alleged or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a client is documented and reported to the County DSS in the county where the client lives, because there is reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult may need protective services (G.S. 108A Article 6; 10A NCAC 27G .0610). Reports are also made to the Health Care Personnel Registry, the LME/MCO and, as required, law enforcement. No staff member may decide that an allegation is 'unfounded' or 'minor' before reporting. (3) INCIDENT LEVELS: Alleged abuse, neglect or exploitation is also an incident under GOV-06. Sexual assault, death, permanent impairment or a threat to safety is a Level III incident under 10A NCAC 27G .0602. (4) STAFF TRAINING: Staff are trained at orientation and at least annually on recognizing, preventing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation (see PER-01). (5) EMPLOYEE CONDUCT: Any employee who abuses, neglects or exploits a client, who fails to report, or who retaliates against a person who reports, is subject to discipline up to and including dismissal and to referral to authorities. (6) TRANSACTIONS WITH CLIENTS: No employee, volunteer, board member or relative of any of them may sell goods or services to, or buy goods or services from, a client, borrow money from or lend money to a client, accept gifts beyond [DOLLAR AMOUNT] nominal value, use a client's property or funds for personal purposes, or employ a client for private work. Client purchases from community vendors are not covered by this restriction. Client money is handled under LIV-02. (7) USE-OF-FORCE GUIDELINES: Staff may not use physical force on a client as discipline, for convenience, or to compel compliance. Seclusion, planned restraint and pain-based techniques are not allowed (see RRI-01 and PRO-01). Staff respond to escalating behavior with de-escalation, redirection, space and calling the QP. If a person faces imminent serious physical harm and no other option exists, staff use only the minimum non-injurious action needed to protect the person, such as stepping between or leaving with others, and call 911. Any physical contact of this kind is reported as an incident the same shift, reviewed by the Administrator within [NUMBER] business days, and addressed with the client and the staff member.

definitions.definition: As defined in 10A NCAC 27C .0102 and applied by this agency: the infliction of physical pain or injury, unreasonable confinement, or mental or emotional harm, including verbal degradation or intimidation, by a caregiver or other person, and sexual contact of any kind.
As defined in 10A NCAC 27C .0102 and applied by this agency: failure to provide the care, supervision, food, shelter, medical care or services a client needs to avoid harm.
Improper use of a client, or of the client's funds, property or resources, for the advantage or benefit of another person.
The state registry of findings against health care personnel, to which staff-related allegations are reported (see HCP-01).
As defined in 10A NCAC 27G .0602, includes death, sexual assault, permanent impairment or a threat to safety.
A situation in which a person is about to suffer serious physical harm.

procedures: At hire and before working alone, each employee receives a copy of this policy and signs an acknowledgment. Training on recognizing, preventing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation is completed at orientation and refreshed at least annually, and documented in the personnel file (see PER-01).

Staff recognize indicators: unexplained injuries, fear of a person, sudden behavior change, missing money or belongings, signs of neglect (hunger, poor hygiene, untreated illness) and disclosures by the client.

Any staff member, volunteer or contractor who sees, suspects or is told of possible abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately makes the client safe, separates the client from any alleged perpetrator, and gets medical care or calls 911 if needed.

The staff member notifies the Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]) or the on-call administrator immediately. The staff member must not first investigate, question witnesses at length, or wait for approval. If the Administrator is alleged to be involved, the staff member goes directly to DSS and the governing body.

Immediately, and in any case on the same day, the Administrator or the staff member makes the report to the County DSS Adult Protective Services in the county where the client lives ([COUNTY DSS PHONE]) and, if a crime may have occurred, law enforcement ([PHONE]). After hours, the report is made to the county's on-call line or law enforcement. The reporter records the name of the person taking the report, the date and the time.

An alleged employee perpetrator is removed from direct client contact and from the schedule pending review. The Administrator documents the action. Where the allegation is against a staff member, it is also reported to the Health Care Personnel Registry as required (see HCP-01).

The Administrator reports to the client's LME/MCO care coordinator and Tailored Plan, and notifies the LRP, and enters the incident in IRIS and completes the required incident reports within the timelines in GOV-06. Where DHSR or another regulator requires notification, the Administrator makes it.
A written incident report is completed by the end of the shift. It describes facts only, names those involved and witnesses, injuries, action taken and everyone notified, with dates and times.

The Administrator preserves evidence (photographs of injuries by medical staff, clothing, schedules, logs) and cooperates fully with DSS, law enforcement, DHSR and the LME/MCO. Staff do not discuss the case with anyone not entitled to know, in line with 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164 and GOV-03.

The Administrator conducts an internal review within [NUMBER] business days and determines whether neglect or abuse by staff occurred, without delaying or replacing DSS or law enforcement action. Findings and corrective actions are documented.
The QP meets with the client and LRP as soon as practicable to explain what is happening, arrange counseling or medical follow-up, and update the person-centered plan and safety supports.

No one is punished for reporting in good faith. Retaliation against a client, employee or volunteer who reports is grounds for dismissal. The Administrator checks within 30 days that no retaliation has occurred and documents the check.

Employees found to have abused, neglected or exploited a client, to have failed to report, or to have violated the transaction rule, are disciplined, up to and including dismissal. The Administrator documents the action in the personnel file and refers to the registry or authorities as required.

Staff who see a violation of the transaction rule (buying, selling, borrowing or lending involving a client) report it to the Administrator. The Administrator reviews it as possible exploitation and reports to DSS when appropriate.

The Administrator logs every allegation, report date, agencies notified, outcome and corrective action in the Abuse/Neglect/Exploitation Log. The QA/QI Committee reviews the log at least quarterly for patterns (see GOV-05).

Clients are told at admission and annually, in plain language and in the client's communication mode, how to report mistreatment to any staff member, the Administrator, DSS, the LME/MCO and the Governor's Advocacy Council (see INF-01 and IR-02).

responsibilities.duty: Protect clients, never abuse, neglect or exploit them, report all suspicions immediately, and follow the transaction rule.

Makes or confirms the DSS, law enforcement, registry, LME/MCO and IRIS reports, removes alleged staff perpetrators from client contact, conducts the internal review, imposes discipline and keeps the log.
Supports the client, notifies the LRP, updates the plan, and completes training.
Adopts this policy, receives quarterly summaries and acts on findings.
Reviews the log, trends and corrective actions.

documentation: Staff acknowledgment of this policy and training records
Incident reports and IRIS entries
Record of each DSS, law enforcement, Health Care Personnel Registry and LME/MCO report with date, time and name of person taking the report
Abuse/Neglect/Exploitation Log
Internal review findings and discipline records
Notification to LRP and client follow-up notes

policies.title: Least Restrictive Alternative
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Qualified Professional, the Program Director and the governing body
policies.purpose: To make sure every client receives services in the least restrictive and most appropriate setting and by the least restrictive methods, with choice, dignity and respect, and that restrictive interventions are never used except as a last resort.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27E .0101 Least Restrictive Alternative (Worksheet item 34). [AGENCY NAME] delivers services in the least restrictive and most appropriate settings and by the least restrictive and most appropriate methods. We (1) promote coping and engagement skills and alternatives to injurious behavior; (2) offer meaningful choices of activities and share decision-making and control with each client; (3) treat each client with dignity and respect at all times; and (4) use restrictive interventions only as a last resort, only when less restrictive options have failed or cannot work in time, and only by trained staff. This home does not allow seclusion, isolation time-out, planned restraint or behavior-control protective devices (see RRI-01). Because the home is a Medicaid home and community-based setting, any limit on a client's freedom, choice, access or privacy is a rights restriction that must go through RRI-01 and RRI-02 and the federal home and community-based settings rule (42 CFR 441.301(c)). Restrictive alternatives are reviewed at each plan review.

definitions.definition: The setting, method or support that gives the client the most freedom and control while still meeting the client's needs and keeping the client and others safe.
An action that limits a client's movement or freedom of choice, such as restraint, seclusion or isolation time-out. Not permitted in this home.
Any limit on a client's rights or freedoms beyond those that apply to all members of the household in the community. See RRI-01.
Use only after all less restrictive options have been tried and failed, or would clearly not work in time to prevent imminent serious harm.
Skills that help a person manage distress, communicate needs and take part in meaningful activity without harm.

procedures: At admission and at each plan review, the QP reviews the client's setting, supports and routines, and asks the client and LRP whether each current limit on freedom, choice, privacy or access is needed.

The QP and the person-centered planning team identify what the client wants and needs, including meaningful daily activity, work, community and relationships, and write them into the plan (see ASM-02).

For every client with behavior that may harm self or others, the QP completes or obtains a functional assessment of what the behavior communicates and builds a proactive plan: coping and engagement skills, communication supports, sensory and environmental changes, and positive reinforcement.

Staff offer meaningful choices daily (meals, activities, schedule, bedroom decor, visitors, outings) and record choices offered and made for clients who have choice-limiting conditions. Staff do not substitute their own preferences for the client's.

When behavior escalates, staff follow the client's plan and use the least restrictive response first: calm voice, offering space, redirection, offering a choice, changing the environment and calling the QP.

Staff do not use restrictive interventions as discipline, for staff convenience or because of low staffing. If staffing is not adequate to meet clients' needs, staff tell the Administrator immediately.
If a person faces imminent danger and nothing less restrictive works, staff protect safety with the minimum action needed, call 911, and follow HRM-01 and GOV-06.

Any proposal to limit a right or freedom, for one client or for the household, is written down by the QP with the reason, the less restrictive alternatives tried, the time limit and a review date, and goes through RRI-01 and RRI-02. No limit is imposed informally.

At every plan review the QP records the review of restrictive alternatives: whether any restriction was used, what less restrictive options were tried, what supports can reduce or end the restriction, and the client's own view.
The QP ends any restriction as soon as it is no longer needed and documents the date and reason.

The Program Director reviews incident reports and rights restrictions at least monthly for signs that the least restrictive alternative was not followed, and reports to the QA/QI Committee quarterly (see GOV-05).
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually, including on de-escalation and engagement skills (see PER-01 and TRN-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures adequate staffing and resources so restrictive methods are never used for convenience, and approves any restriction through RRI-02.
Completes the review of restrictive alternatives at each plan review, builds proactive plans and reviews incidents monthly.
Offer choices, use the least restrictive response, and report any proposed restriction.
Reviews quarterly data and corrective actions.

documentation: Person-centered plan showing choices, supports and review of restrictive alternatives at each review
Written restriction documentation, if any, with less restrictive alternatives tried and review dates
Daily choice and activity notes
Incident reports
Monthly review notes and quarterly QA/QI reports
Staff training records

policies.title: Prohibited Procedures
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors and governing body members
policies.purpose: To clearly prohibit procedures that cause pain or harm to clients, so that no client is subject to them under any circumstances.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27E .0102 Prohibited Procedures (Worksheet item 35). The following are prohibited at [AGENCY NAME] and may not be used for any reason, including discipline, behavior control, convenience or staffing: (1) corporal punishment (G.S. 122C-59); (2) contingent painful body contact; (3) substances that induce painful bodily reactions, excluding Antabuse when prescribed with written consent under CON-01; (4) electric shock, excluding electroconvulsive therapy administered by a medical professional in a health care setting; (5) insulin shock; (6) unpleasant-tasting foodstuffs; (7) contingent application of noxious substances or stimuli, such as loud noise, bad smells or splashing with water; and (8) any potentially physically painful procedure or stimulus used to reduce a behavior, excluding injections prescribed by a physician. In addition, the governing body of [AGENCY NAME] also prohibits as agency policy: withholding food, water, sleep, medication, toileting, or access to personal belongings, or required activity, as punishment; forced or excessive exercise; humiliation, shaming or threats; group punishment; mechanical and chemical restraint; locking a client in a room or area; and any technique that restricts breathing or circulation. Staff who use or knowingly permit a prohibited procedure are subject to discipline up to dismissal and are reported under HRM-01.

definitions.definition: The infliction of physical pain or discomfort on a client as punishment, prohibited by G.S. 122C-59.
Applied in response to a client's behavior in order to change that behavior.
Something unpleasant or harmful, such as a loud noise, bad smell or splashing water, used to reduce behavior.
Use of medication to control behavior or restrict movement when it is not a standard treatment for the person's condition and is not approved by the client or LRP.
A device, such as straps or cuffs, used to restrict a client's movement.

procedures: At hire and before working alone, each employee, volunteer and contractor reads this policy and signs that he or she understands that these procedures are prohibited. The Administrator keeps the signed acknowledgment.

Training on this policy is provided at orientation and at least annually, with examples of each prohibited procedure, including everyday examples such as splashing water, using a hot sauce or taste aversive, or an unplanned 'consequence' (see PER-01 and TRN-01).
Behavior support plans written by or for [AGENCY NAME] are reviewed by the QP before use to confirm no prohibited procedure is included. The QP signs the review.

Staff never use, suggest or allow a prohibited procedure. A staff member who sees a prohibited procedure stops it if safe to do so, makes sure the client is safe, and notifies the Administrator immediately.
Any alleged use is reported under HRM-01 to County DSS and others, and documented as an incident under GOV-06 on the same shift.
Medication such as Antabuse is only used with a prescriber's order and the client's or LRP's written informed consent under CON-01 and is not used as punishment.
The Administrator investigates any alleged violation and removes the staff member from client contact pending review. Confirmed violations lead to discipline up to and including dismissal.

Clients and LRPs are told that these procedures are prohibited as part of the rights information given at admission (see INF-01). Clients may report any such act to any staff member, the Administrator, DSS, the LME/MCO or the Governor's Advocacy Council.
The governing body reviews this policy at least annually and records any additional prohibited procedures it adopts in the manual review log (see REQ-01).
The QA/QI Committee reviews incidents quarterly for any use of prohibited procedures and tracks corrective actions (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, investigates alleged violations, disciplines staff and reports as required.
Reviews behavior plans and trains staff.
Never use a prohibited procedure and report any use immediately.
Adopts this policy and any additional prohibitions, and reviews them annually.

documentation: Staff, volunteer and contractor acknowledgments of this policy
Training records
QP review of behavior plans
Incident reports and abuse/neglect log entries for any alleged violation
Investigation findings and discipline records
Annual governing body review record

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27D .0101 Policy on Rights Restrictions and Interventions
policies.title: Rights Restrictions and Restrictive Interventions: Governing Body Policy
policies.applies_to: The governing body, Administrator, Qualified Professional, Program Director and all staff
policies.purpose: To state the governing body's policy on restricting client rights and on restrictive interventions, so that all staff keep clients safe with dignity and respect, restrict rights only through a documented process, and use medicines that carry serious risk only with safeguards.
policies.policy: This policy implements G.S. 122C-59, 122C-65 and 122C-66 and meets 10A NCAC 27D .0101 Policy on Rights Restrictions and Interventions (Worksheet items 35a, 37, 38, 39, 40 and 41). It is provided to all staff at hire and whenever it changes. [ITEM 35a] The guidelines and procedures below ensure that any restriction of a client's rights and any intervention protects safety, dignity and respect. [ITEM 40 - PERMITTED INTERVENTIONS AND CURRICULUM] The governing body does NOT permit any restrictive intervention in this home. Seclusion, isolation time-out, planned physical restraint and protective devices used for behavior control are explicitly NOT allowed. Because none are permitted, no restrictive-intervention training curriculum is approved or used. Staff are trained in de-escalation and non-physical support only (see TRN-01). If the governing body ever decides to permit any intervention, it may do so only by written resolution that names the intervention, the approved training curriculum and who is trained, and RRI-02, RES-01, RES-02, DEV-01 and TRN-01 must be completed before use. [ITEM 38 - PROHIBITED INTERVENTIONS] In addition to the interventions listed in PRO-01, the following are prohibited in this home: seclusion, isolation time-out, planned physical restraint, mechanical restraint, chemical restraint, and protective devices used for behavior control. [ITEM 41 - WHO INFORMS CLIENTS] The Program Director/Qualified Professional is the position responsible for informing each client and LRP of any restriction that may be used, at admission and whenever a restriction is proposed. [ITEM 39 - 24-HOUR FACILITY] This is a 24-hour facility. Staff may not restrict a client's rights except through a documented restriction under G.S. 122C-62(b) or (d), documented as required by G.S. 122C-62(e). No staff member may restrict a right informally, by house rule, on his or her own, or for staff convenience. [ITEM 37 - HIGH-RISK MEDICATIONS] [AGENCY NAME] follows the safeguards below for prescribing and monitoring medications that present a serious risk, with special focus on neuroleptic (antipsychotic) medications: the prescriber documents the reasons for the medication; the client or LRP gives informed consent (see CON-01); the medication is reviewed regularly; the client is monitored for adverse effects; and a full review is done at least every six months. Medications are never used as punishment, for staff convenience or as a substitute for habilitation. Services are delivered under the least restrictive alternative (see LRA-01).

definitions.definition: A documented limit placed on a client's rights in a 24-hour facility, allowed only under G.S. 122C-62(b) or (d) and documented under G.S. 122C-62(e).
Seclusion, physical restraint, isolation time-out or the use of a protective device for behavior control. Not permitted in this home.
Confining a client alone in a room or area from which the client cannot leave.
An antipsychotic medication, which carries risks such as movement disorders, metabolic effects and sedation.
A staff member who meets the QP requirements for developmental disabilities services and is designated by the Administrator.

procedures: The governing body adopts this policy by written resolution and reviews it at least annually. The Administrator records the date in the manual control log (see REQ-01).
The Administrator gives this policy to every employee at hire, collects a signed acknowledgment, and re-issues it within [NUMBER] days of any change (see INF-02).

At admission, the Program Director/QP tells each client and LRP, in plain language, that this home does not use seclusion, isolation time-out, planned restraint or protective devices for behavior control, and explains how a rights restriction is proposed, reviewed and appealed. This is documented in the record (see INF-01).

Staff identify potential rights restrictions that might arise, such as limits on visitors, phone calls, access to food, or money. Staff do not apply any limit until the QP has documented it as required below.

A rights restriction may be proposed only by the QP, only for a specific reason tied to the client's health, safety or habilitation, and only after less restrictive options have been tried (see LRA-01).

The QP writes the restriction in the client record as required by G.S. 122C-62(e): the right, reason, less restrictive alternatives tried, duration, review date and who was informed. The Executive Director gives written permission as set out in RRI-02 before the restriction takes effect.

The Program Director/QP informs the client and LRP before the restriction starts, gives written notice, explains the appeal process in RRI-02 and the right to contact the Governor's Advocacy Council, and documents this.

If a restriction is applied in an urgent situation to prevent imminent harm, the QP is told immediately and documents the restriction as above within one business day. It is time-limited and ends when the danger ends.

No restriction may be imposed on all residents as a house rule if it takes away a right. House rules are reviewed by the QP and approved by the Administrator to confirm they are consistent with client rights (see IR-01).

If imminent danger occurs, staff do not use any prohibited or non-permitted restrictive intervention. They use de-escalation, call 911 and follow HRM-01 and GOV-06. A physical intervention that occurs despite this policy is treated as a reportable incident and reviewed under RRI-02.

For each client prescribed a neuroleptic or other high-risk medication, the QP confirms before the first dose that the prescriber's reason is documented and that informed consent from the client or LRP is on file (see CON-01).

Medication-trained staff give medication only as prescribed (see MED-02). Staff watch for and record adverse effects, such as stiffness, tremor, restlessness, drowsiness, weight change and abnormal movements, and report them to the prescriber the same day.

The prescriber or consulting clinician performs a periodic review of each high-risk medication, including abnormal-movement screening and relevant lab or health monitoring as ordered. The QP schedules these and records results.

At least every six months the QP arranges a documented review with the prescriber of continued need, dose, side effects and alternatives for each high-risk medication, and reports the date to the Program Director (see MED-04).
The Program Director reviews rights restrictions and high-risk medication reviews at least quarterly and reports to the QA/QI Committee (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts and reviews this policy, and is the only body that may elect to permit any restrictive intervention.
Distributes the policy, grants written permission for 24-hour restrictions as set out in RRI-02, and enforces the prohibitions.
Informs clients and LRPs of restrictions, documents restrictions under G.S. 122C-62(e), and monitors high-risk medication safeguards.
Do not restrict rights or use restrictive interventions, report concerns and monitor for medication side effects.
Documents reasons, obtains consent, monitors and reviews high-risk medications at least every six months.

documentation: Governing body resolution and annual review record
Staff acknowledgments
Documentation of information given to clients and LRPs at admission
Written rights restriction records under G.S. 122C-62(e) with Executive Director's written permission
Prescriber justification, informed consent, side-effect monitoring and six-month review records for high-risk medications
Incident reports and quarterly QA/QI reports

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27D .0101 Policy on Rights Restrictions and Interventions
policies.title: Due Process, Authorization, Review and Debriefing
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, Qualified Professional, Program Director, Client Rights Committee (where required) and all staff
policies.purpose: To give clients due process when a restriction is proposed or imposed, to name who authorizes and reviews restrictions, to protect the client's physical and psychological well-being, and to debrief and plan so any future use is reduced.
policies.policy: This policy meets 10A NCAC 27D .0101 (Worksheet items 42, 43, 44, 45 and 46). Because RRI-01 does not permit restrictive interventions in this home, this policy applies in full to (a) every documented rights restriction, (b) any physical intervention that occurs in an emergency despite RRI-01, and (c) any intervention that the governing body formally elects to permit in the future. [ITEM 42 - DUE PROCESS] A client who refuses a restriction or restrictive intervention is afforded due process: written notice, a stated reason, a review of the decision by someone other than the person who proposed it, and an appeal. The appeal process is: the client or LRP may ask the Administrator for a review within [NUMBER] days, who decides within [NUMBER] business days; if the matter is not resolved, the client may use the agency grievance process in IR-02, ask the LME/MCO care coordinator or Tailored Plan for help, ask the Client Rights Committee for review where the LME/MCO requires one (10A NCAC 27G .0504), and contact the Governor's Advocacy Council at any time. Refusal alone does not result in discharge (see CON-01). [ITEM 43 - WRITTEN PERMISSION] The Executive Director/Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) is the position that gives written permission for any 24-hour restriction, after the QP's written recommendation. [ITEM 44 - REVIEW] The Qualified Professional/Program Director is designated to review every use of a restriction or intervention, and the QA/QI Committee reviews data quarterly. The Client Rights Committee reviews restrictive procedures where the LME/MCO requires it. [ITEM 45 - WELL-BEING] The client's physical and psychological well-being is considered before, during and after any intervention, as set out in the procedures below, including review of health history or a health assessment at admission for conditions that raise risk. [ITEM 46 - DEBRIEFING AND PLANNING] After any use, staff debrief with the client, the LRP and staff, plan to reduce future use, and document and communicate the outcome to the client and LRP. If the governing body ever permits an emergency intervention, the standard in 10A NCAC 27E .0104 applies: use only for imminent danger and never for convenience or staffing; staff may authorize for up to 15 minutes, after which a professional must authorize; adult orders last no more than 4 hours; the client is checked every 15 minutes and monitored for 30 minutes afterward; and each use is documented, notified, logged and reviewed quarterly.

definitions.definition: Notice of a proposed restriction, a stated reason, a review and a route of appeal before or promptly after the restriction takes effect.
A restriction on a client's rights that applies in the 24-hour residence and is documented under G.S. 122C-62.
A structured conversation after an event with the client, LRP and staff about what happened, what each person felt and what can be done differently.
A committee that reviews grievances, alleged rights violations and restrictive procedures where the LME/MCO requires it.
A situation in which a person is about to suffer serious physical harm.

procedures: The QP proposes any restriction in writing to the Administrator, stating the right, the reason, the less restrictive alternatives tried, the duration and the review date (see RRI-01 and LRA-01).
The QP gives the client and LRP written notice of the proposed restriction in plain language and communication mode, explains the reason, and records the client's response, including refusal.

The Administrator reviews the proposal within [NUMBER] business days. If approved, the Administrator signs the written permission before the restriction starts, except in an urgent situation, when it is signed within one business day. No 24-hour restriction takes effect without the Administrator's written permission.

If the client or LRP refuses or objects, the restriction does not proceed on the basis of staff preference alone. The Administrator meets with the client and LRP and re-reviews, and the QP seeks a less restrictive alternative. The client is told of the appeal route and the Governor's Advocacy Council.

If the matter is not resolved, the client or LRP may file a grievance (see IR-02), request review by the Client Rights Committee where the LME/MCO requires one, or contact the LME/MCO care coordinator. The restriction is reviewed within [NUMBER] business days of any appeal, and the outcome is given in writing.

At admission the QP reviews the health history and any health assessment for conditions that raise risk (for example heart or breathing problems, seizures, osteoporosis, pregnancy, obesity, history of trauma, medications that affect balance or breathing) and records them in the plan and on the face sheet so all staff know them.

Before any restriction or intervention, staff consider the client's physical condition and emotional state, trauma history, sensory needs, communication supports and the possible effect on the person, and choose the least restrictive method.

During any physical intervention that occurs in an emergency, staff protect breathing and circulation, never use prone or pain-compliance holds, stay with the client, speak calmly, call 911 if there is any injury or medical concern, and end the physical contact as soon as the danger ends. Under no circumstance is a client left alone while restrained or secluded.

After any intervention, a staff member checks the client for injury, offers medical care, provides comfort and a quiet space, and monitors the client for at least 30 minutes. Any injury is treated and reported under GOV-06. The monitoring is documented.

The staff member writes an incident report by the end of the shift, and notifies the QP, the Administrator and the LRP the same day, within the timelines in GOV-06 (see also HRM-01 where abuse or neglect is suspected).

Within [NUMBER] business days of any event, the QP leads a debriefing with the client, the LRP if the client agrees or the LRP has legal authority, and the staff who were involved. The debriefing covers what led to the event, what happened, what the client felt, what worked and what could have prevented it.

The QP and the team then hold a planning session to reduce future use: identify triggers, update the person-centered plan and proactive supports, teach coping skills, change the environment and staffing as needed, and decide whether any restriction should end or change (see ASM-02).
The QP documents the debriefing and plan in the client record and gives the client and LRP a written or plain-language summary of the outcome. Staff learning points are shared with the team.

The Program Director reviews each restriction at least [every 30 days / at each plan review, whichever is sooner] and ends it when no longer needed. Each review is documented. Any consent for a planned restrictive intervention is limited to six months.

If the governing body ever elects to permit an emergency intervention, no use occurs until the standard in 10A NCAC 27E .0104 is operational: staff authorization for up to 15 minutes, then a qualified professional authorization, orders of no more than 4 hours for adults, checks every 15 minutes, 30 minutes of monitoring afterward, a use log and quarterly review. Training and approvals under RES-01, RES-02, DEV-01 and TRN-01 are completed first.

The QA/QI Committee reviews the restriction and intervention log and debriefing outcomes at least quarterly, looks for patterns, and recommends corrective action to the governing body (see GOV-05). Where required by the LME/MCO, rights-related incidents are reported to the area director within 30 days and to the board within 90 days, and the Client Rights Committee reviews restrictive procedures (10A NCAC 27G .0504).

responsibilities.duty: Gives written permission for 24-hour restrictions, hears appeals, ensures no restriction is imposed without due process, and makes required reports.
Proposes and reviews restrictions, reviews every use, reviews health history for risk, leads debriefing and planning, and documents and communicates the outcome.
Protect well-being before, during and after any event, report the same shift and take part in debriefing.

responsibilities.role: Client Rights Committee (where required by the LME/MCO)
responsibilities.duty: Reviews restrictive procedures, grievances and alleged rights violations.
Reviews restriction and intervention data quarterly.

documentation: Written restriction proposal, notice to client and LRP, and the Administrator's written permission
Record of refusal, appeal, review and outcome
Health history and risk review in the admission record
Incident reports and monitoring notes
Debriefing and planning documentation with the summary given to client and LRP
Restriction and intervention log with quarterly review minutes

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27E .0103 General Policies Regarding Intervention Procedures
policies.title: Intervention Procedures as Therapeutic Treatment
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and contractors of [AGENCY NAME] who are involved in client care, and every client of the Supervised Living 'C' home at [ADDRESS].
policies.purpose: To make sure that no intervention procedure is used with a client unless it is a clinically or medically justified treatment method, determined and authorized by a qualified professional, and never for staff convenience or as punishment.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27E .0103, Worksheet pp.17-18, item 47 (policy with guidelines for intervention procedures as therapeutic treatment methods that are clinically or medically justified and authorized by qualified professionals).

1. Default position. [AGENCY NAME] does not offer intervention procedures as therapeutic treatment by default. No client is subject to any such procedure unless every condition below is met.
2. Clinical or medical justification. An intervention procedure may be used as a treatment method only when it is clinically or medically justified for that client, based on assessment, and documented in the client's record.
3. Who may determine and authorize. Only a physician or a licensed practicing psychologist who is formally trained in the procedure and privileged to use it may determine that the procedure is needed and authorize it. Direct care staff, the Administrator and other non-privileged staff may not determine or authorize an intervention procedure.
4. Never for convenience or punishment. An intervention is never used for staff convenience, to make up for inadequate staffing, as punishment, as retaliation, or as a substitute for a person-centered plan.
5. Least restrictive alternative. Consistent with the least restrictive alternative requirement (see LRA-01), positive and less restrictive approaches must be tried and documented first. The intervention is a last resort used by trained staff.
6. Governing body limits. Because [AGENCY NAME]'s governing body policy on rights restrictions and interventions (RRI-01) implements G.S. 122C-59, -65 and -66, no intervention may be used unless RRI-01 names it as permitted, and then only with the due process, authorization, review and appeal steps in RRI-01 and RRI-02.
7. Documentation. The justification and the authorization are documented in the client's record before the procedure is first used.

definitions.definition: A planned or emergency procedure that restricts a client's movement, freedom or behavior and is used as a treatment or habilitation method, including any restrictive intervention described in RRI-01.
A physician or licensed practicing psychologist who is formally trained in the specific procedure and privileged to determine and authorize it.
Supported by a documented assessment showing the procedure is necessary for the client's treatment or safety and that less restrictive methods were tried or considered and found inadequate.

procedures: The Administrator confirms, at policy adoption and at each annual review, that the governing body has not authorized any intervention procedure in RRI-01. If none is authorized, this policy remains the statement that none is offered.

If a team member, family member or legally responsible person (LRP) asks for an intervention procedure, the requestor tells the Qualified Professional (QP) or Administrator. Direct care staff do not agree to or start any procedure.
The QP refers the request to a physician or licensed practicing psychologist who is formally trained and privileged in the procedure, and records the referral date in the client record.
The QP confirms in writing that the professional is trained and privileged in the specific procedure. Evidence of training and privileging is filed in the professional's contractor file.
The professional completes an assessment and records the clinical or medical justification, the less restrictive methods already tried, the target behavior or condition, and the expected benefit.
The professional documents the determination and authorization in the client record with name, credentials, date and signature. No authorization is accepted verbally or by anyone else.
The QP checks the proposed procedure against RRI-01 and PRO-01. A procedure that is prohibited, or that is not named as permitted in RRI-01, is not carried out.

The QP brings the proposed procedure to the person-centered team and discusses it with the client and LRP. Informed consent is sought and documented per CON-01, and the procedure is written into the individual plan (ASM-02).
Due process, rights-restriction notice, authorization review and appeal steps are carried out under RRI-02 before the first use, except in an emergency covered by RES-01.
The Administrator checks that every staff member who will carry out the procedure has been trained and is current under TRN-01. No untrained staff member carries it out.
The QP reviews the client's response with the authorizing professional at the interval set in the order and in the individual plan, and at least quarterly. Reviews are documented in the record.
The authorizing professional discontinues or revises the procedure when it is no longer clinically justified. The QP records the end date and reason, and informs the client and LRP.

Any use of an intervention outside the written authorization, for convenience, or as punishment is stopped immediately. The Administrator reports it as an incident under GOV-06 and as possible abuse or neglect under HRM-01.
The Administrator reviews every intervention authorization at the annual policy review and through the QA/QI process (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Decides in RRI-01 whether any intervention procedure may be used. Default is that none is offered.
Verifies authorization, training and documentation before any use. Stops unauthorized use and reports it.
Coordinates referral, informed consent, plan entry, due process and reviews.
Determines need and authorizes the procedure in writing, within their training and privileges.
Carry out only authorized procedures they have been trained in. Report concerns to the QP or Administrator at once.

documentation: Written assessment with clinical or medical justification
Signed and dated authorization by the physician or licensed psychologist
Proof of the professional's training and privileging in the procedure
Informed consent and individual plan entry
Due process notices and review records (RRI-02)
Review notes and discontinuation record
Any incident report for unauthorized use (GOV-06)

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27E .0104 Seclusion, Physical Restraint, Isolation Time-Out, and Protective Devices Used for Behavioral Control
policies.title: Restrictive Interventions: Scope, Limits and Emergency Use
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, students and contractors involved in client care or in carrying out restrictive interventions at [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To state the scope of, limits on and emergency rules for seclusion, physical restraint, isolation time-out and protective devices used for behavioral control, and to state that under the current governing body policy (RRI-01) none of these are permitted in this home.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27E .0104, Worksheet pp.18-19, items 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 56, 57 and 58, as follows.

Item 48 (applies to all staff). This policy applies to all staff involved in client care and in implementing restrictive interventions. Staff, volunteers and students must follow it.

Item 49 (guidelines for seclusion, physical restraint, isolation and protective devices for behavioral management). Under RRI-01, [AGENCY NAME] does not permit seclusion, physical restraint, isolation time-out or protective devices used for behavioral control. In an emergency in which a client is in imminent danger of harming self or others, staff use non-physical de-escalation, move other people and hazards away from the situation, and call 911. Staff do not restrain or seclude the client. Sections that follow apply only if the governing body later amends RRI-01 to permit emergency use. They are written so the home is ready and so the surveyor can see the limits that would apply.

Item 50 (limitations). Restrictive interventions may be considered only as a last resort, after less restrictive alternatives have been tried or ruled out in the situation, and only by trained staff, consistent with LRA-01. They may be used only for the shortest time necessary and only while imminent danger continues.

Item 51 (prohibited uses). A restrictive intervention may never be used for coercion, punishment, retaliation, staff convenience or inadequate staffing, and may never be carried out in a way that causes harm or abuse. Any such use is treated as possible abuse or neglect (HRM-01) and is reported (GOV-06).

Item 52 (documentation of acceptable use in the facility). The only acceptable use is the emergency use defined here, and only if RRI-01 has been amended to permit it. Each use is documented as described in RES-02. Today, acceptable use within the facility is none.

Item 56 (emergency use, time limits and authorization). Emergency use is only for imminent danger to self or others. Staff may authorize and begin an emergency intervention for up to 15 minutes. After 15 minutes, a qualified professional authorized under RRI-01 must authorize continuation. For adults, an order lasts no more than 4 hours.

Item 57 (precautions and actions during an intervention). Staff check the client at least every 15 minutes, monitor and document continuously, and monitor the client for 30 minutes after the intervention ends.

Item 58 (discontinuing). Staff end the intervention at any sign of risk to the client's health or safety, and as soon as the client regains behavioral control, whichever happens first.

definitions.definition: Seclusion, physical restraint, isolation time-out, or a protective device used for behavioral control.
Confining a client alone in a room or area from which the client is physically prevented from leaving.
A hold or other physical means that restricts a client's freedom of movement or ability to move the body, used to control behavior.
Separating a client from others in a designated space for a short, limited period to regain behavioral control.
A present, immediate risk that a client will seriously harm self or another person.
A professional identified in RRI-01 as allowed to authorize continuation of an emergency intervention beyond 15 minutes.

procedures: All staff are told of this policy at orientation (PER-01, TRN-01). Each signs that they have read it and understand that restraint and seclusion are not permitted in this home unless RRI-01 is amended.

Staff use the client's individual plan, which names triggers, early warning signs and preferred calming supports, to prevent crises. They offer choices, reduce demands, lower stimulation and use trained de-escalation (TRN-01).

If a client is in imminent danger of harming self or others, the staff member nearest stays calm, moves other clients and hazards away, and calls the on-call supervisor. If danger continues, staff call 911 without delay. [AGENCY NAME] will never delay 911 in order to try a restrictive intervention first.

Staff stay with the client, within safe distance, and give emergency responders the client's name, diagnosis, medications, LRP contact and known triggers. See GOV-08 for the medical emergency process.
