No staff member may use seclusion, physical restraint, isolation time-out or a behavioral protective device while RRI-01 does not permit them. A staff member who does is reported as in procedure 13.

If the governing body amends RRI-01 to permit emergency use, the Administrator confirms before first use that: (a) the amendment is signed and dated; (b) staff are trained and current under TRN-01; (c) the Client Rights Committee and LME/MCO have been told; and (d) authorizers are named.

Under an amended RRI-01, only staff trained and current in the approved curriculum may use an intervention, and only while imminent danger continues. The least restrictive method that is safe is used.

The staff member in charge records the exact time the intervention began and may authorize it for up to 15 minutes. If it must continue, the staff member calls the authorizing professional named in RRI-01 immediately, before the 15 minutes end.

After 15 minutes, no one continues the intervention unless the professional has authorized it. The authorization is written as an order. An adult order lasts no more than 4 hours and is not renewed without a new decision by the professional.

During the intervention, one staff member is assigned to observe and monitor continuously (breathing, color, distress, injury) and to record observations at least every 15 minutes. The client is never left unobserved.

The intervention is discontinued at once if the client shows any sign of physical or emotional risk (such as difficulty breathing, injury, medical distress or panic), or as soon as the client regains behavioral control. Staff call 911 for any medical risk.
For 30 minutes after the intervention ends, staff monitor the client, check for injury, offer comfort and water, and document. A nurse or physician is consulted if there is injury or concern.

Any use of an intervention without authority, for a prohibited reason, or beyond the limits above is stopped at once. The staff member reports to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator reports it under GOV-06 and HRM-01 and starts an investigation within 24 hours.
Completion of documentation, notification, debriefing and review follows RES-02.
The Administrator reviews this policy annually with the governing body and records whether the default (no restrictive interventions) is still in effect.

responsibilities.duty: Decides in RRI-01 whether any emergency use is permitted. Approves any amendment.
Ensures staff know this policy, that training is current and that no unauthorized use occurs. Investigates any use.
Authorizes continuation beyond 15 minutes by written order and sets limits.
Prevent crises, de-escalate, call 911 when needed, never use a prohibited or unauthorized intervention, and document.
Supports staff by phone, confirms 911 was called when required and notifies the Administrator.

documentation: Staff acknowledgment of this policy at orientation
Incident report for every emergency call involving imminent danger (GOV-06)
Written order and time log for any authorized intervention (see RES-02)
15-minute check records and 30-minute post-intervention monitoring record
Investigation record for any unauthorized use
Annual review note on RRI-01 status

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27E .0104 Seclusion, Physical Restraint, Isolation Time-Out, and Protective Devices Used for Behavioral Control
policies.title: Seclusion/Restraint: Staff Roles, Rooms, Documentation, Notification, Review and Data
policies.applies_to: All staff involved in client care, the Administrator, the governing body designee and the Client Rights Committee.
policies.purpose: To state the staff roles, room requirements, documentation, notification, review and data analysis that apply if restrictive interventions are ever used at [AGENCY NAME], and how the home tracks and reports any such use.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27E .0104, Worksheet pp.18-20, items 53, 54, 55, 59, 60, 61 and 62. Under RRI-01, restrictive interventions are not permitted in this home at this time (see RES-01). The provisions below apply to any use that occurs, whether authorized after amendment of RRI-01 or in violation of it.

Item 53 (elements for procedures on seclusion). (a) Positive and less restrictive alternatives are tried first (LRA-01, RES-01). (b) Staff who may take part are identified by name, hold current training in the approved curriculum and have shown competence by evaluation (TRN-01). (c) Staff responsibilities and professional roles during an intervention are set out in procedures 2 to 5 below. (d) Documentation and notification after any intervention follow procedures 7 to 10. (e) Well-being checks and assessment of consequences after the intervention follow procedure 6.

Item 54 (room requirements for seclusion and isolation). [AGENCY NAME] has no seclusion or isolation room. No bedroom, bathroom, closet or other space may be locked, blocked or otherwise used to keep a client from leaving. If a seclusion or isolation room is ever proposed, DHSR must approve it before use, and the governing body must amend RRI-01 first.

Item 55 (documentation in client records). Each use is documented in the client's record, including the rationale, the methods used and the debriefing.

Item 59 (notification). The treatment/habilitation team or designee and a governing body designee are notified within 24 hours of each use. The LRP of a minor or an adult found incompetent is notified immediately unless the LRP has asked not to be notified.

Item 60 (review and reporting). A governing body designee and the Client Rights Committee set the review time frame (at least quarterly), keep client information confidential, investigate unusual or possibly unwarranted patterns of use, and maintain a log with: client name, responsible professional, date, time and type, duration, reason, alternatives considered and why not used, debriefing and planning with client, LRP and staff, and adverse effects.

Item 61 (data collection and analysis). Data from the log are compiled and analyzed as in procedures 12 to 14.

Item 62 (planned intervention). [AGENCY NAME] does not use planned restrictive interventions. If the governing body ever allows them, procedures in 15 to 16 apply.

definitions.definition: The running record of every use of seclusion, physical restraint, isolation time-out or protective device for behavioral control, with the fields required by 10A NCAC 27E .0104.
A structured discussion held with the client, the LRP when appropriate and the staff involved, after an intervention, to understand what happened, check on the client and plan to prevent recurrence.
A restrictive intervention written into a client's individual plan in advance, rather than used only in an emergency.
The person named by the governing body to receive notices and review data under this policy: [GOVERNING BODY DESIGNEE NAME].

procedures: Before any intervention, staff try and document positive, less restrictive alternatives (choices, redirection, reduced stimulation, offering a calm space the client can leave, one-to-one support). The reason an alternative was not effective or not safe is written on the incident form.

Staff roles. The staff member in charge of the shift directs the response and makes the 15-minute decision under RES-01. A second trained staff member is the designated observer and monitors continuously. All other staff keep other clients safe and call for help.

Only staff identified on the current Authorized Staff List (maintained by the Administrator) may take part. A staff member is added only after completing the approved curriculum and the in-person competence evaluation (TRN-01). Competence is re-evaluated at the annual refresher.

The professional named in RRI-01 is responsible for authorizing continuation beyond 15 minutes, seeing or assessing the client as the order requires, and writing the order. Direct care staff do not extend an intervention on their own.
If an intervention is in progress and no authorized professional can be reached before 15 minutes, staff stop and call 911.

After any intervention, the observer checks the client for injury, pain, breathing, emotional distress and need for medical care. The client is monitored for 30 minutes. Staff document findings and consequences. A nurse or physician is consulted for any injury.

Before the end of the shift, the staff member in charge completes an incident report (GOV-06) and a record entry with: the behavior and imminent danger, alternatives tried, method used, start and end times, 15-minute checks, authorizer and order times, and the client's condition afterward.
Within 24 hours the Administrator or QP notifies the treatment/habilitation team or designee and the governing body designee and records the date, time and method of each notice.

Immediately after the intervention, staff notify the LRP of a minor or of an adult found incompetent, unless the LRP has asked not to be notified. Staff record the time of the notice, who was reached and any preference not to be notified.

The QP holds a debriefing with the client, the LRP when appropriate and the staff involved within 2 business days, unless the client's condition delays it. Debriefing notes include what the client says would help and changes to the individual plan.

The Administrator enters the event in the restrictive intervention log within one business day. The log is kept in a locked file with access limited to the Administrator, QP, governing body designee and the Client Rights Committee, to keep client information confidential.

Each quarter, the Administrator compiles data from the log and from incident reports: number of events by client, staff, time of day, day of week, location, type, duration, trigger and adverse effects. If there are none, the quarterly report states that none were recorded.

The governing body designee and the Client Rights Committee (or its LME/MCO-designated equivalent) review the quarterly data at least quarterly. They look for unusual or possibly unwarranted patterns of use, such as repeated use with the same client or staff, use at the same time of day, long durations, or use that may reflect staffing.

Any unusual pattern is investigated, and findings and corrective actions (plan changes, training, staffing) are recorded. Results are given to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05). Rights incidents are reported to the LME/MCO area director within 30 days and to the area board within 90 days where the LME/MCO requires it.

Planned intervention. If the governing body ever permits planned interventions, each one must be: justified and authorized under INT-01; in the individual plan with informed consent (CON-01); reviewed for due process under RRI-02; subject to review by the Intervention Advisory Committee (DEV-01); and reviewed at least quarterly.
Until those steps are met for a specific client, no planned intervention is used. A missing step is treated as unauthorized use and reported under GOV-06.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the Authorized Staff List, log and quarterly data report. Makes 24-hour notifications. Investigates events and patterns.
Directs the response, makes 15-minute decisions, calls the authorizing professional or 911, completes the incident report.
Monitors continuously, records 15-minute checks and 30-minute post-intervention monitoring.
Leads the debriefing, updates the individual plan and notifies the habilitation team.

responsibilities.role: Governing body designee [GOVERNING BODY DESIGNEE NAME]
responsibilities.duty: Receives notice within 24 hours, sets review time frame with the Client Rights Committee and reviews data.
Reviews restrictive procedures and rights incidents and any unusual pattern of use, keeping client information confidential.

documentation: Incident report (GOV-06) and client record entry with rationale, methods and debriefing
Written authorization and time log; 15-minute check sheet; 30-minute monitoring record
Notification record (team, governing body designee, LRP) with dates and times
Restrictive intervention log with all required fields
Quarterly data report and committee review minutes
Investigation records for any unusual pattern
Authorized Staff List and competence evaluations (TRN-01)

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27E .0105 Protective Devices; .0106 Intervention Advisory Committee
policies.title: Protective Devices and Intervention Advisory Committee
policies.applies_to: All staff who use or oversee protective devices, the Administrator, the Client Rights Committee, and any Intervention Advisory Committee that is formed.
policies.purpose: To control any use of protective devices so that each has a documented need, a trained user, a record of observation and a maintenance and cleaning protocol, and to state when an Intervention Advisory Committee is required.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27E .0105 (Worksheet p.20, items 63 and 64) and 10A NCAC 27E .0106 (Worksheet pp.20-21, items 65, 66, 67 and 68).

Item 63 (protective devices procedure). Protective devices are not used for behavioral control (RRI-01, RES-01). If a protective device is used for any other protective purpose, the following apply: (a) there is a documented necessity for the device; (b) the employee using it is trained and competent; (c) observation and interventions are documented in the client record; and (d) the device is maintained and cleaned under the protocol in procedure 8.

Item 64 (Client Rights Committee review). [AGENCY NAME] provides services under contract with the LME/MCO. Any use of a protective device in a client's treatment/habilitation plan is subject to review by the Client Rights Committee. See procedure 6.

Item 65 (Intervention Advisory Committee). An Intervention Advisory Committee must be established for additional safeguards in any facility that uses restrictive interventions as planned interventions. [AGENCY NAME] does not use restrictive interventions as planned interventions, so the committee is not applicable and has not been formed. It will be formed before the first planned intervention if the governing body ever permits one.

Item 66 (membership). If required, membership is documented by name, role and term and is set out in procedure 11.

Item 67 (client information). If required, procedures for how client information is shared with the committee and why are in procedure 12.

Item 68 (training and orientation). If required, committee training and orientation are documented as in procedure 13.

Committee activity is reviewed annually (procedure 14).

definitions.definition: A device or material, such as a helmet, belt or restraint-like support, that limits a client's movement or access to protect the client from injury.
A committee that provides additional safeguards for any facility that uses restrictive interventions as planned interventions.
A restrictive intervention written in advance into a client's individual plan.

procedures: No protective device is used for behavioral control at [AGENCY NAME]. A device that restricts movement may be used only if it is ordered or recommended for a documented protective need, such as a medical need, and is in the individual plan.

Before using a device, the QP records the necessity: the risk of injury, why less restrictive options were not enough, the device type and the times of use. The ordering or recommending professional signs the record.

The Administrator checks that each staff member who will use the device has been trained by a qualified person on the specific device and has shown competence. Competence is documented before first use.
The QP gets informed consent from the client or LRP (CON-01) and puts the device into the individual plan (ASM-02).

Staff observe the client while the device is in use and document the observations and any intervention (skin, circulation, comfort, behavior, time on and off) in the client record at the intervals in the plan.

Client Rights Committee review. Because [AGENCY NAME] operates under contract with an area program (LME/MCO), the QP sends the plan with the protective device to the Client Rights Committee for review before use and at each plan review. The review date and outcome are recorded in the record.
Staff remove the device when the need ends or at any sign of risk. The QP records the end date and reason.

Maintenance and cleaning. Each device is inspected before each use for damage, wear and fit. It is cleaned and disinfected after each use and at least weekly while in use, with the agent in the manufacturer's directions and PER-02. A device with damage is taken out of service and replaced. Cleaning and inspection are logged by date and initials.
Each protective device is assigned to one client. Devices are not shared unless cleaned and disinfected between clients.
The Administrator decides each year whether the governing body has permitted planned restrictive interventions. If not, the IAC section is recorded as not applicable on the annual policy review.

If an IAC is required, the governing body names the members in writing, including: a governing body designee; a qualified professional with expertise in the interventions used; a client, family member or advocate representative who is not an employee; and a representative of the Client Rights Committee. Names, roles, appointment dates and terms are kept in the IAC file. Membership will be checked against 10A NCAC 27E .0106 and with the LME/MCO before the first meeting.

If an IAC is required, client information is given to members only as needed for review, with the client's or LRP's authorization where required (GOV-03). Information is limited to what members need to review the plan's safeguards, in order to protect confidentiality, and is returned or destroyed after the meeting. The reason for each sharing is recorded in the minutes.

If an IAC is required, each member is given an orientation before the first meeting on client rights, confidentiality, the interventions under review and the committee's role. Training, dates, trainer and attendance are documented.
The Administrator reviews committee activity annually (or, if there is no IAC, confirms in writing that none is needed) and reports the review to the governing body and the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether planned interventions are allowed. Appoints the IAC if they are.
Verifies necessity, training, cleaning logs and Client Rights Committee review. Conducts the annual review.
Documents necessity, obtains consent, updates the individual plan and sends the plan for review.
Use devices only as trained, observe and document, inspect and clean devices.
Reviews protective device use in treatment/habilitation plans.
Provides additional safeguards for planned interventions.

documentation: Documented necessity and professional order or recommendation
Staff training and competence records for the device
Informed consent and individual plan entry
Observation notes in the client record
Client Rights Committee review record
Device inspection and cleaning log
IAC membership roster, minutes, confidentiality and sharing record, and training log (if formed)
Annual review note

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27E .0107 Training on Alternatives to Restrictive Interventions; .0108 Training in Seclusion, Physical Restraint, and Isolation Time-Out
policies.title: Training in De-escalation and in Restrictive Interventions
policies.applies_to: All staff, service providers, employees, students and volunteers involved in client care, and all instructors who train them.
policies.purpose: To make sure all people involved in client care are trained in approved de-escalation techniques as alternatives to restrictive interventions, to state that [AGENCY NAME] does not use restrictive interventions, and to set training requirements that would apply if that changes.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27E .0107 (Worksheet p.21, items 69 to 73) and 10A NCAC 27E .0108 (Worksheet p.22, items 74 to 79).

Item 69. All staff, service providers, employees, students and volunteers involved in client care must be trained in an approved de-escalation curriculum, as an alternative to restrictive interventions, before working with clients without direct supervision.

Item 70. All staff complete a formal annual refresher in the approved de-escalation curriculum.

Item 71. Training documentation for all staff is kept at least three years: participants, pass/fail outcome, training dates and instructor names.

Item 72. Instructor qualifications and training requirements are in the section on instructors (procedures 6 to 8).

Item 73. Documentation of alternatives training, and of initial and refresher instructor training, is kept at least three years (procedure 12).

Item 74. Any staff member who uses a restrictive intervention must be trained and current in an approved restrictive-intervention training program. No one else may use one.

Item 75. The approved curriculum for de-escalation is [APPROVED DE-ESCALATION CURRICULUM NAME], an approved curriculum on the list maintained by NC DHHS. [AGENCY NAME] does not use restrictive interventions, and will not use seclusion, physical restraint or isolation time-out (RRI-01, RES-01). No restrictive-intervention curriculum is therefore in use. If the governing body permits emergency use, the curriculum will be named here and in RRI-01 before first use.

Item 76. Prerequisites for staff to use restrictive interventions (if ever permitted) are in procedure 10.

Item 77. If restrictive interventions are ever permitted, all staff authorized to use them successfully complete a formal annual refresher in the approved curriculum.

Item 78. Restrictive-intervention instructors must be retrained at least annually and be currently CPR-trained.

Item 79. Initial and refresher instructor training documentation is kept at least three years.

definitions.definition: A de-escalation or restrictive-intervention training curriculum approved under NC DHHS requirements.
A documented, instructor-led training session in the approved curriculum, completed at least once every 12 months, with a pass/fail outcome.
A person qualified under the approved curriculum to train and evaluate staff in de-escalation or restrictive interventions.

procedures: The Administrator selects [APPROVED DE-ESCALATION CURRICULUM NAME] from the NC DHHS list of approved curricula, confirms the current list before selecting, and records the choice and date in the governing body minutes.

Each new employee, student and volunteer completes the approved de-escalation training before working with clients without direct supervision. Orientation also covers client rights and confidentiality, individual plan needs and bloodborne pathogens as required by 10A NCAC 27G .0202 (see PER-01).

Training is delivered in person by a qualified instructor. A person must pass any written and skills evaluation required by the curriculum. A person who does not pass repeats the training and may not work unsupervised with clients until passing.

Each staff member completes a formal annual refresher in the approved de-escalation curriculum before the anniversary of the last training. The Administrator tracks due dates on the training matrix (REQ-02) and schedules sessions at least 60 days before expiry.
A staff member whose training has lapsed is taken off the unsupervised schedule until the refresher is complete.

Instructor qualifications. A de-escalation instructor must be certified or authorized by the curriculum's developer or sponsor to teach and evaluate the curriculum, in line with NC DHHS requirements. The Administrator verifies this before the first class and annually, and keeps a copy of the instructor's certificate.
Instructors must complete initial instructor training and any refresher the curriculum requires. [AGENCY NAME] keeps proof of dates, trainer and outcome.

An instructor for restrictive interventions (if ever used) must be retrained at least annually and hold current CPR certification. The Administrator checks both dates each year and does not schedule a class when either has lapsed.
Restrictive interventions are not permitted. No staff member is trained to use or may use seclusion, physical restraint or isolation time-out unless the governing body amends RRI-01.

If the governing body permits emergency use, before any staff member may use a restrictive intervention they must: be current in de-escalation training; hold current CPR and first aid/Heimlich certification; have completed the approved restrictive-intervention curriculum in person; have passed the competence evaluation; have been oriented to RES-01 and RES-02; and be listed on the Authorized Staff List. A formal annual refresher in the approved restrictive-intervention curriculum is required of all authorized staff.
The Administrator keeps a training file for each person with: course, curriculum name, dates, hours, pass/fail result, instructor name and signature of the person trained.

Training records, including alternatives training and instructor initial and refresher records, are kept at least three years from the date of training (or longer if another policy or the LME/MCO requires). The records are available to DHSR and the LME/MCO on request.
The Administrator reports the training completion rate to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05) each quarter and reviews this policy and the curriculum annually.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the curriculum and the decision that restrictive interventions are not used.
Selects curriculum and instructors, schedules training, tracks due dates, keeps records and takes staff off unsupervised duty when training has lapsed.
Teaches and evaluates staff under the curriculum. Keeps own qualifications current.
Complete initial and annual training and use de-escalation instead of restrictive interventions.

documentation: Curriculum selection and governing body minutes
Individual training file (course, dates, pass/fail, instructor name)
Instructor qualification, initial and refresher records, and CPR card
Staff training matrix (REQ-02)
Authorized Staff List (only if restrictive interventions are ever permitted)
Quarterly training report to QA/QI

policies.title: Suspension, Expulsion and Involuntary Discharge
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME], all clients and legally responsible persons of the Supervised Living 'C' home, and the LME/MCO care coordinator.
policies.purpose: To make sure no client lives in fear of unwarranted suspension or expulsion, to set the narrow criteria for any discharge that is not mutually agreed, and to document the steps taken to find alternative services.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 10A NCAC 27D .0102, Worksheet pp.22-23, items 80, 81 and 82.

Item 80. Each client is free from threat or fear of unwarranted suspension or expulsion from the facility. Staff may not use the threat of suspension, expulsion or discharge to control behavior or to gain compliance. A client who is found to have been threatened is protected, and the staff member is subject to corrective action.

Item 81 (criteria). Suspension, expulsion or any other form of discharge that is not mutually agreed upon may be considered only when: (a) the client's behavior poses an imminent and serious danger to self or others that cannot be managed with the supports available even after the plan has been reviewed and revised; (b) the client's needs have changed so the home can no longer safely meet them, as shown by assessment; (c) the client or LRP does not pay or provide required agreed-upon room and board and the client's Medicaid-covered services are not at issue, after the steps in the fee policy (GOV-07) are done; (d) the home's license, certification or contract ends (CNT-01); or (e) the client needs a higher level of care that cannot be provided in the home. A discharge may never be used for convenience, as punishment, because of a complaint or grievance, because the client exercised a right, or because of the client's diagnosis alone.

Item 82 (documentation). When suspension, expulsion or involuntary discharge is considered, [AGENCY NAME] documents: the time frame for resuming services after a suspension; the specific conditions and timeline for resuming services; staff efforts to identify alternative services that meet the client's needs and the designation of those services; and any necessary discharge plan.

Federal home and community-based settings requirements (42 CFR 441.301(c)) are respected. The client keeps the protections of the home's agreement and of due process, and the LME/MCO care coordinator is involved before any involuntary action, except in an emergency threatening health or safety.

This policy is explained to each client or LRP within 72 hours of admission and the LME/MCO is notified of any suspension or discharge (procedures 1 and 11).

definitions.definition: A temporary stop of a client's residence or services in the home, with a defined time frame and conditions for return.
An end to the client's residence in the home that the client or LRP has not agreed to.
Any discharge not mutually agreed upon by the client or LRP and the home.
A guardian or other person with legal authority to make decisions for the client.
The Tailored Plan that authorizes and pays for the client's Innovations Waiver Residential Supports and coordinates care.

procedures: Within 72 hours of admission, the QP explains this policy to the client and the LRP in plain language, with communication supports as needed (INF-01, IR-01), and documents the date, who was present and the client's questions in the record (10A NCAC 27D .0201).

Staff never threaten suspension, expulsion or discharge. Any staff member who hears or sees such a threat reports it to the Administrator the same day, and it is handled as a rights concern under HRM-01 and IR-02.

When a behavior or situation might lead to suspension or discharge, the QP calls the person-centered team and the LME/MCO care coordinator within 2 business days. The team reviews the individual plan, assessment, medications, health, environment and staffing to identify supports that would let the client stay.
The team documents the supports tried and the results. The less restrictive alternatives (LRA-01) are tried first, and the person is involved in the discussion with the support they need.
If suspension or discharge still seems needed, the Administrator checks the criteria in item 81. If no criterion is met, the action is not taken.

If a client is in immediate danger, staff follow RES-01 (call 911) and the client may be temporarily away from the home for safety. This is a suspension only when it is recorded as such under the next steps, and the client's bed and belongings are kept.

For any suspension, the Administrator writes a notice stating the reason, the start date, the time frame for resuming services, the specific conditions for returning and the timeline, and the supports offered during the suspension. A copy goes to the client, LRP, care coordinator and the record.

The QP and care coordinator identify alternative services and place(s) that meet the client's needs (for example another residential provider, crisis services, respite, behavioral health or a hospital if medically necessary) and record who was contacted, the date, and the outcome. The service(s) designated for the client are named in the record.

If discharge that is not mutually agreed is proposed, the Administrator gives written notice to the client, LRP and LME/MCO per GOV-02 stating the reason, the effective date, the person's right to grieve and appeal (IR-02), the right to contact the Governor's Advocacy Council and the LME/MCO, and the alternative services identified.

The QP writes a discharge plan with the client, LRP and team. It states the new setting, transportation, transfer of medications, funds and belongings (LIV-02, MED-03), records transfer (GOV-03), and follow-up for continuity of care (CNT-01).
The Administrator notifies the LME/MCO of every suspension and every non-mutual discharge by the next business day, in writing, and follows any LME/MCO requirements for transition and authorizations.

The client and LRP may grieve the decision under IR-02. The home continues services until the grievance process, plan for a safe transition and alternative placement are done, unless there is imminent danger.
The client does not leave without a safe place to go and the transport and supports needed. The home does not discharge a client to homelessness.
When a suspension ends, the QP meets with the client and LRP to confirm that the conditions were met, restores services on the date given in the notice and updates the individual plan.
The Administrator logs every suspension and non-mutual discharge, reports each to the QA/QI Committee (GOV-05) and reviews trends and causes, including staffing and supports, at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether criteria are met, issues notices, notifies the LME/MCO, and logs and reports every action.
Explains the policy at admission, leads the team review, identifies alternative services and writes the discharge plan.
Takes part in the team review, helps identify alternatives and authorizes services.
Do not threaten suspension or discharge, report concerns and support the client through any transition.
Reviews the log and any trends, and approves this policy.

documentation: Record of admission-day explanation of this policy within 72 hours
Team review notes and supports tried
Written suspension notice with time frame, conditions and timeline for resuming services
Record of efforts to identify alternative services and designated services
Discharge plan and notice to client, LRP and LME/MCO
Grievance records, if any (IR-02)
Suspension and discharge log and QA/QI report

policies.title: Health Care Personnel Registry and Criminal Record Checks
policies.applies_to: All applicants and employees, including relief and contract staff, with possible direct access to clients or their property; Administrator, Program Director and the person who keeps personnel files
policies.purpose: To keep clients safe by confirming that no unlicensed staff member with possible direct access to clients or their property has substantiated findings on the North Carolina Health Care Personnel Registry (HCPR). To set out how [AGENCY NAME] vets staff, how it reports allegations and cooperates with investigations, how it submits investigation results, and how it documents each step.
policies.policy:
This policy meets the Health Care Personnel Registry policy item (G.S. 131E-256; Worksheet p.23, item 83). It covers the agency's responsibility to vet all unlicensed staff with possible direct access to clients or their property through the HCPR, report-allegation procedures, investigation procedures, submission of investigation results, and documentation requirements.

[AGENCY NAME] checks every unlicensed staff member who may have direct access to clients or their property through the HCPR. This includes full-time, part-time, relief, contract and agency-supplied staff. The check is done before the person works alone with clients or has access to client property. In every case the HCPR check is finished within 90 days of the licensure review, which is the outer limit. A criminal record check is completed for every staff member within 180 days of the application review. [AGENCY NAME] does not employ or contract with anyone who has substantiated HCPR findings (10A NCAC 27G .0202). Applicants must disclose any convictions, and the Administrator reviews every disclosure and every criminal record result before the person has unsupervised access to clients. Staff must be at least 18 years old. The agency reports every allegation of abuse, neglect, exploitation or misappropriation of client property by an unlicensed staff member to the HCPR, cooperates fully with the investigation, and submits the results of its own investigation. Every result and every step is kept in the personnel file. This policy works together with HRM-01 (abuse, neglect and exploitation) and GOV-06 (incident reporting).

definitions.definition: The Health Care Personnel Registry kept by the NC Division of Health Service Regulation under G.S. 131E-256. It lists health care personnel with substantiated findings of abuse, neglect, exploitation, misappropriation of property or other listed findings.

definitions.term: Unlicensed staff with possible direct access
definitions.definition: Any employee, relief worker, contractor or volunteer who is not a licensed professional and who may provide care to clients or handle clients' belongings, funds or medications.
A finding entered on the HCPR after the state has investigated and confirmed an allegation against the person.
A report or reasonable suspicion that a staff member abused, neglected or exploited a client, or misappropriated client property.

procedures: The Administrator identifies every position with possible direct access to clients or their property and lists it in the HCPR Vetting Roster kept with the personnel records.
The Applicant disclosure form asks about every conviction and pending charge. The Administrator reviews each completed form before a conditional offer is made.

Before the person works alone with clients or has access to client property, the Program Director queries the HCPR for the applicant and prints or saves the result with the date and the name of the person who ran it.
If the HCPR shows a substantiated finding, the Administrator does not hire the person, or removes the person from the schedule at once if already employed. The Administrator documents the decision.
In every case, the HCPR check is finished within 90 days of the licensure review (the outer limit). The Administrator checks the Vetting Roster monthly during start-up for any gaps.
The Administrator starts the criminal record check for each staff member on or before the first day of employment. Every check is completed within 180 days of the application review.

The Administrator reviews each criminal record result and compares it with the applicant's disclosure. Any conviction is evaluated for its relationship to the job, its recency and client safety. The evaluation is written and signed.
No staff member may work alone with clients until the HCPR result is on file and the Administrator has recorded a written clearance. Until then, a cleared staff member directly supervises the person.
The Program Director re-checks the HCPR for every unlicensed staff member at least once a year at annual evaluation. The date and result are added to the personnel file.

Any staff member who hears of or suspects abuse, neglect, exploitation or misappropriation by a coworker tells the Administrator or Program Director immediately. If both are unreachable, the staff member follows the chain of command in GOV-01. The staff member also follows the reporting steps in HRM-01.
The Administrator protects clients first. The accused staff member is removed from client contact while the allegation is reviewed.

The Administrator reports the allegation to the HCPR within the timeframe the HCPR requires. [AGENCY NAME]'s own limit is the same business day, and never later than 24 hours after learning of it. The agency uses the HCPR's current report form and keeps a copy.

The Administrator completes a documented internal investigation. It includes written statements, review of client records and schedules, and interviews. Findings are submitted to the HCPR in the form and by the deadline it sets. The agency's own target is 5 working days.

The Administrator cooperates with HCPR, DHSR, law enforcement, the county DSS and the LME/MCO. This includes supplying records, making staff available for interviews and following any written instruction.
The Administrator also files any required incident report (see GOV-06) and tells the client's guardian and care coordinator as that policy requires.
When the HCPR notifies the agency of its determination, the Administrator places it in the personnel file. The Administrator applies any substantiated finding as in step 4 and records the decision.
The Program Director gives the Administrator a quarterly HCPR and criminal record check status report. The QA/QI Committee reviews it (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy. Reviews disclosures and criminal records, makes hire and removal decisions, reports allegations and submits investigation results to the HCPR.
Runs HCPR queries, keeps the Vetting Roster current, re-checks annually and keeps the personnel files complete.
Disclose convictions truthfully, report suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation or misappropriation immediately and cooperate with investigations.
Reviews quarterly status reports and corrects gaps.

documentation: Dated HCPR query result for each applicant and each annual re-check, with the name of the person who ran it
Applicant disclosure of convictions and the Administrator's signed evaluation
Criminal record check result and completion date
Written clearance to work alone with clients
HCPR Vetting Roster
Allegation report copy, internal investigation file, submission of results and the HCPR determination
Signed job description (10A NCAC 27G .0202)

policies.category: G.S. 122C-63 Continuity of Care for Individuals
policies.title: Continuity of Care: Closure and Discharge Notification
policies.applies_to: Program Director, Administrator, care coordinator liaison and all staff involved in discharge, transfer or closure
policies.purpose: To make sure no client loses needed services because the facility closes or the client is discharged. This policy names the position that notifies the LME/MCO and sets the notice period and transition steps.
policies.policy:
This policy meets the Continuity of Care policy item (N.C.G.S. 122C-63; Worksheet p.23, item 84). It names the staff position of this facility for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities that will notify the LME/MCO serving the client's county of residence of the intent to close the facility or discharge a client who may need continuing care, at least 60 days before the closure or discharge.

The Program Director is the designated position. The Program Director notifies the LME/MCO serving the client's county of residence in writing at least 60 days before [AGENCY NAME] closes or discharges a client who may need continuing care. When the Program Director is absent or vacant, the Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) acts in that role. The agency also gives DHSR 30 days' written notice before closing the facility (10A NCAC 27G .0404). The 60-day LME/MCO notice is the longer period, so it controls timing. The agency does not wait to start transition planning. It plans with the care coordinator, the client, family and guardian so that services continue without a gap. A decision not to renew the license at the end of the calendar year, when licenses expire (G.S. 122C-23), is treated as a closure and triggers the same notices.

definitions.definition: Services, supports, medications, treatments or residential placement a client still needs after leaving this facility.
The Local Management Entity/Managing Care Organization (Tailored Plan) serving the client's county of residence: Alliance Health, Partners Health Management, Trillium Health Resources or Vaya Health.
Ceasing to operate the facility, whether voluntary, by license non-renewal, or by order. It includes a decision not to renew at the end of the license period.
A written plan for moving the client to a new living setting and services, with dates, responsible people and the supports to be provided.

procedures: When the Administrator decides to close the facility, or the team decides to discharge a client who may need continuing care, the Administrator tells the Program Director the same day and records the decision with its date.

The Program Director writes to the LME/MCO serving the client's county of residence at least 60 days before the planned closure or discharge date. The notice gives the client's name and Medicaid ID, the reason, the planned date, the client's known continuing care needs and the contact person. One notice is sent per LME/MCO when clients come from different counties.
The Program Director sends the notice in a way that proves delivery (secure email with read receipt, or certified mail) and files the proof in the client record.

For a facility closure, the Administrator also gives DHSR 30 days' written notice of closure (10A NCAC 27G .0404). The Administrator sends it no later than the day the LME/MCO notice goes out, so that the DHSR notice is never late.

Within 5 working days of the LME/MCO notice, the Program Director contacts the client's care coordinator, the client, the legally responsible person and family (with the client's consent) to begin transition planning.

The team holds a transition meeting. It reviews the client's person-centered plan (ASM-02), health and medication needs, behavior supports, day program, transportation, preferences and the new setting. It records who will do what and by when.

The Program Director arranges for the client to visit the new setting, where possible, and gives the receiving provider a transfer packet. The packet includes the current plan, the medication list and last MAR, health information, rights restrictions in effect, and contact lists, all with the required authorization (GOV-03).

Staff prepare the client for the move at his or her own pace, using plain language and the person's usual communication method. They support the client's right to take his or her own clothing and possessions (LIV-02).

The Program Director transfers or arranges for the safe handling of medications, personal funds and belongings. The inventory is checked and signed by the client or guardian and by a receiving staff member.
The Program Director follows the discharge notice, appeal and due process steps in GOV-02 and SUS-01 whenever the discharge is involuntary.

In an emergency discharge, such as a medical emergency, hospital admission or court order, the Program Director notifies the LME/MCO as soon as possible, in any case the same business day. The Program Director sends the written notice soon after. Staff do not leave a client without a safe place to go.
For the first 30 days after discharge, the Program Director follows up with the care coordinator to confirm the client's services started. Any problems are reported to the Administrator.

The Program Director enters the dates of every notice, meeting and transfer in the continuity of care log and the client record. The Administrator reviews the log before the closure or discharge date.
The QA/QI Committee reviews every closure or discharge notice at its next meeting to check that the 60-day and 30-day notices were on time (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Notifies the LME/MCO at least 60 days ahead, leads transition planning and keeps the continuity of care log.
Decides on closure, gives DHSR 30 days' written notice, acts for the Program Director when absent and approves the transition plan.
Coordinates the new service plan with the LME/MCO and receiving provider.
Prepare the client for the move, pack belongings and complete the inventory.

documentation: Dated written notice to the LME/MCO and proof of delivery
Written 30-day notice to DHSR for closure and proof of delivery
Transition plan and transition meeting notes
Transfer packet checklist and authorizations
Belongings, funds and medication hand-off inventory with signatures
Continuity of care log and 30-day follow-up note
Discharge summary in the client record

policies.category: Treatment Rights in 24-hour Facilities: G.S. 122C-61 and G.S. 122C-62 Additional Rights
policies.title: Treatment Rights and Adult Client Rights in a 24-Hour Facility
policies.applies_to: All clients, legally responsible persons, guardians, family and visitors; all staff; Administrator and Program Director
policies.purpose: To state the treatment rights and the additional adult rights that apply to every person living in this 24-hour facility, and to say how staff protect and support those rights every day.
policies.policy:
This policy meets item 84 [G.S. 122C-61], Treatment Rights in 24-hour Facilities (N.C.G.S. 122C-61; Worksheet p.24); item 85, Adult client rights (N.C.G.S. 122C-62; Worksheet p.24); and item 86, Minor client rights (N.C.G.S. 122C-62; Worksheet p.25), which is addressed in the not-applicable statement below.

Item 84 [G.S. 122C-61]. Every client receives necessary treatment for physical ailments. Staff arrange prompt medical, dental and other health care and follow the medical preparedness plan (GOV-08). Every client has the right to an individualized discharge plan, which is built into the person-centered plan (ASM-02). If treatment or services are discontinued unexpectedly, for example because of a hospitalization, loss of a provider, a funding change or an emergency, staff handle it under the client's plan and the continuity of care steps in CNT-01 and GOV-02. They notify the guardian and care coordinator and arrange the care the client needs so there is no gap.

Item 85. Adult clients have the following rights. (a) Confidential phone calls, made and received in private. (b) Visitors between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. as the state minimum. At least 6 hours of visiting are available daily, including at least 2 hours after 6:00 p.m. Visiting does not take precedence over the client's therapies or treatment. (c) The right to communicate and meet, under appropriate supervision when the plan requires it, with individuals of the client's choice. (d) Visits outside the facility, unless there are commitment or court-order issues. (e) Time outdoors every day and access to exercise facilities several times a week. (f) The right to keep and use personal clothing and possessions. (g) Religious worship. (h) Retaining a driver's license, unless prohibited by law or court order. (i) Individual private storage space.

The state-law visiting hours are a minimum only. Under the HCBS settings rule (42 CFR 441.301(c) and 441.710), clients may have visitors at any time. [AGENCY NAME] limits visitors only through a documented modification in the client's person-centered plan, with the required justification and consent (see IR-01 and RRI-01). Any other limit on these rights is a rights restriction that must follow RRI-01 and RRI-02.

Item 86. Minor clients' rights under G.S. 122C-62 are not applicable to this facility. This is a Supervised Living 'C' home that serves adults only (10A NCAC 27G .5601). The agency does not admit minors. Minors and adults may not live together. If a minor were ever referred, the Program Director would decline admission and refer the family to the LME/MCO.

definitions.definition: Medical, dental, behavioral and other care that a licensed professional or the client's plan shows is needed for the client's physical or mental health.
The part of the person-centered plan that describes where the client will go next, with what supports, and what must happen first.
A guardian or other person with legal authority to make decisions for the client.
Any limit on a right listed in this policy. It is allowed only when authorized and documented under RRI-01 and RRI-02.

procedures: At admission and within 72 hours of arrival, the Program Director gives each client and legally responsible person a rights summary and tells them of the right to contact the Governor's Advocacy Council (10A NCAC 27D .0201). Staff explain it in plain language and the client's usual communication method.

Within the same 72 hours, staff explain the house rules, confidentiality, grievance procedure, fees, and suspension and search policies, as required by 10A NCAC 27D .0201. The client or guardian signs, and a copy goes in the client record (see INF-01).

Staff also give written notice of the right to contact the LME/MCO, DMH/DD/SAS, DHSR, the county DSS and Disability Rights North Carolina (10A NCAC 27G .7002). The notice includes [LME/MCO PHONE] and [DHSR COMPLAINT HOTLINE NUMBER]. The same information is posted in a public place in the home (IR-02).

Staff arrange each client's necessary physical health care. Appointments are scheduled, transportation is arranged (GOV-04), and the outcome is recorded in the client record. Medication needs are met under MED-02.

When a client has a new health problem, injury or change in condition, staff contact the physician or call 911 as the medical preparedness plan directs. They notify the guardian and care coordinator the same day.

At each plan meeting, the team reviews and updates the individualized discharge plan with the client and guardian. The plan states the planned next setting, needed supports and who is responsible (ASM-02).

If treatment or services are suddenly discontinued, the Program Director tells the client, guardian, care coordinator and LME/MCO within one business day. The team arranges substitute services immediately and records the plan.

Each client has a private telephone available. Staff help the client place and receive calls in private. Staff do not listen to or limit calls unless a rights restriction has been authorized under RRI-02.

Staff welcome visitors. Visitors are never turned away between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. and are accommodated at other times unless the client's plan documents a modification. Visits are arranged around the client's therapies, and staff offer another time if a therapy conflicts. The agency makes sure that at least 6 hours of visiting are possible each day, including 2 after 6:00 p.m.

Staff support clients in communicating and meeting with people of their choice. Supervision is used only when the client's plan says so and for the reason stated. Staff support visits outside the home unless a commitment or court order prevents it.

Staff offer outdoor time every day, weather permitting, and record it or any refusal in the daily notes. Exercise opportunities are offered at least several times a week through walks, community fitness options or in-home activities.

Staff help each client keep and use personal clothing and possessions (LIV-02), and give each client individual private storage space such as a locked or lockable drawer, closet or cabinet. The client holds the key unless a documented restriction applies.
Staff support each client's religious worship, including transportation to services of the client's choice, and respect the right not to worship.

A client who holds a driver's license keeps it unless prohibited by law or court order. Staff do not hold licenses. The team supports the client in arranging safe transportation if the client does not drive.

Before applying any limit to a right in this policy, the Administrator follows RRI-01 and RRI-02: least restrictive alternative, written justification, informed consent, time limits and review. Staff never restrict a right as punishment or for staff convenience.

The Program Director checks monthly that rights are being honored by reviewing the daily notes, visitor log and complaints. Findings go to the periodic internal review (PIR-01) and the QA/QI Committee.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, approves any rights restriction under RRI-01 and RRI-02 and makes sure the home posts required notices.
Gives and explains rights information within 72 hours, arranges health care, reviews the discharge plan and monitors rights compliance monthly.
Honor each right daily, support private calls and visits, offer outdoor time and exercise, and record refusals and concerns.
Helps the team update the individualized discharge plan and arrange substitute services.
May use these rights, ask questions, make complaints and consent to or refuse any proposed modification.

documentation: Signed rights summary acknowledgment and the date given (within 72 hours)
Record of the 72-hour explanation of house rules, confidentiality, grievances, fees, suspension and search policies
Written notice of the right to contact the LME, DMH/DD/SAS, DHSR, DSS and Disability Rights North Carolina
Health care appointments and outcomes in the client record
Individualized discharge plan within the person-centered plan
Notes on any unexpected discontinuation of treatment and the substitute plan
Visitor log, outdoor and exercise notes, and any plan modification with justification and consent
Documentation of any authorized rights restriction (RRI-02)

policies.title: Living Environment, Health, Hygiene and Grooming
policies.applies_to: All clients, all direct support staff, Program Director, Administrator and maintenance personnel
policies.purpose: To give every client a safe, comfortable, private home that the client can make his or her own, and to make sure personal care and grooming are provided with dignity, privacy and respect for rights.
policies.policy:
This policy meets item 87, Living Environment (10A NCAC 27F .0102; Worksheet p.25) and item 88, Health, Hygiene and Grooming (10A NCAC 27F .0103; Worksheet pp.25-26).

Item 87, Living Environment. [AGENCY NAME] provides each client a living environment that promotes comfort, privacy and personalization. Clients have uninterrupted sleep, personal privacy, and the ability to personalize their living space. The physical home meets 10A NCAC 27G .0304. Single bedrooms have at least 100 square feet and double bedrooms at least 160 square feet, with no more than two clients per room and clients in a shared room being of the same sex. There is at least one full bathroom for every five persons living in the home, counting staff and their family. Hot water at taps used by clients is kept between 100°F and 116°F. Mattresses are fire-retardant. Clients do not sleep in an unfinished basement or attic. Cooling is not required in 24-hour homes of six or fewer, but the agency takes reasonable steps to keep the home comfortable. The home complies with the NC Building Code and the agency keeps documented evidence of compliance with fire, sanitation and building codes, including the annual fire inspection (10A NCAC 27G .0301). Smoking is prohibited inside the facility, and signs are posted.

Item 88, Health, Hygiene and Grooming. Staff support each client's personal health, hygiene and grooming in a way that respects the client's rights and dignity, including the right to dignity, privacy and humane care. Each client has regular opportunities for personal hygiene, access to hygiene products, and facilities that ensure privacy. Staff assist only as much as the person needs, as written in the person-centered plan, and always honor the person's preferences and culture.

definitions.definition: Letting a client choose how his or her bedroom and personal areas look, with their own furniture, decorations, bedding, photos and belongings, within fire and safety rules.
The client's right to be alone, to dress, bathe and toilet without being seen, and to keep personal space and belongings private.
Items such as soap, shampoo, toothbrush and toothpaste, deodorant, razors, menstrual products, incontinence supplies and other personal care items.
A bathroom with a toilet, sink and a tub or shower.

procedures: Before admission, the Program Director confirms that the bedroom assigned meets the size, occupancy and same-sex requirements (single 100 square feet, double 160 square feet, no more than two per room). The measurement is recorded in the home's environment file.

The Program Director confirms the home has at least one full bathroom per five persons, counting staff and their family who live there. The count is recalculated whenever a client or staff member moves in or out.
The Administrator checks that every bed has a fire-retardant mattress. Receipts or manufacturer labels are kept. No client is assigned a room in an unfinished basement or attic.

Maintenance staff test hot water at client sinks, tubs and showers weekly with a thermometer and record the results on the water temperature log. If water is outside 100–116°F, the Program Director arranges adjustment or repair the same day and keeps clients from using unsafe water in the meantime.

Within 7 days of admission, the client is invited to personalize his or her bedroom. Staff help choose and hang decorations, bring in furniture and bedding, and arrange belongings. Limits apply only for fire safety, and the reason is explained to the client.

Staff protect uninterrupted sleep. Routine checks at night are quiet and brief, lights and noise are kept low, and staff do not wake clients for staff convenience. Any needed overnight checks must be in the person's plan.
Staff knock and wait for permission before entering a client's bedroom or bathroom, except in an emergency. Bedroom and bathroom doors close, and the client decides who may enter his or her room.

The Administrator posts no-smoking signs at each entrance and in the common areas. Staff, clients and visitors may smoke only outside, away from entrances and windows, and the agency does not allow smoking inside.
The Program Director keeps the annual fire inspection, sanitation report and building-code compliance evidence on file (10A NCAC 27G .0301). The Administrator tracks renewal dates.
Staff check weekly that the home is clean, free from odors and in good repair. The Program Director arranges repairs. Grounds are kept clean and free of insects and rodents.
Each client has the opportunity to bathe or shower, wash hair, brush teeth, shave, care for nails and dress daily and as often as he or she chooses. Staff offer help and respect refusals.

Each client has his or her own hygiene products stored in a place of the client's choice. If the client cannot buy them, the agency makes sure they are provided, and it never uses their absence as a reason to withhold anything. Supplies are checked at least weekly.

When personal care help is needed, staff provide only the help written in the person-centered plan. They explain what they are doing, ask permission, cover the person, use the same-gender staff preference where possible, and keep the door closed.
Staff respect each client's grooming choices, including hairstyles, clothing, makeup, facial hair and cultural or religious practices. They teach skills when the plan includes them.
Staff document personal care, refusals and any skin, nail, dental or other health concern in the daily notes. They report health concerns to the Program Director and arrange care (see TXR-01).

During the monthly rights check, the Program Director talks with each client about comfort, privacy, sleep and personal space and records any concerns. Problems are reported under PIR-01 and corrected within 30 days.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure the home meets 10A NCAC 27G .0304 and building, fire and sanitation codes, and keeps inspection records.
Assigns rooms, confirms bathroom counts, supervises hot water checks and repairs, and monitors privacy, sleep and personal care.
Protect privacy and sleep, support personalization and offer personal care help with dignity as the plan directs.
Test and record water temperatures, repair problems and keep the home and grounds clean and safe.

documentation: Bedroom measurement and occupancy record and bathroom count
Fire-retardant mattress receipts or labels
Weekly water temperature log
Annual fire inspection, sanitation report and building-code compliance file
No-smoking sign check
Personalization record in the client file
Daily personal care notes and hygiene supply checks
Monthly client interview notes and corrective actions

policies.title: Personal Funds, Clothing and Possessions
policies.applies_to: All clients, legally responsible persons, representative payees, direct support staff, Program Director, Administrator and the person who keeps client funds records
policies.purpose: To protect each client's personal clothing and possessions and to safeguard and properly account for any personal funds that [AGENCY NAME] handles or helps the client to manage.
policies.policy:
This policy meets item 89, Storage and Protection of Clothing and Possessions (10A NCAC 27F .0104; Worksheet p.26) and item 90, Client's Personal Funds (10A NCAC 27F .0105; Worksheet p.26).

Item 89. [AGENCY NAME] makes every effort to protect each client's personal clothing and possessions. Each client has storage space for them. Staff help each client develop and keep an inventory of belongings, and they document and monitor personal belongings. Staff do not use, borrow, sell or keep client property. A client's possessions are removed or limited only through an authorized rights restriction under RRI-01 and RRI-02, and never for punishment or convenience.

Item 90. Staff help clients manage and invest their personal funds, including through personal fund accounts, in a way that fits each client's abilities and choices. Funds are never commingled. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a separate ledger for each client with receipts for every deposit and withdrawal. When facility employees manage a client's funds, the record states who manages them and why, and no deduction is made without written authorization from the client or legally responsible person. The agency does not charge a client more than the client can pay. Medicaid does not pay room and board. Room and board is usually paid from the client's income, such as SSI, which is $994 per month for an individual in 2026. Charges follow GOV-07. The Administrator verifies these procedures against the full text of 10A NCAC 27F .0104 and .0105 before adopting this policy and each time the policy is reviewed.

definitions.definition: Money that belongs to the client, including benefits, wages, gifts and allowances, whether the client keeps it, or the agency holds or tracks it.
Mixing a client's money with another client's money or with agency money. It is not allowed.
A dated written list of the client's clothing and valuables that is kept in the client record and kept current.
A person or organization appointed by the Social Security Administration to receive and manage a client's benefits.

procedures: On the day of admission, staff and the client (and guardian if any) make a written inventory of clothing and possessions. Items of value or special importance are described in detail. Each person signs and dates it, and a copy goes in the client record.
Staff update the inventory whenever an item is added, lost, damaged or removed, and at least quarterly with the client. Changes are dated and initialed.

Each client has a private place to keep clothing and belongings, and lockable storage for valuables if requested (see TXR-01). Staff do not enter personal storage without the client's permission, except in an emergency or as authorized under SRH-01.

If a possession is lost, damaged or missing, staff report it to the Program Director the same day. The Program Director looks into it and writes a report. Suspected theft or exploitation is reported under HRM-01 and GOV-06.
Staff label clothing in a way the client agrees to and see that laundry is returned to its owner. Clients choose their own clothing and are not required to wear a uniform or share clothing.

At admission, the Program Director asks the client and legally responsible person who manages the client's money. The answer is recorded in the client record and reviewed at each plan meeting. The least restrictive arrangement is used first.
If the client manages his or her own money, staff offer teaching and support in budgeting, saving and investing as the plan states. Staff do not take control of funds the client can manage.
If the agency holds or manages funds for a client, the Administrator obtains written authorization from the client or legally responsible person that states who may handle the money and how.
The agency opens a separate ledger for each client. Staff record each deposit and withdrawal with the date, amount, purpose, balance and staff signature. Receipts are attached for every purchase.

Client money is kept apart from agency money and other clients' money, in a locked place with limited key access. It is never commingled. Agency or staff money is never lent to or borrowed from a client.
Two staff count and reconcile each client's cash against the ledger at least monthly, and both sign. Any difference is reported to the Administrator at once and investigated.

No deduction, fee, charge or loan repayment is taken from a client's funds without prior written authorization from the client or legally responsible person that states the amount and purpose. The agency does not charge a client more than the client can pay.

Room and board charges follow the fee agreement and GOV-07. The Administrator keeps the agreement in the client record and checks that the charges fit the client's income. Medicaid-covered services are never billed to the client.
Staff give each client or guardian a statement of the account at least quarterly and on request. The client or guardian may inspect the ledger and receipts at any time.
When a client leaves the facility, staff give the client or legally responsible person the money and possessions held, check them against the ledger and inventory, and get a signed receipt.
The Administrator reviews every client ledger quarterly, and the QA/QI Committee reviews the results annually (GOV-05). Concerns are corrected within 30 days.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, verifies it against 10A NCAC 27F .0104 and .0105, reviews ledgers quarterly and investigates differences.
Oversees inventories and ledgers, assigns staff for counts, and investigates lost property.
Help with inventories, protect belongings, record every transaction with receipts and report problems immediately.
Decide how funds are managed, give written authorization for deductions and may review records at any time.

documentation: Dated, signed admission inventory and updates
Report of any lost, damaged or missing item and the investigation
Record of who manages each client's funds and written authorization
Separate ledger for each client with receipts
Monthly two-signature cash reconciliation
Written authorization for each deduction
Fee agreement and quarterly account statements
Signed receipt for funds and possessions returned at discharge

policies.title: Facility Pools and Facility Animals (Conditional)
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Program Director, all staff, clients, visitors and anyone who brings an animal into the home
policies.purpose: To keep clients safe around swimming pools and animals. This policy says that the home has no pool, sets the conditions that apply if one is added, and sets rules for animals, including rabies vaccination proof.
policies.policy:
This policy meets item 91, Facilities With Pools (Worksheet heading 'Facilities With Pools'; Worksheet p.27) and item 92, Facility Animals (Worksheet heading 'Facility Animals'; Worksheet p.27). Both are conditional items.

Item 91, Facilities With Pools. The home at [ADDRESS] has no swimming pool, hot tub or other constructed water feature. If [AGENCY NAME] ever adds a pool, it will first obtain approval from the DHSR Construction Section. No client may use the pool until that approval is in writing. The pool must also meet the NC Building Code and the site and grounds rules (10A NCAC 27G .0301 and .0303). Before use, the Administrator will add written supervision and safety measures to this policy, covering staff supervision ratios, lifesaving equipment, barriers and locked access, rules for swimming, staff trained in CPR, and each client's swimming ability.

Item 92, Facility Animals. Animals are allowed in the home only with the Administrator's approval, after the Program Director has considered the wishes, allergies, fears, health and safety of every client living there. A client's choice to have a pet is supported where it can be done safely. Clients, visitors and staff who bring owned dogs, cats or ferrets onto the premises must show proof of current rabies vaccination. [AGENCY NAME] documents and verifies that proof and keeps vaccination records for all pets on the premises. Animals are kept clean, are healthy and do not create a risk to clients. Grounds are kept safe and clean and free of insects and rodents (10A NCAC 27G .0303).

definitions.definition: Any dog, cat, ferret or other animal that lives at the home or visits it, whether owned by a client, staff member, visitor or the agency.
A current certificate or record signed by a licensed veterinarian that shows the animal's identification, the vaccine date and the date the next vaccine is due.
A dog (or other animal as the law allows) trained to do work or tasks for a person with a disability. Service animals are covered by IR-01, not by the pet approval process.

procedures: The Administrator confirms and records that the home has no pool. A pool may not be built, installed, rented or opened to clients without prior written DHSR Construction Section approval and a revised version of this policy.

If a pool is added, the Administrator gives DHSR 30 days' written notice of the renovation before work starts (10A NCAC 27G .0404), submits plans to the DHSR Construction Section and keeps the approval letter on file.

Before any pool use, the Administrator adopts written safety measures: a locked barrier or fence, a rescue device, a first-aid kit, posted rules, an emergency plan, a staff-to-client supervision ratio set by the client's swimming skills, and at least one CPR-trained staff member within reach at all times.
A client wishing to have an animal, or a person wanting to bring one, asks the Program Director first. The Program Director records the request and the animal's species, name and owner.

The Program Director asks every housemate and the guardians about allergies, fears, asthma or past bites, and records the answers. If any client has a medical problem or objection, the animal is not allowed or is kept out of shared areas.

Before a dog, cat or ferret comes onto the premises, the owner gives the Program Director proof of rabies vaccination. The Program Director checks the animal's description, the vaccine date, the expiration date and the veterinarian's signature or stamp.
The Program Director verifies the proof by calling or contacting the veterinary office if anything appears unclear. The date of verification and the person who verified it are recorded.

The Program Director enters the animal in the Pet Register with owner, species, vaccination dates, next due date and any restrictions, and keeps a copy of the proof. The register covers all pets on the premises, including visiting animals that stay.

A visitor or staff member bringing a dog, cat or ferret for a visit shows proof at the door. If proof is not available, the animal does not enter. Only brief visits are allowed until proof is checked and the register updated.

The Program Director reviews the Pet Register monthly. At least 30 days before a vaccine expires, the owner is reminded to renew it. An animal whose vaccination has lapsed is removed from the home until proof of renewal is shown.

Owners are responsible for feeding, grooming, litter and waste cleanup, veterinary care and licensing, as local rules require. Staff help clients who own pets as the plan states. Animal food and waste are kept away from food preparation areas, and animals are kept out of the kitchen during meal preparation and medication areas.
Staff and clients wash their hands after touching animals or cleaning up after them (PER-02). Litter boxes and animal areas are cleaned at least daily. The Program Director checks sanitation weekly.

If an animal bites, scratches or injures anyone, staff give first aid, seek medical care, separate the animal, and report the incident under GOV-06. The Program Director contacts the local health department as it directs and informs the owner. The animal is not allowed back until the Administrator has reviewed the case.
The Administrator may remove any animal that is aggressive, ill, causes allergic reactions, or threatens client safety or sanitation, after talking with the owner and affected clients.

Service animals are admitted according to IR-01. Staff may ask only the questions the law allows. The Program Director may still ask for vaccination records as a standard health step for any animal in the home.

responsibilities.duty: Approves or removes animals, seeks DHSR Construction Section approval for any pool and adopts pool safety rules.
Collects and verifies vaccination proof, keeps the Pet Register, checks sanitation and asks about allergies and fears.
Check proof at the door, supervise contact between clients and animals, keep areas clean and report bites or problems.
Provides proof of rabies vaccination, keeps the animal healthy and cleans up after it.

documentation: Statement that the home has no pool (annual review note); if a pool is added, DHSR Construction Section approval letter and written pool safety measures
Pet approval request and allergy and fear screening
Rabies vaccination proof and record of verification for each dog, cat or ferret
Pet Register covering all pets on the premises, with next due dates
Monthly register review and sanitation checks
Incident reports for any bite or injury (GOV-06)

policies.category: 10A NCAC 27G .3605 Medication and Mobile Units Only
policies.title: Medication and Mobile Units: Not Applicable Statement
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator, Qualified Professional, and the licensure reviewer
policies.purpose: To state, with the reason, that the rule for medication and mobile units does not apply to this home, and to set the conditions under which [AGENCY NAME] will reassess that statement.
policies.policy: This policy meets Worksheet item 93, Medication and Mobile Units policy (service provisions, location and service capacity, operations and service delivery), 10A NCAC 27G .3605, Worksheet p.27. The item is NOT APPLICABLE to [AGENCY NAME]. Reason: 10A NCAC 27G .3605 applies only to medication and mobile units, which are a separate type of service from a residential facility. [AGENCY NAME] is licensed as a Supervised Living facility with a 'C' designation under 10A NCAC 27G .5601. That is a 24-hour home environment serving adults whose primary diagnosis is a developmental disability. The core rules in 10A NCAC 27G .0100-.0900 apply to the home, and the service rules in .5600 modify or expand them (10A NCAC 27G .0101). The home does not operate a medication unit, does not dispense medication to outside patients, and does not deliver services from a mobile unit. Services are delivered only at the licensed premises and in the community with clients. Medication handled in the home for residents is governed by policies MED-01 through MED-04. Transportation of clients is governed by GOV-04. If the service model changes, this statement will be reviewed and a compliant policy written before the new service begins.

definitions.definition: A separately licensed service type covered by 10A NCAC 27G .3605. It is not a Supervised Living home.
A 24-hour home serving adults whose primary diagnosis is a developmental disability (10A NCAC 27G .5601).
A worksheet item that does not apply to the licensed service, stated with a written reason.

procedures: The Administrator confirms at licensure submission that the facility type on the application is Supervised Living, 'C' designation, and that no medication unit or mobile unit service is listed.
The Administrator enters 'Not applicable' for Worksheet item 93 on the MH Licensure Policies and Procedures Worksheet and cites this policy as the reason.
