The Administrator places this policy in the manual in numerical order, so the reviewer can tick off item 93 without searching.
Staff do not transport or dispense medication to people who do not live in the home, and do not operate any mobile or off-site medication service.
Medication used by residents follows MED-01 through MED-04 only. Those policies do not create a medication unit.
Before adding any new service, location or program, the Administrator and governing body decide whether a different rule, including .3605, would apply.

If a new service would trigger .3605 or another service rule, the Administrator gives DHSR written notice as required by LIC-01 and does not start the service until the licensing requirements are met.
The Administrator reviews this statement at each annual manual review (REQ-01) and whenever the service model changes.
The Administrator records the review date and outcome on the manual review log.

responsibilities.duty: Approve this statement and any change in the service model that would affect it.
Keep the statement accurate, complete the worksheet entry, and perform annual and change-driven reviews.
Tell the Administrator if any proposed activity looks like a medication or mobile unit service.

documentation: Completed Worksheet entry for item 93 marked Not Applicable
Manual review log with review dates
Governing body approval record

policies.title: Policies and Procedures Manual: Control, Review and Licensure Submission
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator, Qualified Professionals, and all staff who use the manual
policies.purpose: To control the content, version, review and submission of the Policies and Procedures Manual so that the version reviewed by DHSR is the version staff follow.
policies.policy: This policy meets Required Materials for Licensure Review, 'Policy and Procedures' (item RM-PP): the facility's Policies and Procedures Manual, submitted with the MH Licensure Policies and Procedures Worksheet as the first item in the submission order. [AGENCY NAME] will submit its manual with the completed worksheet, listed first in the required materials. The Administrator will apply for the license at least 30 days before planned operation and will disclose every owner holding 5% or more of the business (10A NCAC 27G .0402). The initial license fee for a residential facility of 6 or fewer beds is $350. The license is not issued until the fee is paid, and licenses expire at the end of the calendar year (N.C.G.S. 122C-23). DHSR gives applicants 6 months to complete the program review, and [AGENCY NAME] will respond to DHSR requests within that period so the application is not rescinded or denied. The manual is a controlled document. It is reviewed at least annually and revised after any change in rule, rate or accreditation requirement. Renewal each year requires the fee, fire report, sanitation report and ownership list (10A NCAC 27G .0404).

definitions.definition: A policy or manual with a version number, effective date, approver and revision history, so only the current version is in use.

definitions.term: MH Licensure Policies and Procedures Worksheet
definitions.definition: The DHSR worksheet that lists each required policy item and the page of the manual where it is met.
Any person or entity holding 5% or more ownership, who must be disclosed to DHSR.

procedures: The Administrator assigns each policy an ID, title, version number and effective date, and keeps a master index.
The Administrator completes the MH Licensure Policies and Procedures Worksheet and writes the policy ID and page for every official item, so a reviewer can tick each one off.
The Administrator assembles the submission packet with the Policies and Procedures Manual and worksheet first, in the order DHSR lists the required materials.
The Administrator identifies all owners holding 5% or more and lists them on the application.

The Administrator submits the application at least 30 days before the planned start of operation, with the $350 fee for a home of 6 or fewer beds, because DHSR will not issue the license until the fee is paid.
The Administrator logs the date the application is received and calendars the 6-month program review deadline, plus an internal check at 60 days and 120 days.
The Administrator answers each DHSR request for revision in writing within 10 business days and sends a revised page with its policy ID and new version number.
The governing body approves the manual and signs the approval page before submission and after any substantive revision.

The Administrator reviews the whole manual at least once every 12 months and also within 30 days after any change in rule, Medicaid rate or bulletin, accreditation requirement, ownership, or service model.
The Administrator records each review, who took part, what changed and the new version on the revision log.
The Administrator keeps one current master copy at the home and one electronic copy, and removes superseded copies from use but archives them for the retention period.
New staff read and sign for the manual sections that apply to their job at orientation, and again when a policy they must follow is revised (see PER-01).
Before each annual renewal, the Administrator confirms that the fee, fire report, sanitation report and ownership list are ready and that the manual matches current practice.
If DHSR conducts an unannounced review, the Administrator or Qualified Professional on duty gives the reviewer the current manual immediately.

responsibilities.duty: Approve the manual and each substantive revision and receive the annual review report.
Own the manual, complete the worksheet, submit the application, calendar all deadlines, and run the annual review.
Review policies in their area for accuracy and tell the Administrator when practice and policy differ.
Read and follow assigned policies and report unclear or outdated policy to a supervisor.

documentation: Master policy index with versions and effective dates
Completed MH Licensure Policies and Procedures Worksheet
Governing body approval page
Revision and annual review log
Application submission record with fee receipt and ownership list
Staff acknowledgement signatures

policies.title: Required Staff Training Matrix and Special Populations Curriculum
policies.applies_to: All employees and contract staff who work in the home, the Administrator, and Qualified Professionals who supervise or train
policies.purpose: To set out the training every staff member must complete, who delivers it, and when, and to describe the Special Populations curriculum for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD).
policies.policy: This policy meets the Required Materials for Licensure Review 'Staff Training Requirements' (all required), items RM-TR-1 General Orientation Training, RM-TR-2 Client Rights Training, RM-TR-3 Confidentiality Training, RM-TR-4 Population-Specific Training, RM-TR-5 De-escalation Training (all staff), RM-TR-6 Seclusion, Physical Restraint & Isolation Time-Out Training (if applicable; in-person), RM-TR-7 Medication Administration Training (if applicable; in-person), RM-TR-8 CPR (cannot be online only) and RM-TR-9 First Aid; and the 'Training Curriculum' item RM-CUR, Special Populations Training curriculum matching the population served. Under 10A NCAC 27G .0202, staff training covers orientation, client rights and confidentiality, the needs in each client's plan, and bloodborne pathogens, and at least one staff member trained in first aid, CPR and the Heimlich maneuver is on site. [AGENCY NAME] sets a higher standard: every direct support staff member is trained in CPR and first aid before working alone with clients. A Direct Support Professional must have a GED or diploma and a supervision plan made at hire and reviewed annually, and non-Qualified Professionals are supervised by a Qualified Professional with experience in the population served (10A NCAC 27G .0104; see PER-03). Training dates, trainer and content are documented for every person. Matrix summary: orientation, rights, confidentiality, I/DD population training, de-escalation, CPR and first aid are required for all direct care staff. Medication administration training is required for any staff who administer medication. Seclusion, restraint and isolation time-out training is required only if [AGENCY NAME] uses those interventions.

definitions.definition: Training on the needs, supports, communication, health and behavior of adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, matched to the people served.
Training with a live instructor and hands-on practice, not online only. Required for CPR, medication administration and any restraint training.
Unlicensed staff who have been trained by an RN or pharmacist and approved in writing to administer medications (10A NCAC 27G .0209).
A staff member who meets the QP definition in 10A NCAC 27G .0104 for the population served.

procedures: Before a new employee works alone with a client, the Administrator verifies and documents the following: General Orientation (RM-TR-1), Client Rights (RM-TR-2), Confidentiality (RM-TR-3), the I/DD Population-Specific Training in the Special Populations curriculum (RM-TR-4), De-escalation Training (RM-TR-5), CPR (RM-TR-8) and First Aid (RM-TR-9).

General orientation covers: job description, which the employee and supervisor sign (10A NCAC 27G .0202); the manual; the fire and disaster plans; incident reporting; abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting; and the individual plans of the clients to be served.

Client rights training is delivered by a Qualified Professional and covers the rights policies in this manual. Confidentiality training covers the client record, release of information and what may not be shared.

CPR and first aid are taught by a certified instructor with hands-on skills practice. Online-only CPR is not accepted. The Administrator keeps a copy of each card and tracks expiration dates, so a trained staff member is on site at all times.
The Administrator provides bloodborne pathogens training at hire and every year, consistent with 29 CFR 1910.1030 and PER-02.
De-escalation training is required for all staff, including relief and part-time staff, before working alone, and is repeated as TRN-01 directs.

Medication administration training (RM-TR-7): the home stores and administers client medications, so only licensed persons, or unlicensed staff who have been trained in person by an RN or pharmacist and privileged, may administer (10A NCAC 27G .0209). The Administrator keeps the trainer's name and credentials and the privileging date.

Seclusion, physical restraint and isolation time-out training (RM-TR-6): [AGENCY NAME] does not use seclusion or isolation time-out. Physical restraint is used only in an emergency, for imminent danger, and never for convenience or staffing (10A NCAC 27E .0104). Any staff who may be involved in a restraint must first complete in-person training from a qualified trainer. If no staff are trained, no restraint is used and the staff follow emergency procedures in HRM-01 and RES-01.
The Administrator keeps a training matrix listing every staff member, each required course, completion date and renewal date, and reviews it monthly.
The Administrator removes from the schedule, or from the task requiring it, any staff member whose required training has expired until it is renewed.

The Special Populations curriculum (RM-CUR) is written for adults with I/DD. It covers: person-centered thinking and habilitation; communication, including augmentative systems; behavior as communication and positive supports; seizure recognition and response; dysphagia and choking prevention; mobility, positioning and adaptive equipment; common health conditions and signs of illness; medication side effects; dignity, choice and community inclusion; and recognizing abuse, neglect and exploitation.
The curriculum names the trainer, the length of each module, learning objectives and a competency check. Each staff member signs a roster for each session.
The Administrator updates the curriculum annually and whenever a client with a new need is admitted, such as tube feeding or a mobility device.
Staff who supervise others must be Qualified Professionals with experience in the I/DD population (10A NCAC 27G .0104). Supervision plans are made at hire and reviewed annually (PER-03).
The Administrator keeps the curriculum, sign-in rosters, certificates and the training matrix in the personnel file or training binder for DHSR review.

responsibilities.duty: Schedule and verify all required training, maintain the matrix, and keep rosters and curricula ready for review.
Deliver or oversee client rights, confidentiality, population-specific and de-escalation training and complete competency checks.
Train unlicensed staff in medication administration in person and document competency.
Complete all required courses, sign rosters and keep CPR and first aid current.

documentation: Staff training matrix
Training rosters with date, trainer and content
CPR and first aid cards
Medication administration training and privileging records
Special Populations curriculum with objectives and competency checks
Signed job descriptions
Supervision plans

policies.title: Licensure, Certification, Accreditation and Provider Agreements
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator and designated Qualified Professional
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] holds and keeps every license, accreditation and provider agreement it needs before serving clients and at all times afterward.
policies.policy: No one may establish or operate a licensable facility without first applying for and receiving a DHSR license (10A NCAC 27G .0401). [AGENCY NAME] will not admit a second adult before the license is issued, because operating a licensable facility without a license is a Class H felony with a fine of $1,000 per day (N.C.G.S. 122C-28). A separate license is required for each premises, and the home's capacity is never more than six clients (10A NCAC 27G .0404). The application includes the LME/MCO letter of support (N.C.G.S. 122C-23.1) and the fee, because the license is not issued until it is paid. Licenses expire on December 31. The initial license may run up to 15 months, and renewal is annual (N.C.G.S. 122C-23). Renewal requires the fee, fire report, sanitation report and ownership list. DHSR inspects without notice about every 12 months. The DHSR complaint hotline number is posted in a public place. [AGENCY NAME] gives DHSR 30 days' written notice of renovation, capacity, program, location, ownership or name changes and of closure. If DHSR issues provisional status for 30 days to 6 months, it is posted and disclosed to clients (10A NCAC 27G .0405). Because Innovations Residential Supports requires national accreditation, [AGENCY NAME] will meet it: for new enrollments after April 20, 2026, and for existing providers by April 20, 2027, confirming the accreditor in the NCTracks Provider Permission Matrix.

definitions.definition: NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation, Mental Health Licensure & Certification Section, which licenses the home.
A letter from the LME/MCO for the home's county, required with the DHSR application for residential facilities other than ICF/IID.
A license of 30 days to 6 months that DHSR may issue instead of a full license; it must be posted and disclosed to clients.
The number of clients the license allows; for this home, no more than six.

procedures: The Administrator obtains the LME/MCO letter of support and local zoning approval for the home's address before submitting the DHSR application (REQ-01).
The Administrator pays the license fee with the application and does not admit any client until the license is in hand. No second adult is admitted before issuance.

The Administrator posts the original license in a public place in the home, along with the DHSR complaint hotline number [DHSR COMPLAINT HOTLINE NUMBER], which the Administrator verifies against the current DHSR notice.
The Administrator records the licensed capacity at admission and never admits above it, including temporary, respite or emergency stays.
The Administrator keeps a licensure calendar: December 31 expiration, the fire inspection, the sanitation inspection, the ownership list update and the fee payment.
At least 60 days before December 31, the Administrator requests the fire and sanitation reports and prepares the renewal packet so renewal is filed and the license does not lapse.
When DHSR arrives unannounced, the person in charge admits the surveyor, calls the Administrator at [PHONE], and gives the surveyor access to records, the premises and staff.

For any renovation, capacity change, program change, change of location, change of ownership or name, or closure, the Administrator sends written notice to DHSR at least 30 days in advance and informs the LME/MCO.
A change of premises requires a new license for the new premises. The Administrator does not move clients until it is issued.
If DHSR issues provisional status, the Administrator posts it immediately, tells each client or legally responsible person in writing, and documents the notice in the record.
The Administrator writes and submits a plan of correction by the DHSR deadline and tracks each corrective action to completion.

The Administrator confirms the national accreditation requirement for Innovations Residential Supports in the NCTracks Provider Permission Matrix, selects an accreditor from the permitted list, and completes the application in time for the April 20, 2026 and April 20, 2027 deadlines as they apply.
The Administrator reports accreditation status to the LME/MCO and keeps the accreditation certificate on file.
The Administrator keeps copies of the license, provider agreements, letter of support and accreditation documents in the administrative file and gives a status report at each governing body meeting.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure licensure and accreditation are in place and funded, and review the licensure status report.
Apply for, renew and amend licenses; give required notices; manage accreditation; post the license and hotline.
Admit surveyors, notify the Administrator and never exceed capacity.

documentation: DHSR license and renewal records
LME/MCO letter of support
Licensure calendar
Fire and sanitation reports
Ownership list
Notices to DHSR
Provisional status notices to clients (if any)
Accreditation certificate and NCTracks confirmation
Plans of correction

policies.title: Medicaid Compliance, Billing, Service Documentation, EVV and DCW Attestation
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator, billing staff, Qualified Professionals and Direct Support Staff who document services
policies.purpose: To ensure that [AGENCY NAME] bills Medicaid only for services that are authorized, delivered and documented, and meets its contract, attestation and monitoring obligations.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides NC Innovations Waiver Residential Supports under the approved 1915(c) waiver (CMS No. 0423.R04.00), paid through the LME/MCO Tailored Plan. Medicaid does not pay room and board, which is paid from the client's own income and any other eligible support. [AGENCY NAME] contracts with each Innovations Tailored Plan LME/MCO that authorizes services for its clients. It bills only authorized days, at the authorized level and code (the Alliance schedule uses H2016, T2014, T2020 and H2016 HI; the Administrator confirms codes and rates with each plan). Every billed day is supported by a service note and the client's plan. Billing is never changed to meet a rate or avoid a denial, and no record is altered. The home will follow the HCBS setting requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c). For the Residential Supports direct care worker (DCW) add-on of $7.68 per diem (S.L. 2026-41), [AGENCY NAME] files the attestation with the LME/MCO and tracks the use of funds for DCW wages. The Administrator confirms with the LME/MCO whether the add-on is already in the plan's rate. The Administrator confirms in writing whether electronic visit verification (EVV) applies to Residential Supports and, if it does, completes onboarding with the state's vendor in line with 42 USC 1396b(l). Level II (non-death) and Level III incidents and Level II deaths are reported to the LME within 72 hours, and quarterly summaries are submitted (10A NCAC 27G .0604); see GOV-06. The LME monitors providers using incident history, complaints and QI activities, and corrections are due within 60 days of the monitoring report (10A NCAC 27G .0608). DMH/DD/SAS may suspend funding authorization when health, safety or welfare is in immediate jeopardy, and a hearing request does not stay the order (10A NCAC 26C .0503). It may revoke authorization after written warning for substantial failure to comply, including altered documents or missed plan-of-correction deadlines (10A NCAC 26C .0504). Staff pay and hours are handled in line with applicable wage and hour law, including 29 CFR Part 552 where it applies.

definitions.definition: The LME/MCO's approval of the service, level, units and dates that [AGENCY NAME] may bill for a client.
A daily payment for Residential Supports, billed once per authorized day.
The $7.68 per diem Residential Supports add-on that must be used for direct care worker wages and attested to the LME/MCO.
Electronic visit verification, an electronic record of service delivery required for certain Medicaid services.
A written plan with dates for fixing the deficiencies in a monitoring report.

procedures: The Administrator holds a current provider agreement with each Tailored Plan LME/MCO whose clients are served and keeps the agreement, fee schedule and billing manual on file.
Before billing a client, the billing staff member confirms the authorization: service, level, units, start and end dates and the client's Medicaid ID.
Direct support staff complete a daily service note for each client each day, with date, staff signature or initials, activities and progress toward plan goals, and any change in condition.
The Qualified Professional reviews notes at least weekly for completeness and consistency with the plan and corrects gaps by dated late entry. Original entries are never erased or backdated.
Billing staff bill only days for which a note and authorization exist, at the authorized level and code, and do not bill days the client was hospitalized or away unless the plan's rules allow it.
The Administrator reconciles claims against remittances monthly, investigates denials and repays any overpayment within the period the LME/MCO requires.

The Administrator confirms in writing with each LME/MCO whether EVV applies to Residential Supports and keeps the response. If it applies, staff are trained and onboarding is completed before billing continues.
The Administrator obtains the attestation form for the DCW add-on, confirms whether the $7.68 is already in the plan's rate, and files the attestation by the LME/MCO's deadline.
The Administrator keeps a DCW funds tracking sheet showing add-on revenue and the wage amounts paid to direct care workers, and reviews it each month with the governing body treasurer.
The Administrator reports Level II and III incidents to the LME within 72 hours on the Secretary's form and sends the quarterly summary on time (GOV-06).
When the LME issues a monitoring report, the Administrator writes a plan of correction, finishes corrections within 60 days of the report, and keeps evidence for each item.
The Administrator tracks every plan-of-correction deadline on the licensure calendar. A missed deadline is escalated to the governing body at once, since it can lead to loss of funding authorization.

If notified of a funding suspension or revocation warning, the Administrator informs the governing body the same day, secures client safety and continuity of care with the LME/MCO, and contacts counsel.

Staff are told that altering, backdating or fabricating a record is grounds for discipline and may be reported. Staff may report billing concerns to the Administrator or the governing body without retaliation.
The Administrator provides compliance refresher training on documentation and billing to staff at hire and annually (PER-01).

responsibilities.duty: Oversee compliance, receive monthly billing and DCW funds reports, and act on monitoring findings.
Maintain agreements, file attestations, confirm EVV, supervise billing and manage plans of correction.
Verify authorization and documentation before each claim and reconcile payments.
Review service notes for quality and completeness.
Write accurate, same-day service notes.

documentation: Provider agreements and authorizations
Daily service notes
Claims and remittance reconciliations
DCW attestation and funds tracking sheet
Written EVV determination from the LME/MCO
Incident reports and quarterly summaries
LME monitoring reports and plans of correction

policies.title: Individual Rights, HCBS Settings Requirements, Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and contract staff; all clients and their legally responsible persons
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act
policies.purpose: To protect each client's rights and community living choices as a resident of a home funded by the Innovations Waiver, and to ensure equal access without discrimination.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides Residential Supports under the Innovations Waiver (CMS No. 0423.R04.00) in a home that meets the home and community-based settings requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c) and 42 CFR 441.710. Each client has a residency agreement, privacy, choice of roommate and daily schedule, and access to food at any time. Each client has meals that are nutritious, and activities suitable to their age that the clients help plan (10A NCAC 27G .0208). A right may be modified only through a documented, individualized plan modification, the least restrictive method, and informed consent, and never for staff convenience (10A NCAC 27E .0101). [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate on the basis of disability, race, color, national origin, sex, age, religion or any other protected status, in line with the ADA and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. Interpreters and accessible formats are provided at no cost, and reasonable accommodations are made. Each client or legally responsible person receives a rights summary and is told about the right to contact the Governor's Advocacy Council. Within 72 hours of admission, house rules, confidentiality, grievance, fees, suspension and search policies are explained and the explanation is documented (10A NCAC 27D .0201). Clients are told in writing that they may contact the LME, DMH/DD/SAS, DHSR, DSS and Disability Rights North Carolina (10A NCAC 27G .7002). For Special Assistance recipients, [AGENCY NAME] submits the DSS-1464 Civil Rights Compliance Form on request (10A NCAC 27G .5604).

definitions.definition: Federal requirements that a home be integrated in the community and support choice, privacy, dignity and control over daily life.
A documented, individualized change to a rights-related HCBS requirement, with the reason, less intrusive methods tried, time limit, and consent.
Information provided in a form a person can use, such as plain language, large print, pictures, audio or Braille.
A change in a rule, practice or service that gives a person with a disability equal access.

procedures: At admission, the Qualified Professional gives the client and legally responsible person the rights summary, explains it in the person's preferred language and format, and tells them of the right to contact the Governor's Advocacy Council.

Within 72 hours of admission, the Qualified Professional explains house rules, confidentiality, grievance, fees, suspension and search policies, and documents the explanation, date, method and who attended in the client record.

The Administrator provides each client a residency agreement that states the client's rights, the house rules, the fees and the conditions for leaving the home, and reviews it with the client and guardian.
Staff support privacy: knocking and waiting before entering a bedroom or bathroom, private calls and mail, and a lockable bedroom door where the plan provides it.
Each client chooses a roommate where shared bedrooms are used, and may ask to change. The Administrator documents the request and tries to honor it.

Staff support each client in choosing their own schedule for waking, meals, activities, visitors and community outings, within safety needs in the plan. Food and drink are available at any time, and meals are nutritious (10A NCAC 27G .0208).
Clients help plan the activities, menus and outings through house meetings, and the minutes are kept. Activities fit the age of the clients.
Vehicles used to carry clients with physical disabilities have secure adaptive equipment, and the driver checks it before each trip (GOV-04).

A rights modification is allowed only when the interdisciplinary team documents the specific need, positive interventions tried, less intrusive methods, a time limit and review date, and obtains informed consent. Restrictions follow RRI-01, RRI-02 and LRA-01. No rights are restricted for staff convenience.

Staff provide qualified interpreters, including sign language, and translated or accessible materials at no cost. They never ask a client's family or other clients to interpret, except in an emergency or if the client asks.
The Administrator makes reasonable accommodations on request, such as a ramp, a communication board, extra time or a modified procedure, and documents the request and decision.

The Administrator gives each client written information about the right to contact the LME, DMH/DD/SAS, DHSR, DSS and Disability Rights North Carolina, with phone numbers, and posts it in a public place in the home.
The Qualified Professional documents that the client received the information and checks understanding, repeating it as needed.
For each client who receives State/County Special Assistance, the Administrator keeps the required forms signed by a Qualified Professional and submits DSS-1464 when requested.
The Administrator reviews rights compliance as PIR-01 requires and corrects any practice that interferes with client rights. Staff who discriminate or violate rights are subject to discipline.

responsibilities.duty: Adopt this policy and ensure the home meets HCBS settings and nondiscrimination requirements.
Ensure rights information, accommodations, interpreters, DSS-1464 and postings are provided.
Explain rights, document the 72-hour review and manage plan modifications.
Respect privacy, choice and dignity daily and report rights concerns.

documentation: Signed rights summary and 72-hour explanation record
Residency agreement
Written notice of right to contact the LME, DMH/DD/SAS, DHSR, DSS, Disability Rights NC and the Governor's Advocacy Council
House meeting minutes
Plan modification records with consent
Interpreter and accommodation log
DSS-1464 and Special Assistance forms

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All clients, legally responsible persons and guardians, family members, and all staff of [AGENCY NAME] Supervised Living (C designation) homes serving adults with developmental disabilities, including NC Innovations Residential Supports clients.
policies.purpose: To give every client a simple, written way to raise a complaint or grievance and get a fair, timely response without fear of retaliation. To make sure clients know they may also go directly to outside agencies. To meet the governing body policy requirement for a grievance procedure (10A NCAC 27G .0201), the written notice of outside contacts (10A NCAC 27G .7002), and the client rights and complaint referral provisions that apply to contract agencies (10A NCAC 27G .0504 and .0606).
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] maintains a written grievance procedure, adopted by the governing body under 10A NCAC 27G .0201, that gives the name and contact information of the person who receives grievances and describes the help available to a client who wants to file one. Staff give the procedure to each client, and the legally responsible person where there is one, at admission, and explain it in a way the client can understand. Staff repost it in the home and give it again on request.

Clients may raise a complaint with the agency at any time, orally or in writing, and staff will help a client who needs assistance to write it down, speak it, or have it recorded. Clients may also complain directly, at any time and without first using the agency's process, to the LME/MCO, DMH/DD/SAS, the Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR), the county Department of Social Services (DSS), or Disability Rights North Carolina (10A NCAC 27G .7002). The agency gives clients this information in writing and will not discourage, delay, screen or condition the use of any outside contact.

No client, family member, guardian, or staff member will be threatened, punished, discharged, transferred, restricted, or otherwise retaliated against for filing or supporting a grievance or complaint. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination.

The LME decides within 5 working days of receiving a complaint whether to handle it informally or investigate, and the informal-process letter is due within 15 working days (10A NCAC 27G .7002). The agency will cooperate fully and promptly with any LME/MCO, DHSR, DSS or Disability Rights NC review. Where the LME/MCO requires a Client Rights Committee, the agency will form one and will report rights incidents to the area director within 30 days and to the area board within 90 days as required (10A NCAC 27G .0504). Rule-related complaints about the agency may be forwarded by the LME to DHSR (10A NCAC 27G .0606), and the agency will respond to DHSR as it would to any licensure complaint.

Any grievance that alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, or a serious injury is not handled as an ordinary grievance. It is reported immediately under HRM-01 and GOV-06.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction by or for a client about the services, staff, home environment, rights, or treatment, made orally or in writing, whether or not the person uses the word 'grievance.'
The person designated by the governing body to receive, log, and track grievances and ensure the response timelines in this policy are met. Named in the grievance procedure given to clients.
The Local Management Entity/Managed Care Organization (Tailored Plan) that covers the home's county, administers the Innovations waiver, and receives client complaints about the agency.
The LME/MCO, DMH/DD/SAS, DHSR, county DSS, and Disability Rights North Carolina, to which a client may complain directly.
Any adverse action or threat taken because a person filed, supported, or took part in a grievance or complaint.
A committee, formed if the LME/MCO or area board requires it of contract agencies, that reviews grievances, alleged rights violations, and restrictive procedures.

procedures: At admission, the Qualified Professional or designee gives the client, and the legally responsible person or guardian if any, a copy of the written grievance procedure. It lists the name and contact information of the Grievance Coordinator and describes the help available in filing a grievance. The reviewer documents the delivery in the client record (see INF-01).

At the same admission meeting, the staff member gives the client the written list of outside contacts: the LME/MCO, DMH/DD/SAS, DHSR (Mental Health Licensure & Certification Section, 2718 Mail Service Center, Raleigh, NC 27699-2718), county DSS, and Disability Rights North Carolina. The list shows each agency's current telephone number as [PHONE]. The staff member explains in plain language that the client may call any of them at any time without going through the agency first, and records that this was explained.

The grievance procedure and the outside contact list are posted in a common area of each home at a height and in a format accessible to clients. The Program Director checks this at least monthly and replaces any missing or outdated copy. Both documents are provided in the client's preferred language, in plain language or pictures where needed, and in other accessible formats on request (see IR-01).

Any staff member who receives a complaint, whether oral, written, or through another person, accepts it without argument or judgment. The staff member offers help to write it, speak it, or record it, and gives it to the Grievance Coordinator the same day, or the next working day if the Coordinator is unavailable. Staff may not screen out, hold back, or try to talk a client out of a complaint.

If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, a rights violation involving a restrictive intervention, or an injury, the staff member first makes sure the client is safe. The staff member then notifies the Program Director immediately. The Program Director starts the reporting steps in HRM-01 and GOV-06 (including Health Care Personnel Registry and incident reporting as applicable) before any grievance review begins.

The Grievance Coordinator enters each grievance in the Grievance Log on the day it is received. The entry records the date, client, who raised it, a summary in the complainant's own words, whether the complaint was oral or written, and any help given. The Coordinator gives the complainant a written or otherwise accessible acknowledgment within 2 working days.

The Grievance Coordinator assigns the grievance to a reviewer who was not directly involved in the issue. If the complaint is about the Program Director or the Coordinator, it goes directly to the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the governing body chair. The reviewer meets with the complainant, listens to the concern, and asks what outcome the client wants.

The reviewer gathers the facts: interviews staff and others involved, reviews relevant records, and may observe the home. The reviewer takes immediate steps if a client's health, safety, or rights are at risk. The reviewer avoids using any person alleged to be involved in the issue as a source of the review.

The agency gives a written response to the complainant within 10 working days of receipt. If more time is needed, the Coordinator tells the complainant why and gives a new date, and the review does not run beyond 30 days without the written approval of the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME]. The response states what was found, what will be done, who will do it and by when, and reminds the complainant of the right to take the matter to the LME/MCO or any outside agency listed in step 2.

If the complainant is not satisfied, the Coordinator offers a second-level review by the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or, for matters involving the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], by the governing body chair, and gives a written result within 10 working days. The agency also offers to help the complainant contact an outside agency, including by supplying a phone and privacy to place a call, writing materials, postage, or help writing the complaint.

When the agency learns that a client has complained to the LME/MCO, DHSR, DSS, DMH/DD/SAS, or Disability Rights NC, the Program Director logs it and cooperates with the agency's requests. The LME decides within 5 working days whether to handle the complaint informally or investigate, and the informal-process letter is due within 15 working days. The agency provides requested records and staff interviews promptly and does not interfere with or retaliate against the client or witnesses.

If the LME/MCO or area board requires the agency to have a Client Rights Committee, the governing body appoints it and it reviews grievances, alleged rights violations, and restrictive procedures. The agency reports rights incidents to the area director within 30 days and to the area board within 90 days, in the form the LME/MCO prescribes. The Grievance Coordinator tracks these deadlines in the Grievance Log.

Staff do not treat a grievance as a reason to restrict, transfer, discharge, or change the services of the client who filed it. Any proposed action affecting a client who has an open grievance is reviewed in advance by the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], who documents that it is unrelated to the grievance. Any suspected retaliation is reported to the Grievance Coordinator or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and investigated as a separate grievance.

The Grievance Coordinator provides a quarterly summary of grievances (numbers, types, homes, outcomes, timeliness, and trends, without unnecessary client identifiers) to the QA/QI Committee (see GOV-05) and to the governing body. The governing body records its review in minutes, which are kept permanently. The QA/QI Committee uses the trends to make corrective changes.

Annually, the governing body reviews this policy, the grievance procedure, and the outside contact list, and updates them where a contact, rule, or LME/MCO requirement has changed. Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (see INF-02 and PER-01).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and the written grievance procedure; reviews quarterly grievance summaries and records them in permanent minutes; annually reviews the policy; appoints a Client Rights Committee if the LME/MCO requires it.
Ensures the procedure is implemented; handles second-level reviews and complaints about the Program Director or Coordinator; prevents retaliation; ensures cooperation with outside agencies.

Receives and logs grievances; sends acknowledgments and responses within the stated timelines; tracks LME/MCO and outside agency complaints and rights-incident reporting deadlines; prepares quarterly summaries.

Gives the procedure and outside contact list at admission and records it; keeps postings current in each home; starts HRM-01 and GOV-06 reporting when a complaint alleges abuse, neglect, or exploitation; assigns or serves as reviewer.
Accept every complaint, help clients put it in writing or voice it, pass it to the Coordinator the same day or next working day, and never discourage or retaliate.
Reviews grievance trends and timeliness and recommends corrective action (see GOV-05).
May file a grievance orally or in writing at any time, may take it to the LME/MCO or any listed outside agency directly, and may ask for help at any step.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment in the client record that the grievance procedure and outside contact list were received and explained at admission
Grievance Log with date received, summary, assignee, acknowledgment date, response date, outcome, and any second-level review
Written acknowledgment and written response letters, or documentation of an accessible alternative format used
Review file: interview notes, records reviewed, and corrective actions with responsible person and completion date
Records of contacts from the LME/MCO, DHSR, DSS, DMH/DD/SAS, or Disability Rights NC, and the agency's responses
Client Rights Committee minutes and rights-incident reports to the area director (30 days) and area board (90 days), where applicable
Quarterly grievance summaries to the QA/QI Committee and governing body minutes, kept permanently
Monthly posting check record for each home

required_items.text: Procedure defining delegation of management authority for the agency's operation and services (chain of command).
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0201 Governing Body Policies; Worksheet p.2

required_items.text: Procedure for criteria for discharge of the client from the facility/agency: reasons a client might be discharged, and the notice period and recipients of the notice.

Procedure on Client Record Management: transportation of records, safeguarding against loss, tampering and defacement, authorized-user access at all times, confidentiality, and providing access to information for clients.
Procedure with guidelines for safe transportation of clients, tailored to individual needs, including securing and accessing emergency information in transit.

Procedures on the composition and activities of a QA/QI committee. Activities include: monitoring and evaluating quality of care, outcomes and service utilization; a written QA/QI plan; professional/clinical supervision by a qualified professional; strategies for improving care; review of staff qualifications and granting of treatment/habilitation privileges; review of all fatalities of active clients in area-operated or contracted residential programs; and adoption of operational and programmatic performance standards.
Procedures for reporting Level I, II and III incidents, including specific measures to prevent similar incidents and how the agency will implement IRIS (Incident Response Improvement System).

Client Fee Assessment and Collection Procedure: how clients or legal representatives are informed of all fees for assessment, treatment and habilitation, and practices for assessing and collecting fees.
Procedures for the agency's medical preparedness plan and how it will be used in a medical emergency.
Procedures on use of volunteers: whether used, services provided, training, supervisor, and how client confidentiality is ensured.
Policy on training for professional and paraprofessional staff: what training is provided and how ongoing staff education is ensured.
Policy on identifying, reporting, investigating and controlling infectious and communicable diseases affecting staff and clients, including training on infectious diseases and blood-borne pathogens.

Policy on implementing and documenting an individualized supervision plan for all paraprofessional staff upon hire. It must specify who develops the plan, the staff's areas of need and methods to address them, and that the plan is reviewed and signed by both staff member and supervisor.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0204 Competencies and Supervision of Paraprofessionals; Worksheet p.4

required_items.text: Admission and Assessment policy: procedure for an admission assessment before services, including presenting problem, needs and strengths, provisional/admitting diagnosis with an established diagnosis within 30 days, social/family/medical history, evaluations appropriate to needs, and documented strategies when services start before the plan is in place.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0205 Assessment and Treatment/Habilitation or Service Plan; Worksheet pp.4-5

required_items.text: Policy on developing a treatment/habilitation plan within 30 days of admission (or before, if applicable), with the client and/or legally responsible person. It must include anticipated outcomes with projected dates, strategies, responsible staff, an at-least-annual review schedule, the basis for evaluating outcomes, and written consent or a written statement of why consent was not obtained.

Emergency Plans and Supplies policy: a written fire safety plan for each facility and an area-wide disaster plan approved by the appropriate local authority; plans accessible to staff and evacuation procedures/routes posted; fire and disaster drills at least quarterly in 24-hour facilities, repeated for each shift; drills simulating actual fire emergencies; basic first aid supplies available.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0207 Emergency Plans and Supplies; Worksheet pp.5-6

required_items.text: The P&P manual documents that the agency chooses NOT to administer medications, and that it will not prescribe, handle, dispense, administer, transport, dispose of or store medications. Complete only if the home does not handle medications.

Medication Dispensing procedure: dispensing only by a registered pharmacist, physician or other person authorized by law and registered with the NC Board of Pharmacy; only on a written order from a licensed M.D.; no stock of prescription drugs for dispensing except in emergencies without hiring a pharmacist; take-home methadone by R.N.s only (applies only to programs licensed to distribute methadone).
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Medication Dispensing Procedures; Worksheet p.6

required_items.text: Medication Packaging and Labeling procedures: manufacturer's label and visible expiration date on non-prescription containers not dispensed by a pharmacist; tamper-resistant packaging for prescriptions (including samples); prescription labels showing client name, prescriber, dispensing date, directions, drug name/strength/quantity/expiration, and pharmacy or dispensing location details and dispensing practitioner.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Medication Packaging and Labeling Procedures; Worksheet p.7

required_items.text: Medication Administration procedures: administration only on a written order from a legally authorized prescriber; self-administration only if authorized in writing by the physician; administration by licensed personnel or unlicensed staff trained by an R.N., pharmacist or other qualified professional; a current MAR for each client, documented immediately after administration (client name, drug name/strength/quantity, instructions, date and time, name or initials of administering person); client requests for medication changes documented and filed with the MAR, followed by physician consultation.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Medication Administration Procedures; Worksheet pp.7-8

required_items.text: Medication Disposal procedures: disposal to prevent diversion or accidental ingestion; a disposal record (client, drug, strength, quantity, date and method, signature of the person disposing and the witness); methods for non-controlled substances (incineration, flushing into septic/sewer, or transfer to a local pharmacy); remaining medication disposed of promptly or held no more than 30 days after discharge unless the client is expected to return.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Medication Disposal Procedures; Worksheet p.8

required_items.text: Medication Storage procedures: a securely locked cabinet in a clean, well-lit, ventilated room at 59-86 degrees F; refrigerator at 36-46 degrees F, with medications in a separate locked compartment if food is also stored; separate storage for each client and for external vs. internal use; secure storage if a physician approves self-medication.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Medication Storage Procedures; Worksheet pp.8-9

required_items.text: Medication Review procedure: 6-month drug review by a physician or pharmacist for clients on psychotropic medications; findings and any corrective action recorded in the client record.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Medication Review Procedures; Worksheet p.9

required_items.text: Medication Error procedures: how errors and significant adverse drug reactions are reported immediately to the client's physician or pharmacist, and how a client's refusal of medication is documented.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27G .0209, Medication Errors Procedures; Worksheet p.9

required_items.text: Search and Seizure policy: conditions for searching a client or living space, including procedures for seizing belongings or property in the client's possession.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27D .0103 Search and Seizure Policy; Worksheet p.9

required_items.text: The search and seizure policy documents that clients will be free from unwarranted invasion of privacy.

The policy states every search and seizure is documented, including scope of search, reason, procedures followed, description of any property seized, and an account of the disposition of seized property.
Policy on how the governing body ensures a compliance review of Client Rights Rules implementation at least every 3 years, with the 3 most recent written review reports kept.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27D .0104 Periodic Internal Review; Worksheet p.10

required_items.text: Informing Clients policy: written summary of rights (G.S. 122C Art. 3) to client and legally responsible person; right to contact Disability Rights NC; timely notification (24-hour facilities within 72 hours, explained at the client's level of understanding); information to be provided (rules and penalties, confidentiality protections G.S. 122C-52 through 56, how to get a copy of the treatment/habilitation plan, and governing body policies on fee assessment/collection, grievance procedures with contact info and assistance, suspension and expulsion, and search and seizure); special considerations for restrictive interventions and restricted rights (behavior management systems, potential restrictions, notification after emergency use, notification of legally responsible persons, notification of rights restrictions); documentation in the client record that rights were fully explained.

Informing Staff policy: how staff are informed about Client Rights and how documentation is maintained, plus a procedure requiring each staff member to sign an acknowledgment of receipt, kept on file.

Social Integration policy (day/night or 24-hour facilities): guidelines for encouraging and facilitating appropriate social interaction among clients and with community non-clients. It covers encouragement of participation, no prohibition of social interaction unless a written restriction is in the client record, and what counts as appropriate interactions.

Client Self-Governance policy (day/night or 24-hour facilities): client input in facility governance with mechanisms for feedback; development of client self-governance groups; meeting and communication protocols between clients and staff; training and support for clients and staff.

Informed Consent policy: informing clients about benefits, risks, alternatives, length of consent validity and withdrawal procedures (consent for planned restrictive intervention not to exceed six months); written consent per G.S. 122C-57(f) or Subchapter 27E .0100 planned interventions, and for drugs such as Antabuse and Depo-Provera when used for non-FDA-approved uses; right to consent or refuse under G.S. 122C-57(d), with refusal not used as the sole ground for termination except as stated; documentation of informed consent in the client record.

Protection From Harm, Abuse, Neglect or Exploitation policy: protection from harm per G.S. 122C-66; definitions and prohibition of abuse and neglect per 10A NCAC 27C .0102; transaction policies on sale or purchase of goods or services involving clients; use of force guidelines; employee conduct repercussions including dismissal; staff training on recognizing, preventing and reporting; documentation and reporting procedures.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27D .0304 Protection From Harm, Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation; Worksheet p.14

required_items.text: Least Restrictive Alternative policy: services delivered in the least restrictive and most appropriate settings and methods; promotion of coping and engagement skills; meaningful activity choices; shared decision-making; restrictive interventions only as a last resort, with dignity and respect, by trained personnel.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27E .0101 Least Restrictive Alternative; Worksheet p.15

required_items.text: Prohibited Procedures policy: clear prohibition of banned interventions, including corporal punishment (G.S. 122C-59), contingent painful body contact, substances that induce painful bodily reactions (excluding Antabuse), electric shock (excluding medically administered ECT), insulin shock, unpleasant-tasting foodstuffs, contingent noxious substances (noise, bad smells, splashing with water), and any potentially physically painful procedure or stimulus used to reduce a behavior (excluding prescribed injections).
Policy with clear guidelines and procedures for restricting client rights and implementing interventions that ensure safety, dignity and respect; provided to all staff.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27D .0101 Policy on Rights Restrictions and Interventions; Worksheet p.16 (numbered '35a' in the document)

required_items.text: Procedures on how ALL instances of alleged or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of clients are documented and reported to the County Department of Social Services.
Procedures and safeguards for prescribing medications that present a serious risk to the client, with special focus on neuroleptic medications.
Identify in the policy any restrictive interventions prohibited from use within the facility.
If the facility operates 24 hours, outline the circumstances and procedures prohibiting staff from restricting a client's rights.
Policy outlining the permitted restrictive interventions and the approved training curriculum; if none are permitted, the policy must explicitly say they are not allowed.
Policy identifies the staff member (position) responsible for informing the client of any restrictions that may be used.
Policy documents that clients who refuse restrictive interventions are afforded due process. (Worksheet pp.16-22: the highlighted items apply if the agency uses restrictive interventions.)
Policy includes the staff position responsible for giving written permission for 24-hour restrictive interventions. (Highlighted; applies if restrictive interventions are used.)
Policy designates the specific staff responsible for review of the use of restrictive interventions. (Highlighted; applies if restrictive interventions are used.)

Policy states what considerations are given to the client's physical and psychological well-being before, during and after a restrictive intervention, including review of health history or a health assessment at admission for pre-existing conditions or limitations that raise risk. (Highlighted; applies if restrictive interventions are used.)

Policy guidelines for debriefing and planning sessions with clients and legally responsible persons to reduce future use: debriefing process, planning process, and documentation/communication to the client and LRP after use. (Highlighted; applies if restrictive interventions are used.)

Policy with guidelines for intervention procedures as therapeutic treatment methods that are clinically or medically justified and authorized by qualified professionals (determination and authorization only by a physician or licensed practicing psychologist formally trained and privileged in the procedure). (Highlighted.)
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27E .0103 General Policies Regarding Intervention Procedures; Worksheet pp.17-18

required_items.text: Policy states that it applies to all staff involved in client care and in implementing restrictive interventions. (Highlighted.)
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27E .0104 Seclusion, Physical Restraint, Isolation Time-Out, and Protective Devices Used for Behavioral Control; Worksheet p.18

required_items.text: Guidelines for the use of seclusion, physical restraint, isolation and protective devices for behavioral management. (Highlighted.)
Procedures outlining limitations on the use of restrictive interventions. (Highlighted.)
Guidelines on prohibited uses, such as coercion, punishment, retaliation, staff convenience or inadequate staffing; interventions must not cause harm or abuse.
Documentation outlining the acceptable use of restrictive interventions within the facility.

Elements for procedures on use of seclusion: positive, less restrictive alternatives tried first; how staff are identified, trained and evaluated for competence; staff responsibilities and professional roles during interventions; documentation and notification protocols after any restrictive intervention; and (continued on p.19) procedures for well-being checks and assessing consequences after the intervention. (Highlighted.)
Guidelines on room requirements for Seclusion and Isolation, if used (DHSR must approve the room).
Guidelines for documenting use of restrictive interventions in client records, including rationale, methods and debriefing. (Highlighted.)
Guidelines for emergency use of restrictive interventions, including time limits and authorization procedures. (Highlighted.)
Guidelines on precautions and actions during restrictive interventions, including continuous monitoring and documentation. (Highlighted.)
Procedures for discontinuing restrictive interventions at any indication of risk to health or safety or once the client gains behavioral control. (Highlighted.)

Notification within 24 hours of the treatment/habilitation team or designee after each use, a governing body designee, and immediate notification of the legally responsible person of a minor or incompetent adult unless they asked not to be notified. (Highlighted.)

Review and Reporting procedures: review time frame set by a governing body designee and the Client Rights Committee, with confidentiality; investigation of unusual or possibly unwarranted patterns of use; a log of client name, responsible professional, date/time/type, duration and reason, alternatives considered and why not used, debriefing and planning with client/LRP/staff, and adverse effects. (Highlighted.)
The agency's data collection and analysis procedures on the use of seclusion and physical restraint. (Highlighted.)
The agency's procedures if planned intervention is used. (Highlighted.)

Protective Devices procedure: necessity for the device; employee using it is trained and competent; observation and interventions documented in the client record; protocol for maintenance and cleaning.

Procedure documenting that, if the facility is operated by or under contract with an area program, use of protective devices in the treatment/habilitation plan is subject to Client Rights Committee review.
An Intervention Advisory Committee shall be established for additional safeguards in a facility that uses restrictive interventions as planned interventions. (Highlighted.)
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27E .0106 Intervention Advisory Committee; Worksheet p.20

required_items.text: Document who is required to join the agency's Intervention Advisory Committee. (Highlighted.)
Procedure governing the Intervention Advisory Committee, detailing how client information is disseminated and the reasoning for it. (Highlighted.)
Procedure documenting the specific training and orientation given to the Intervention Advisory Committee. (Highlighted.)

Policy documents that all staff, service providers, employees, students and volunteers involved in client care must be trained in approved de-escalation techniques as alternatives to restrictive interventions.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27E .0107 Training on Alternatives to Restrictive Interventions; Worksheet p.21

required_items.text: Policy documents a formal annual refresher in an approved de-escalation curriculum for all staff.
Procedures for keeping documentation of alternatives-to-restrictive-intervention training for all staff for at least three years (participants, pass/fail outcomes, training dates, instructor names).
Policy documents the instructor's qualifications and training requirements.
Procedures for maintaining documentation of alternatives training and of initial and refresher instructor training for at least three years.
Policy states that any staff using restrictive interventions must be trained and current in an approved restrictive-intervention training program. (Highlighted.)
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27E .0108 Training in Seclusion, Physical Restraint, and Isolation Time-Out; Worksheet p.22

required_items.text: Documentation of the approved curriculum for restrictive interventions used; if none are used, a policy stating the agency will not use restrictive interventions. (Highlighted.)
Show where in the policy the prerequisite training requirements for staff to use restrictive interventions are outlined. (Highlighted.)
Policy documents a formal annual refresher in an approved restrictive intervention, successfully completed by all staff. (Highlighted.)
Policy states that restrictive-intervention instructors must be retrained at least annually and be currently CPR-trained. (Highlighted.)
Procedures for maintaining initial and refresher instructor training documentation for at least three years. (Highlighted.)
Suspension and Expulsion policy states each client shall be free from threat or fear of unwarranted suspension or expulsion from the facility.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27D .0102 Suspension and Expulsion Policy; Worksheet p.22

required_items.text: Policy outlines criteria for suspension, expulsion or other forms of discharge that are not mutually agreed upon.

Policy sets documentation requirements: time frame for resuming services after a suspension; specific conditions and timeline for resuming services; staff efforts to identify alternative services meeting the client's needs, and designation of those services; any necessary discharge plan.

Health Care Personnel Registry policy: the agency's responsibility to vet all unlicensed staff with possible direct access to clients or their property through the HCPR, and how it will handle report-allegation procedures, investigation procedures, submission of investigation results, and documentation requirements.
required_items.cite: G.S. 131E-256 Health Care Personnel Registry (HCPR); Worksheet p.23

required_items.text: Policy on which staff position of a facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities will notify the LME/MCO serving the client's county of residence of the intent to close the facility or discharge a client who may need continuing care, at least 60 days before the closure or discharge.
required_items.cite: N.C.G.S. 122C-63 Continuity of Care; Worksheet p.23 (the document numbers this '84')

required_items.text: Policy documenting that every client in a 24-hour facility receives necessary treatment for physical ailments, with guidelines on the right to necessary treatment, the right to an individualized discharge plan, and unanticipated discontinuation of treatment.
required_items.cite: N.C.G.S. 122C-61 Treatment Rights in 24-hour Facilities; Worksheet p.24 (the document also numbers this '84', so the id here is disambiguated)

required_items.text: Policy outlining adult clients' rights: confidential phone calls; visitors 8:00 a.m.-9:00 p.m. for at least 6 hours daily, 2 after 6:00 p.m., not taking precedence over therapies; communicating and meeting under appropriate supervision with individuals of their choice; visits outside the facility unless commitment or court-order issues; time outdoors daily and access to exercise facilities several times a week; keeping and using personal clothing and possessions; religious worship; retaining a driver's license unless prohibited; individual private storage space.
required_items.cite: N.C.G.S. 122C-62 Additional Rights in 24-hour Facilities; Worksheet p.24

required_items.text: Policy outlining minor clients' rights under G.S. 122C-62 (phone calls, supervised visitors, mail, special education and vocational training, outdoor play and recreation, personal clothing and possessions, religious worship, storage space, spending a reasonable sum of their money, driver's license). Likely not applicable to a 'C' (adult) home, but the worksheet's 'No/N/A' rule requires a comment explaining why.

Living Environment policy: how the agency provides each client a living environment that promotes comfort, privacy and personalization, with guidelines ensuring uninterrupted sleep, personal privacy and the ability to personalize living space.

Health, Hygiene and Grooming policy: guidelines for personal health, hygiene and grooming care that respect client rights and dignity, including the right to dignity, privacy and humane care, opportunities for personal hygiene, access to hygiene products, and facilities that ensure privacy.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27F .0103 Health, Hygiene and Grooming; Worksheet pp.25-26

required_items.text: Guidelines and procedures for staff to safeguard clients' personal clothing and possessions: efforts to protect belongings, how employees help clients develop and keep an inventory, and procedures for documenting and monitoring personal belongings.
required_items.cite: 10A NCAC 27F .0104 Storage and Protection of Clothing and Possessions; Worksheet p.26

required_items.text: Client's Personal Funds policy: guidelines for assisting clients with managing and investing personal funds, including assistance with personal fund accounts, management of funds by facility employees, and authorization for deductions.

SOURCES AND LIMITS. DHSR's Policy & Procedure Worksheet is the single official checklist for the policy content. It is a general mental-health worksheet that cites 10A NCAC 27G .0200, 27D, 27E, 27F and the statutes. It has no items drawn from the Supervised Living rules (10A NCAC 27G .5601-.5604). I could not retrieve the .5600 rule text itself, so no .5600-specific policy items are listed. Item text above is condensed from the form because of quoting limits; the item numbering and rule cites follow the form, and the PDF has the exact wording. The form numbers two different items '84' (G.S. 122C-63 on p.23 and G.S. 122C-61 on p.24); I disambiguated them with bracketed cites. It also has an item '35a'.

HOW IT IS SUBMITTED. Per the Application Packet, do NOT send the P&Ps with the license application. After the zoning, LME/MCO letter of support, floor plan and photo items are in and DHSR Construction has done the physical plant review, the Licensure & Training team contacts the applicant to begin the program review. The applicant has six months from that first contact to finish it; DHSR describes the manual as the licensee's own and says it is returned for revision if incomplete or incorrect.

WORKSHEET RULES (Submission Guidelines, REV 7-22-25):
- Submit the P&P manual as ONE PDF and the worksheet as a SEPARATE PDF.
- List the exact manual page number for each required policy.
- If you answer 'No' or 'N/A', explain why in the comment box.
- Worksheets must be complete and correct; incomplete or incorrect ones are returned.
- Flowcharts are not accepted as policy documents.
- If the agency uses restrictive interventions, complete the highlighted areas on worksheet pages 16-22. I marked those items '(Highlighted)', but the highlighting is hard to read in the PDF text, so confirm against the PDF.
- The slide deck says the worksheet is a guide, not a substitute for the regulations. The Application Packet says to build the P&Ps from 10A NCAC Ch. 26 Subch. C and Ch. 27 Subchs. C, D, E, F and G.

SUBMISSION ORDER. The Required Materials list says to submit documents in the order listed: P&P manual and worksheet; personnel records; staff training; training curriculum; instructor credentials; disaster plan. The 'Substance Abuse Waiver Training' group applies to SUD services only. A written disaster plan with verification from local Emergency Management is required; the county Emergency Management office confirms in writing that the plan was reviewed.

APPLICABILITY TO A SUPERVISED LIVING 'C' HOME (adult DD, 24-hour residential):
- Item 86 (minors' rights) is likely N/A because the population is adults.
- Item 93 (medication and mobile units) is N/A.
- Items 91 (pools) and 92 (animals) apply only if the home has a pool or allows animals.
- Medication items 17-23 apply if the home handles medications; item 16 is the opt-out statement used only if it does not.
- The restrictive-intervention items (35a-79) apply as written if restrictive interventions are used. If none are used, items 40 and 75 require an explicit statement that they are not allowed.
- Item 84 [G.S. 122C-63] is written for facilities serving individuals with intellectual disabilities, so it applies to a 'C' home.

SEPARATE FROM POLICY CONTENT. Staff records, resumes, license verifications, HCPR and criminal checks, instructor credentials, NCID username, application forms, ownership information, fees, floor plan and photos, zoning letter, LME/MCO letter of support, and the fire and sanitation inspections are paperwork, not policy content. The walk-through checklist is a separate pre-licensure inspection. The slide deck says all staff must be hired and in place before a license is granted.
